Meaning: "other than the path of those who have earned anger."

He has dispensed with mentioning the first term of the construct (the path) by the second, the context of the discourse indicating it, which is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Guide us to the straight path, the path of those upon whom You have bestowed favor﴾. Then He said: ﴿other than those who have earned anger﴾. Some have claimed that the (lā) in His saying ﴿nor of those who are astray﴾ is superfluous, and that the sense of the statement in their view is: "other than those who have earned anger and those who are astray," and they cited the verse of al-'Ajjaj: "In a well, where there was no Hur, nor was he aware" (the verse is in Tafsir al-Tabari, 1/190). That is, "in a well of Hur." The correct view is what we have already mentioned. For this reason Abu 'Ubayd al-Qasim ibn Sallam narrated in his book Fada'il al-Qur'an, from Abu Mu'awiyah, from al-A'mash, from Ibrahim, from al-Aswad, from 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him, that he used to recite: "ghayri al-maghdubi 'alayhim wa ghayri al-dallin" (Fada'il al-Qur'an, p. 162). This is a sound chain of transmission. Likewise it is related from Ubayy ibn Ka'b that he recited in the same way. That is to be understood as having come from them by way of explanation (tafsir), and it indicates what we have said: that the (lā) was brought only to emphasise the negation, lest it be supposed that it is conjoined to ﴿those upon whom You have bestowed favor﴾, and to distinguish between the two ways, so that each of them may be avoided. For the way of the people of faith includes knowledge of the truth and acting upon it; the Jews lacked action, and the Christians lacked knowledge. For this reason anger is attributed to the Jews and straying to the Christians, because whoever knows and abandons deserves anger, unlike one who does not know. The Christians, though intending something, did not find its way, because they did not approach the matter from its proper gate, which is following the true Messenger, so they went astray. Both the Jews and the Christians are astray and have earned anger, but the most distinctive attribute of the Jews is anger, as He said concerning them: ﴿those whom Allah has cursed and upon whom He has become angry﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 60], and the most distinctive attribute of the Christians is straying, as He said: ﴿They have certainly gone astray before and led many astray and have strayed from the sound way﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 77]. This is also what the hadiths and reports have come with, and it is clear and evident.

Imam Ahmad said: Muhammad ibn Ja'far narrated to us, Shu'bah narrated to us, saying: I heard Simak ibn Harb say: I heard 'Abbad ibn Hubaysh narrate from 'Adi ibn Hatim, who said: The cavalry of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ came and seized my aunt and some people. When they were brought to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ they were lined up before him, and she said: "O Messenger of Allah, the one who would vouch for me has gone far away, and my child has cut off from me, and I am an old, elderly woman with no one to serve me, so be gracious to me, may Allah be gracious to you." He said: "Who is your vouchee?" She said: "'Adi ibn Hatim." He said: "The one who fled from Allah and His Messenger!" She said: "Be gracious to me." When he returned, and a man was beside him, you would think him to be 'Ali, he said: "Ask him for a mount," so she asked him and he ordered it for her. She said: "He did a deed that your father would not have done, for so-and-so came to him and received from him, and so-and-so came to him and received from him." So I went to him, and there with him was a woman and children, or a child, and she mentioned their closeness to the Prophet ﷺ. He said: I knew that he was not a king like Chosroes or Caesar. Then he said:
"O 'Adi, what keeps you from saying, 'There is no god but Allah'? Is there any god other than Allah?" He said: What keeps you from saying, "Allah is greatest"? Is there anything greater than Allah, mighty and majestic?" He said: So I embraced Islam, and I saw his face light up with joy, and he said: "Those upon whom anger is earned are the Jews, and those who are astray are the Christians." And he related the hadith. At-Tirmidhi related it from the hadith of Simak ibn Harb and said: "Hasan gharib; we know it only from his hadith." I say: Hammad ibn Salamah has also related it from Simak, from Murri ibn Qatari, from 'Adi ibn Hatim, who said: I asked the Messenger of Allah ﷺ about the words of Allah: ﴿other than those who have earned anger﴾, and he said: "They are the Jews." ﴿nor those who are astray﴾, and he said: "The Christians are those who are astray." Likewise Sufyan ibn 'Uyaynah related it from Isma'il ibn Abi Khalid, from al-Sha'bi, from 'Adi ibn Hatim with the same. This hadith of 'Adi has been narrated by several routes, and it has many wordings, the mention of which would be lengthy.

'Abd al-Razzaq said: Ma'mar narrated to us, from Budayl al-'Uqayli, who said: 'Abd Allah ibn Shaqiq informed me that one who heard the Prophet ﷺ, while he was at Wadi al-Qura, and he was on his horse, told him that a man from Banu al-Qayn asked him: "O Messenger of Allah, who are these?" He said: "Those upon whom anger is earned," and he pointed to the Jews, "and those who are astray are the Christians." Al-Juraydi, 'Urwah, and Khalid al-Hadhdha' also related it from 'Abd Allah ibn Shaqiq, but they transmitted it as mursal, and did not mention the one who heard the Prophet ﷺ. In the narration of 'Urwah the one who heard is named as 'Abd Allah ibn 'Umar, but Allah knows best.

Ibn Mardawayh related, from the hadith of Ibrahim ibn Tahman, from Budayl ibn Maysarah, from 'Abd Allah ibn Shaqiq, from Abu Dharr, who said: I asked the Messenger of Allah ﷺ about "those upon whom anger is earned," and he said: "The Jews." I said: "Those who are astray?" He said: "The Christians." Ibn Hajar said in al-Fath (8/159): "Ibn Mardawayh related it with a hasan chain from Abu Dharr."

As-Suddi said, from Abu Malik, and from Abu Salih, from Ibn 'Abbas, and from Murrah al-Hamdani, from Ibn Mas'ud, and from some companions of the Prophet ﷺ: ﴿other than those who have earned anger﴾ are the Jews, ﴿nor those who are astray﴾ are the Christians.

Al-Dahhak and Ibn Jurayj said, from Ibn 'Abbas: ﴿other than those who have earned anger﴾ are the Jews, ﴿nor those who are astray﴾ are the Christians.

Likewise said al-Rabi' ibn Anas, 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Zayd ibn Aslam, and others. Ibn Abi Hatim said: I know of no difference among the exegetes on this.

The evidence for what these imams said, that the Jews are those upon whom anger is earned and the Christians are those who are astray, is the hadith already cited, and His saying, in addressing the Children of Israel in Surat al-Baqarah: ﴿Evil is that for which they have sold themselves, that they should disbelieve in what Allah has sent down, out of insolent envy that Allah should send down His bounty upon whom He wills of His servants. So they returned having earned anger upon anger, and for the disbelievers is a humiliating punishment﴾ [al-Baqarah: 90]. And He said in al-Ma'idah: ﴿Say: Shall I inform you of something worse than that as recompense from Allah? Those whom Allah has cursed and upon whom He has become angry and made of them apes and swine and servants of Taghut. Those are worse in position and further astray from the sound way﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 60]. And He said: ﴿Cursed were those who disbelieved among the Children of Israel upon the tongue of Dawud and 'Isa, son of Maryam, because they disobeyed and were transgressing. They did not prohibit one another from wrongdoing that they committed. Wretched was what they used to do﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 78-79].

In the Sirah (see Ibn Hisham, al-Sirah al-Nabawiyyah, 1/224) it is related from Zayd ibn 'Amr ibn Nufayl that when he set out with a group of his companions for Syria seeking the upright religion (al-din al-hanif), the Jews said to him: "You will not be able to enter with us until you take your share of the anger of Allah." He said: "I flee from the anger of Allah." The Christians said to him: "You will not be able to enter with us until you take your share of the wrath of Allah." He said: "I cannot do that." So he remained upon his natural disposition (fitrah), kept away from the worship of idols and the religion of the polytheists, and did not join either the Jews or the Christians. As for his companions, they became Christians and entered the religion of Christianity, because they found it closer to the religion of the Jews at that time. Among them was Waraqah ibn Nawfal, until Allah guided him through His Prophet, and when He sent him, he believed in what he had found of revelation, may Allah be pleased with him.

(Issue) The sound position among the scholars is that it is excused to neglect the precise articulation distinguishing the (ḍād) from the (ẓāʾ), because their points of articulation are close. The ḍād's point of articulation is from the beginning of the edge of the tongue and what adjoins it of the molars, while the point of articulation of the ẓā' is from the tip of the tongue and the tips of the upper front teeth. Also, each of the two letters is among the voiced letters, the fricative letters, and the emphatic letters. For all this, substituting one for the other has been excused for one who cannot distinguish between them, and Allah knows best. As for the hadith, "I am the most eloquent of those who pronounced the ḍād," it has no basis, and Allah knows best.

Section: This noble surah, which consists of seven verses, includes the praise and glorification of Allah and extolling Him through the mention of His Most Beautiful Names, which entail His Supreme Attributes; and the mention of the Return, which is the Day of Judgement; and the guidance of His servants to ask Him and to supplicate to Him, and to disavow their own power and strength; and to sincerely devote worship to Him and to affirm His oneness in divinity, blessed and exalted is He, and to exalt Him above having any partner, equal, or like; and to their asking Him for guidance to the straight path, which is the upright religion, and their being made firm upon it, until this leads them to crossing the physical bridge (sirat) on the Day of Resurrection, which leads them to the gardens of bliss in the company of the Prophets, the truthful ones, the martyrs, and the righteous.

It also includes encouragement toward righteous deeds, so that they may be with their people on the Day of Resurrection, and warning against the paths of falsehood, lest they be gathered with their travellers on the Day of Resurrection, namely those upon whom anger is earned and those who are astray. How excellent is the attribution of bestowing favour to Him in His saying, ﴿the path of those upon whom You have bestowed favour﴾, and the omission of the agent in the case of anger in His saying, ﴿other than those upon whom anger is earned﴾, although He is in reality the agent of that, as He said: ﴿Have you not seen those who took as allies a people upon whom Allah has become angry?﴾ [al-Mujadilah: 14], and the verse...

And likewise, the attribution of misguidance is to the one who commits it, even though it is He who misguides them by His decree, as the Exalted said: ﴿Whomever Allah guides, he is the one rightly guided, and whomever He misguides, you will never find for him any protecting friend to guide him.﴾ [Al-Kahf: 17]. And He said: ﴿Whomever Allah misguides, there is none to guide him, and He leaves them in their transgression, wandering blindly.﴾ [Al-A'raf: 186]. And there are other verses indicating that He, glorified is He, alone holds guidance and misguidance. This is not as the Qadariyyah sect (the Qadariyyah, who deny divine predestination) and those who follow their path say, that it is the servants who choose that and do it, and they argue for their innovation (bid'ah) with an ambiguous (mutashabih) verse of the Qur'an, and leave aside what is explicit in refuting them. This is the condition of the people of misguidance and error. It has been reported in the authentic hadith: "When you see those who follow what is ambiguous in it, those are the ones whom Allah has named, so beware of them" [[Related by al-Bukhari in his Sahih, no. (4547), and Muslim in his Sahih, no. (2665), from the hadith of 'A'ishah, may Allah be pleased with her.]]. That is, in His saying: ﴿As for those in whose hearts is deviation, they follow that which is ambiguous of it﴾ [Al 'Imran: 7]. So there is no sound proof for an innovator in the Qur'an, praise be to Allah, because the Qur'an came to distinguish the truth from falsehood, separating guidance from misguidance, and there is no contradiction or discrepancy in it, for it is from Allah, a revelation from the All-Wise, the Praiseworthy [[In (ج، ط، ب): "the All-Knowing (khabir)".]].

**Section**

It is recommended for one who recites al-Fatihah to say after it: "Amin" [like: Yasin] [[Addition from (ج، ط).]], and it is also said "Amin" with a short vowel [like: yamin] [[Addition from (ج، ط).]]. Its meaning is: "O Allah, answer." The evidence for this is what Imam Ahmad, Abu Dawud and al-Tirmidhi reported from Wa'il ibn Hujr, who said: "I heard the Prophet (ﷺ) recite: ﴿not of those who have evoked anger, nor of those who are astray﴾, and he said: 'Amin,' prolonging his voice with it." In Abu Dawud's version: "he raised his voice with it" [[Al-Musnad (4/316), Sunan Abi Dawud no. (932), Sunan al-Tirmidhi no. (248).]]. Al-Tirmidhi said: "This is a hasan hadith." It is also narrated from 'Ali, Ibn Mas'ud and others.

And from Abu Hurayrah, who said: "When the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) recited ﴿not of those who have evoked anger, nor of those who are astray﴾, he would say: 'Amin,' until he could be heard by those near him in the first row." Abu Dawud and Ibn Majah related it, and Ibn Majah added: "the mosque would resound with it" [[Sunan Abi Dawud no. (934), Sunan Ibn Majah no. (853).]]. Al-Daraqutni also related it and said: "This is a hasan isnad."

And from Bilal that he said: "O Messenger of Allah, do not precede me with Amin." Related by Abu Dawud [[Sunan Abi Dawud no. (937).]].

Abu Nasr al-Qushayri [[In (أ): "al-Tustari".]] transmitted from al-Hasan and Ja'far al-Sadiq that they both doubled the letter mim in "Amin," as in: ﴿nor those making for the Sacred House﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 2].

Our companions (the Shafi'i scholars) and others said: This is recommended for one outside the prayer, and it is emphasized for the one praying, whether he is alone, an imam, or a follower, and in all circumstances, due to what came in the two Sahihs from Abu Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with him, that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "When the imam says Amin, then say Amin, for whoever's Amin coincides with the Amin of the angels, his previous sins will be forgiven." And in Muslim's version: that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "When one of you says in the prayer: Amin, and the angels in the heaven say: Amin, and one of them coincides with the other, his previous sins will be forgiven" [[Sahih al-Bukhari no. (780), Sahih Muslim no. (410).]]. [It was said: this means whoever's Amin coincides with the Amin of the angels in time; it was said: in the answering; it was said: in the quality of sincerity] [[Addition from (ج، ط، أ، و).]]. And in Sahih Muslim from Abu Musa, traced to the Prophet: "When he (i.e., the imam) says: ﴿nor of those who are astray﴾, then say: Amin, and Allah will answer you" [[Sahih Muslim no. (404).]]. Juwaybir reported from al-Dahhak, from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "I said: O Messenger of Allah, what is the meaning of Amin?" He said: "O Lord, do it" [[Also related by al-Tha'labi in his tafsir, as in al-Durr al-Manthur (1/45), through al-Kalbi from Abu Salih from Ibn 'Abbas, similar. Both isnads are weak.]]. Al-Jawhari said: the meaning of Amin is: "Thus let it be." Al-Tirmidhi said: its meaning is: "Do not disappoint our hope." Most scholars said: its meaning is: "O Allah, answer us." Al-Qurtubi related from Mujahid, Ja'far al-Sadiq and Hilal ibn Kaysan that Amin is one of the names of Allah, the Exalted. It is also related from Ibn 'Abbas as a marfu' report, but it is not sound, as said by Abu Bakr ibn al-'Arabi al-Maliki [[Tafsir al-Qurtubi (1/128).]].

The companions of Malik said: the imam does not say Amin, and the follower says it, due to what Malik related from Sumayy, from Abu Salih, from Abu Hurayrah, that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "And when he (i.e., the imam) says: ﴿nor of those who are astray﴾, then say: Amin," and the hadith continues [[Al-Muwatta' (1/87), and al-Bukhari in his Sahih no. (796) and Muslim in his Sahih no. (409) related it through Malik.]]. They also took as support the hadith of Abu Musa: "And when he recites: ﴿nor of those who are astray﴾, then say: 'Amin'."

We have already mentioned in what is agreed upon: "When the imam says Amin, then say Amin," and that the blessings and peace of Allah be upon him used to say Amin when he recited ﴿not of those who have evoked anger, nor of those who are astray﴾ [[In (ج): "They used to say Amin behind him when he recited."]].

Our companions differed about saying Amin audibly for the follower in the audibly recited prayers. The essence of the disagreement is that if the imam forgets to say Amin, the follower says it audibly, by unanimous agreement. If the imam says it audibly, then the new (jadid) opinion is that the follower does not say it audibly, and this is the position of Abu Hanifah and a narration from Malik, because it is a remembrance among the remembrances, so it is not said audibly, like the rest of the prayer's remembrances. The old (qadim) opinion is that he says it audibly, and this is the position of Imam Ahmad ibn Hanbal and the other narration from Malik, due to what has preceded: "until the mosque resounds."

And we have another third opinion: if the mosque is small, the follower does not say it audibly, because they hear the imam's recitation; and if it is large, he says it audibly so that Amin reaches those in the corners of the mosque. And Allah knows best.

Imam Ahmad related in his Musnad, from 'A'ishah, may Allah be pleased with her, that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) mentioned the Jews in her presence and said: "They will never envy us for anything as they envy us for the Friday that Allah guided us to, and they went astray from it, and for the qiblah that Allah guided us to, and they went astray from it, and for our saying behind the imam: Amin" [[Al-Musnad (6/135).]]. Ibn Majah related it, and its wording is: "The Jews have never envied you for anything as they envied you for the greeting (salam) and the Amin" [[Sunan Ibn Majah no. (856), through Hammad ibn Salamah, from Suhayl, from Abu Salih, from his father, from 'A'ishah, traced to the Prophet. al-Busiri said in al-Zawa'id (1/297): "This is a sahih isnad, all of whose narrators Muslim relied upon."]]. And from Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn Majah has: that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "The Jews have never envied you for anything as they envied you for saying Amin, so increase your saying of Amin" [[Sunan Ibn Majah no. (857), through Yazid ibn Subayh, from Talhah ibn 'Amr, from 'Ata', from Ibn 'Abbas, traced to the Prophet.]]. In its isnad is Talhah ibn 'Amr, and he is weak.

Ibn Mardawayh related from Abu Hurayrah that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Amin is the seal of the Lord of the worlds upon His believing servants" [[Also related by Ibn 'Adi in al-Kamil (6/440) through Mu'ammal, from Abu Umayyah ibn Ya'la, from al-Maqburi, from Abu Hurayrah. Ibn 'Adi said: "No one narrates it from Abu Umayyah ibn Ya'la, though he is weak, except this Mu'ammal."]]. And from Anas, who said: the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "I have been given Amin in the prayer and at supplication, which none before me was given, except Musa. Musa would supplicate and Harun would say Amin, so seal your supplications with Amin, for Allah will answer it for you" [[Also related by al-Harith ibn Abi Usamah, no. (167), Bughyat al-Ba'ith, through a mawla of Khalid, from Anas ibn Malik. Zurbi ibn 'Abd al-Rahman is weak.]].

I say: From here some of them drew an argument concerning this noble verse, which is the saying of the Exalted: ﴿And Musa said: "Our Lord, You have given Pharaoh and his chiefs adornment and wealth in the life of this world, our Lord, so that they may mislead from Your way. Our Lord, obliterate their wealth and harden their hearts so they will not believe until they see the painful punishment." He said: "Your supplication has been answered, so remain upright and do not follow the path of those who do not know."﴾ [Yunus: 88, 89]. He mentioned the supplication from Musa alone, and from the context of the speech there is what indicates that Harun said Amin, so he took the position of one who supplicated, due to His saying: ﴿Your supplication has been answered﴾ [Yunus: 89]. This indicates that whoever says Amin to a supplication is as if he said it himself. Therefore those who said: the follower does not recite, because his Amin on the recitation of al-Fatihah is equivalent to reciting it. And for this reason the hadith came: "Whoever has an imam, the imam's recitation is his recitation." And Bilal used to say: "Do not precede me with Amin." This position indicates that the follower has no recitation to perform in the audibly recited prayers. And Allah knows best.

For this reason Ibn Mardawayh said: Ahmad ibn al-Hasan related to us, 'Abd Allah ibn Muhammad ibn Sallam related to us, Ishaq ibn Ibrahim related to us, Jarir related to us, from Layth ibn Abi Sulaym, from Ka'b, from Abu Hurayrah, who said: the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "When the imam says: ﴿not of those who have evoked anger, nor of those who are astray﴾ and says Amin, then the Amin of the people of the earth coincides with the Amin of the people of the heaven, Allah forgives the servant his previous sins. And the example of one who does not say Amin is like that of a man who fought with a people, and they drew lots, and their arrows came out, but his arrow did not come out. He said: 'Why did my arrow not come out?' It was said to him: 'You did not say Amin'" [[Also related by Abu Ya'la in his Musnad (11/296) from Abu Khaythamah from Jarir, and Layth ibn Abi Sulaym is weak.]].

[In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful] [[Addition from (ج، ط).]]

**Tafsir of Surat al-Baqarah**

Twenty-five thousand and five hundred letters, six thousand one hundred and twenty words, and two hundred and eighty-six verses, according to the count of the Kufans and the count of 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, may Allah be pleased with him.

**Mention of what has been reported regarding its virtue**

Imam Ahmad said: 'Arim related to us, Mu'tamir related to us, from his father, from a man, from his father, from Ma'qil ibn Yasar, that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Al-Baqarah is the hump (sanam) and summit of the Qur'an. With each of its verses there descended eighty angels, and the verse: ﴿Allah, there is no deity except Him, the Ever-Living, the Sustainer of existence﴾ [al-Baqarah: 255] was extracted from beneath the Throne and joined to it, or it was joined to Surat al-Baqarah. Ya-Sin is the heart of the Qur'an; no man who desires Allah and the Hereafter recites it except that he is forgiven. Recite it over your dead." Ahmad alone related it [[Al-Musnad (5/26).]].

Ahmad also related it from 'Arim, from 'Abd Allah ibn al-Mubarak, from Sulayman al-Taymi, from Abu 'Uthman, and he is not al-Nahdi, from his father, from Ma'qil ibn Yasar, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Recite it over your dead," meaning Ya-Sin [[Al-Musnad (5/26). Abu 'Uthman was not declared reliable except by Ibn Hibban, and his father is unknown. It has become clear that the hadith is disordered (mudtarib), its transmission having varied from Sulayman al-Taymi.]].

Previously, we clarified the identity of the unnamed narrator in the first report through this chain. Abu Dawud, al-Nasa'i and Ibn Majah narrated this hadith in this form in the second report.[[Sunan Abi Dawud, no. (3121); al-Sunan al-Kubra of al-Nasa'i, no. (10913); Sunan Ibn Majah, no. (1448).]]

al-Tirmidhi narrated it from the report of Hakim ibn Jubayr, in which there is weakness, from Abu Salih, from Abu Hurayrah, who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Everything has a summit (sanam), and the summit of the Qur'an is al-Baqarah. In it is a verse that is the chief of the verses of the Qur'an: the Verse of the Throne (Ayat al-Kursi)."[[Sunan al-Tirmidhi, no. (2878). al-Hakim narrated it in al-Mustadrak (2/259) through the route of Hakim ibn Jubayr with the same wording.]]

In Musnad Ahmad, Sahih Muslim, al-Tirmidhi and al-Nasa'i, from the report of Suhayl[[In A: "Sahl".]] ibn Abi Salih, from his father, from Abu Hurayrah, that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Do not make your houses graves. Indeed, the house in which Surat al-Baqarah is recited, the Shaytan does not enter."[[Al-Musnad (2/284); Sahih Muslim, no. (780); Sunan al-Tirmidhi, no. (2877); al-Sunan al-Kubra of al-Nasa'i, no. (8015).]] al-Tirmidhi said: Hasan sahih (good and sound).

Abu 'Ubayd al-Qasim ibn Salam said: Ibn Abi Maryam narrated to me, from Ibn Lahi'ah, from Yazid ibn Abi Habib, from Sinan ibn Sa'd, from Anas ibn Malik, who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Indeed, the Shaytan leaves the house when it hears Surat al-Baqarah being recited in it."[[Fada'il al-Qur'an (p. 121).]]

Sinan ibn Sa'd, and it is said the reverse (Sa'd ibn Sinan). Ibn Ma'in deemed him trustworthy, but Ahmad ibn Hanbal and others considered his hadith unfamiliar (istankara).

Abu 'Ubayd said: Muhammad ibn Ja'far narrated to us, from Shu'bah, from Salamah ibn Kuhayl, from Abu al-Ahwas, from Abd Allah, meaning Ibn Mas'ud, who said: "Indeed, the Shaytan flees from the house in which Surat al-Baqarah is heard." It was narrated by al-Nasa'i in al-Yawm wa al-Layla, and al-Hakim narrated it in his al-Mustadrak from the hadith of Shu'bah.[[Fada'il al-Qur'an of Abu 'Ubayd (p. 121); al-Sunan al-Kubra of al-Nasa'i, no. (10800); al-Mustadrak (2/260).]] Then al-Hakim said: Its chain is sahih, though the two (Bukhari and Muslim) did not narrate it.

Ibn Mardawayh said: Ahmad ibn Kamil narrated to us, Abu Isma'il al-Tirmidhi narrated to us, Ayyub ibn Sulayman ibn Bilal narrated to us, Abu Bakr ibn Abi Uways narrated to me, from Sulayman ibn Bilal, from Muhammad ibn Ajlan, from Abu Ishaq, from Abu al-Ahwas, from Abd Allah ibn Mas'ud, who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "I would not find any one of you placing one of his legs over the other, singing, and leaving Surat al-Baqarah to be recited. Indeed, the Shaytan flees from the house in which Surat al-Baqarah is recited. And the emptiest of houses is the one empty of the Book of Allah."

In the same form, al-Nasa'i narrated it in al-Yawm wa al-Layla, from Muhammad ibn Nasr, from Ayyub ibn Sulayman, with the same chain.[[Al-Sunan al-Kubra of al-Nasa'i, no. (10799). al-Tabarani narrated it in al-Mu'jam al-Awsat, no. (3292), Majma' al-Bahrayn, through the route of Hullu ibn al-Sarri, from Abu Ishaq, from Abu al-Ahwas, from Abd Allah, as a marfu' (attributed to the Prophet ﷺ). But Shu'bah contradicted both of them (Ibn Ajlan and Hullu ibn al-Sarri), narrating it from Abu Ishaq, from Abu al-Ahwas, from Abd Allah, as a mawquf (stopping at the Companion). It was narrated by Ibn al-Durays in Fada'il al-Qur'an, no. (176). Shu'bah is the most trustworthy of people concerning Abu Ishaq. Ibn al-Durays also narrated it in no. (165) through the route of Ibrahim, from Abu al-Ahwas, from Abd Allah, as a mawquf.]]

al-Darimi narrated in his Musnad, from Ibn Mas'ud, who said: "There is no house in which Surat al-Baqarah is recited except that the Shaytan leaves it with a fart (durat)."[[Sunan al-Darimi, no. (3375).]] He also said: "Indeed, everything has a summit, and the summit of the Qur'an is Surat al-Baqarah. And indeed, everything has a core (lubab), and the core of the Qur'an is al-Mufassal."[[Sunan al-Darimi, no. (3377).]] He also narrated, through the route of al-Sha'bi, who said: Abd Allah ibn Mas'ud said: "Whoever recites ten verses of Surat al-Baqarah in a night, no Shaytan will enter that house that night: four from its beginning, the Verse of the Throne, two after it, and three from its end." In another report: "Neither the Shaytan nor anything disliked will approach him or his family that day, and they are not recited over a madman except that he recovers."[[Sunan al-Darimi, no. (3383).]]

And from Sahl ibn Sa'd, who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Indeed, everything has a summit, and the summit of the Qur'an is al-Baqarah. Whoever recites it in his house at night, the Shaytan will not enter his house for three nights, and whoever recites it in his house by day, the Shaytan will not enter his house for three days."

It was narrated by Abu al-Qasim al-Tabarani, Abu Hatim, and Ibn Hibban in his Sahih.[[Al-Mu'jam al-Kabir (6/163); Sahih Ibn Hibban, no. (1727), Mawarid edition.]]

al-Tirmidhi, al-Nasa'i and Ibn Majah narrated from the hadith of Abd al-Hamid ibn Ja'far, from Sa'id al-Maqbari, from Ata', mawla (client) of Abu Ahmad, from Abu Hurayrah, who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ sent a detachment (ba'th), and they were many in number. He asked them to recite, and he asked each one of them, meaning what Qur'an he had with him. He came upon a man among them who was the youngest in age, and he said: "What do you have with you, so-and-so?" He said: "With me is such-and-such and Surat al-Baqarah." He said: "Do you have Surat al-Baqarah?" He said: "Yes." He said: "Go, for you are their commander." A man of their nobles said: "By Allah, what prevented me from learning al-Baqarah was only that I feared I would not be able to uphold it." The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Learn the Qur'an and recite it, for the likeness of the Qur'an for one who learns it, recites it and stands by it, is like a leather bag filled with musk, whose fragrance spreads everywhere. And the likeness of one who learns it and then sleeps while it is in his chest is like a leather bag tied shut over musk."[[Sunan al-Tirmidhi, no. (2876); al-Sunan al-Kubra of al-Nasa'i, no. (8749).]]

This is the wording of al-Tirmidhi's narration. Then he said: This is a hasan hadith. Then he narrated it from the hadith of al-Layth, from Sa'id, from Ata', mawla of Abu Ahmad, as a mursal (a report in which the Companion is omitted from the chain), and Allah knows best.[[In J: "Allah tabaraka wa ta'ala knows best".]]

al-Bukhari said: al-Layth said: Yazid ibn al-Had narrated to me, from Muhammad ibn Ibrahim, from Usayd ibn Hudayr, who said: While he was reciting Surat al-Baqarah at night, and his horse was tethered beside him, the horse began to move. He stopped, and it calmed. He recited again, and the horse moved again. He stopped, and it calmed. Then he recited again, and the horse moved again, so he left off. His son Yahya was near it, and he feared that it would harm him. When he took him, he raised his head toward the sky until he could no longer see it. In the morning, he told the Prophet ﷺ, and he said: "Recite, O Ibn Hudayr." He said: "I feared, O Messenger of Allah, that it would trample Yahya, who was near it. So I raised my head and went to him, then I raised my head to the sky, and there was something like a canopy in which were the likenesses of lamps, and I went out until I could no longer see it." He said: "Do you know what that was?" He said: "No." He said: "Those were angels who drew near to your voice. If you had continued reciting, the morning would have come, and people would have looked at them, and they would not have hidden from them."[[Sahih al-Bukhari, no. (5018).]]

Thus Imam al-'Alim Abu 'Ubayd al-Qasim ibn Salam narrated it in the Book of the Virtues of the Qur'an, from Abd Allah ibn Salih and Yahya ibn Bukayr, from al-Layth with it.[[Fada'il al-Qur'an (p. 26).]]

It was also narrated through another route from Usayd ibn Hudayr, as previously mentioned.[[In J, T, B, A, W: "other routes".]][[Previously takhrij in Fada'il al-Qur'an.]] And Allah knows best.

Something similar happened to Thabit ibn Qays ibn Shammas, may Allah be pleased with him. This is what Abu 'Ubayd [al-Qasim][[Addition from T.]] narrated: Abbad ibn Abbad narrated to us, from Jarir ibn Hazim, from Jarir[[In J, B: "from his uncle Jarir".]] ibn Yazid, that the elders of the people of Madinah narrated to him that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ was told: "Have you not seen Thabit ibn Qays ibn Shammas? Last night his house kept shining with lamps." He said: "Perhaps he recited Surat al-Baqarah." Thabit was asked, and he said: "I recited Surat al-Baqarah."[[Fada'il al-Qur'an of Abu 'Ubayd (p. 27); its takhrij was also previously mentioned in Fada'il al-Qur'an.]]

This is a good chain, except that it contains an ambiguity (ibham, unnamed narrators), and it is mursal. And Allah knows best.

[Mention] [[Addition from A, W.]] of what has been reported concerning its virtue together with Al 'Imran.

Imam Ahmad said: Abu Nu'aym narrated to us, Bashir ibn Muhajir narrated to us, Abd Allah ibn Buraydah narrated to me, from his father, who said: I was sitting with the Prophet ﷺ when I heard him say: "Learn Surat al-Baqarah, for taking it up is a blessing, leaving it is regret, and the idle (al-batalah) cannot master it." Then he was silent for a while, then he said: "Learn Surat al-Baqarah and Al 'Imran, for they are the two bright ones (al-Zahrawan), they shade their companion on the Day of Resurrection, as if they were two clouds, or two shades, or two flocks of birds in ranks. And indeed, the Qur'an will meet its companion on the Day of Resurrection when he rises from his grave, like a pale man, and he will say to him: 'Do you recognize me?' He will say: 'I do not know you.' He will say: 'I am your companion, the Qur'an, which made you thirsty in the midday heat and kept your night awake. Indeed every merchant is behind his trade, and today you are behind every trade.' Then he will be given the kingdom in his right hand and eternity in his left, a crown of dignity will be placed on his head, and his two parents will be clothed in two garments, the like of which the people of the world could not stand before. They will say: 'With what have we been clothed with this?' It will be said: 'With your child's taking up the Qur'an.' Then it will be said: 'Recite and ascend the stairs and chambers of Paradise.' So he will continue ascending as long as he recites, whether reciting quickly (hadhdh) or measured (tartil)."

Ibn Majah narrated part of it from the hadith of Bashir ibn al-Muhajir, and this chain is good according to the conditions of Muslim, for Muslim narrated from this Bashir. Ibn Ma'in deemed him trustworthy, and al-Nasa'i said: "There is nothing wrong with him." However, Imam Ahmad said of him: "He is munkar al-hadith (his narrations are rejected), his hadith has been examined and it brings strange things." al-Bukhari said: "He contradicts in some of his hadith." Abu Hatim al-Razi said: "His hadith is written down but not used as evidence." Ibn Adi said: "He narrated what is not followed by others." al-Daraqutni said: "He is not strong."

I say: However, parts of it have corroborating reports. Among them is the hadith of Abu Umamah al-Bahili. Imam Ahmad said: Abd al-Malik ibn Amr narrated to us, Hisham narrated to us, from Yahya ibn Abi Kathir, from Abu Salam, from Abu Umamah, who said: I heard the Messenger of Allah ﷺ say: "Recite the Qur'an, for it will intercede for its people on the Day of Resurrection. Recite the two bright ones, al-Baqarah and Al 'Imran, for they will come on the Day of Resurrection as if they were two clouds, or as if they were two shades, or as if they were two flocks of birds in ranks, pleading on behalf of their people (on the Day of Resurrection)." Then he said: "Recite al-Baqarah, for taking it up is a blessing, leaving it is regret, and the idle (al-batalah) cannot master it."[[Al-Musnad (5/249).]]

It was narrated by Muslim in the Book of Prayer from the hadith of Mu'awiyah ibn Salam, from his brother Zayd ibn Salam, from his grandfather Abu Salam Mamtur al-Habashi, from Abu Umamah Sudayy ibn Ajlan [al-Bahili],[[Addition from J, B, A, W.]] with it.[[Sahih Muslim, no. (804).]]

al-Zahrawan: the two shining ones. al-Ghayayah: what shades you from above. al-Firq: a portion of a thing. al-Sawaff: those arranged in ranks and pressed together. al-Batalah: sorcerers. The meaning of "la tastatii'uha" (they cannot master it) is that they cannot memorize it; it was also said: it cannot penetrate its reciter. And Allah knows best.

The Prophet's companion An-Nawwas ibn Sam'an (Nawwas ibn Sam'an)... [translation follows]

And among these is the hadith of An-Nawwas ibn Sam'an. Imam Ahmad said: Yazid ibn Abd Rabbih related to us, al-Walid ibn Muslim related to us, from Muhammad ibn Muhajir, from al-Walid ibn Abd al-Rahman al-Jurashi, from Jubayr ibn Nufayr, who said: I heard An-Nawwas ibn Sam'an al-Kilabi say: I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) say: "The Qur'an will be brought on the Day of Resurrection, and its people who used to act by it will be brought with it. Surah al-Baqarah and Surah Al 'Imran will go before them." The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) struck three parables for them, which I have not forgotten since: "It is as if they were two clouds, or two dark shades, with a gap of light between them, or as if they were two flocks of birds in ranks, pleading on behalf of their companions."

Muslim related it from Ishaq ibn Mansur, from Yazid ibn Abd Rabbih, with the same chain.

At-Tirmidhi related it from the hadith of al-Walid ibn Abd al-Rahman al-Jurashi, with the same chain, and said: "Hasan gharib."

Abu Ubayd said: Hajjaj related to us, from Hammad ibn Salamah, from Abd al-Malik ibn Umayr, who said: Hammad said: I think he narrated it from Abu Munib, from his paternal uncle, that a man recited al-Baqarah and Al 'Imran, and when he finished his prayer, Ka'b said to him: "Did you recite al-Baqarah and Al 'Imran?" He said: "Yes." He said: "By Him in whose hand my soul is, in them is the Name of Allah which, when He is called upon by it, He responds." He said: "Tell me of it." He said: "No, by Allah, I will not tell you. If I told you, you would quickly call upon Him with a supplication by which both you and I would be destroyed."

Abu Ubayd also said: Abd Allah ibn Salih related to us, from Mu'awiyah ibn Salih, from Salim ibn Amir, that he heard Abu Umamah say: "A brother of yours saw in a dream that people were walking up through a rugged, long mountain cleft, and on the top of the mountain were two green trees calling out: 'Is there among you one who recites Surah al-Baqarah? Is there among you one who recites Surah Al 'Imran?' When the man said, 'Yes,' they drew near to him with their branches, until he clung to them and they carried him over the mountain."

Abu Ubayd also said: Abd Allah ibn Salih related to us, from Mu'awiyah ibn Salih, from Abu Imran, that he heard Umm al-Darda' say: "A man among those who recited the Qur'an raided his neighbour, killed him, and he was executed for it. The Qur'an kept slipping away from him, surah by surah, until al-Baqarah and Al 'Imran remained, a week each. Then Al 'Imran slipped away from him, and al-Baqarah remained for a week. It was said to her: 'What is said is not changed in My presence, and I am not unjust to the servants' (Qaf: 29). She came out like a great cloud."

Abu Ubayd said: I think he meant that the two were with him in his grave, defending him and keeping him company, and they were among the last of the Qur'an that remained with him.

He also said: Abu Musahhir al-Ghassani related to us, from Sa'id ibn Abd al-Aziz al-Tanukhi, that Yazid ibn al-Aswad al-Jurashi used to narrate: "Whoever recites al-Baqarah and Al 'Imran in a day, is cleared of hypocrisy until evening, and whoever recites them in a night is cleared of hypocrisy until morning." He said: He used to recite them every day and night apart from his portion.

Also: Yazid related to us, from Waqa' ibn Iyas, from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, who said: Umar ibn al-Khattab (may Allah be pleased with him) said: "Whoever recites al-Baqarah and Al 'Imran in a night, he will be (or it will be written that he is) among the devout (al-qanitin)."

There is a break in its chain, but it is established in the two Sahihs (al-Sahihayn) that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) recited both of them in one rak'ah.

Mention of what has been reported concerning the virtue of the Seven Long (al-Sab' al-Tiwal):

Abu Ubayd said: Hisham ibn Isma'il al-Dimashqi related to us, from Muhammad ibn Shu'ayb, from Sa'id ibn Bashir, from Qatadah, from Abu al-Malih, from Wathilah ibn al-Asqa', from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "I was given the Seven Long (surahs) in place of the Torah, I was given the Mi'in in place of the Gospel, I was given the Mathani in place of the Psalms, and I was favoured with the Mufassal."

This is a gharib hadith, and Sa'id ibn Bashir is weak in narration.

Abu Ubayd also related it from Abd Allah ibn Salih, from al-Layth, from Sa'id ibn Abi Hilal, who said: "It reached us that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said..." and mentioned it, and Allah knows best. Then he said: Isma'il ibn Ja'far related to us, from Amr ibn Abi Amr, client of al-Muttalib ibn Abd Allah ibn Hantab, from Habib ibn Hind al-Aslami, from Urwah, from Aisha, from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "Whoever takes the Seven is a scholar (habr)."

This too is gharib. Habib ibn Hind ibn Asma' ibn Hind ibn Harithah al-Aslami narrated from him Amr ibn Abi Amr and Abd Allah ibn Abi Bakrah. Abu Hatim al-Razi mentioned him and did not mention any criticism of him, and Allah knows best.

Imam Ahmad also related it from Sulayman ibn Dawud and Husayn, both from Isma'il ibn Ja'far, with the same chain. He also related it from Abu Sa'id, from Sulayman ibn Bilal, from Habib ibn Hind, from Urwah, from Aisha, that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Whoever takes the first seven of the Qur'an is a scholar (habr)."

Ahmad said: Husayn related to us, Ibn Abi al-Zinad related to us, from al-A'raj, from Abu Hurayrah, from the Prophet (ﷺ), the like of it.

Abd Allah ibn Ahmad said: "I think this (is narrated) from his father, from al-A'raj, but it was so in the book without 'Abi' (my father); my father omitted it, or it is thus a mursal." Then Abu Ubayd said: Husham related to us, Abu Bishr informed us, from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, concerning the words of the Exalted: ﴿And We have certainly given you seven of the oft-repeated (verses)﴾ (al-Hijr: 87), he said: "They are the Seven Long: al-Baqarah, Al 'Imran, al-Nisa', al-Ma'idah, al-An'am, al-A'raf, and Yunus." He said: Mujahid said: "They are the Seven Long." Likewise said Makhul, Atiyyah ibn Qays, Abu Muhammad al-Farisi, Shaddad ibn Ubayd Allah, and Yahya ibn al-Harith al-Dhimari, in interpreting the verse this way, and in enumerating them, and that Yunus is the seventh.

Section

Al-Baqarah is entirely Medinan without disagreement. Some scholars said: it contains a thousand reports, a thousand commands, and a thousand prohibitions.

Those who counted said: its verses are two hundred and eighty-seven, its words six thousand one hundred and twenty-one, and its letters twenty-five thousand five hundred, and Allah knows best.

Ibn Juraij said, from Ata', from Ibn Abbas: "Surah al-Baqarah was revealed in Medina."

Khusayf said, from Mujahid, from Abd Allah ibn al-Zubayr, who said: "Surah al-Baqarah was revealed in Medina."

Al-Waqidi said: Al-Dahhak ibn Uthman related to me, from Abu al-Zinad, from Kharijah ibn Zayd ibn Thabit, from his father, who said: "al-Baqarah was revealed in Medina."

Likewise said many of the imams, scholars and exegetes, and there is no disagreement on it.

Ibn Mardawayh said: Muhammad ibn Ma'mar related to us, al-Hasan ibn Ali ibn al-Walid al-Farisi related to us, Khalaf ibn Hisham related to us, Ubays ibn Maymun related to us, from Musa ibn Anas ibn Malik, from his father, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Do not say 'Surah al-Baqarah' or 'Surah Al 'Imran' or 'Surah al-Nisa'', and likewise (for) the whole Qur'an; rather say: 'the surah in which al-Baqarah is mentioned', and 'the one in which Al 'Imran is mentioned', and likewise (for) the whole Qur'an."

This is a gharib hadith whose raising (to the Prophet) is not sound. Isa ibn Maymun here is Abu Salamah al-Khawwas, who is weak in narration and not to be relied upon. It is established in the two Sahihs from Ibn Mas'ud that he threw the pebble at Jamrah from the bottom of the valley, with the House on his left and Mina on his right, and then said: "This is the place of the one upon whom Surah al-Baqarah was revealed." Both (Bukhari and Muslim) recorded it.

Ibn Mardawayh related, from the hadith of Shu'bah, from Aqil ibn Talhah, from Utbah ibn Farqad, who said: The Prophet (ﷺ) saw among his companions a lagging, and said: "O companions of Surah al-Baqarah!" I think this was on the day of Hunayn, when they turned back in retreat, and he ordered al-Abbas, who called out to them: "O companions of the Tree!", meaning the people of the Pledge of al-Ridwan. In another narration: "O companions of al-Baqarah!", to rouse them by it, and they began to come back from every direction. Likewise on the day of Yamamah with the companions of Musaylimah, when the Companions were fleeing because of the density of the Banu Hanifah host, the Muhajirun and the Ansar began calling out to one another: "O companions of Surah al-Baqarah!", until Allah granted them victory. May Allah be pleased with all the companions of the Messenger of Allah.

* *

The exegetes have differed concerning the disjointed letters found at the beginnings of surahs. Some of them said: they are among what Allah has kept to Himself in knowledge, so they referred their knowledge to Allah and did not explain them [related by al-Qurtubi in his tafsir from Abu Bakr, Umar, Uthman, Ali and Ibn Mas'ud, may Allah be pleased with them all; and said by Amir al-Sha'bi, Sufyan al-Thawri and al-Rabi' ibn Khuthaym, and preferred by Abu Hatim ibn Hibban].

And some of them explained them, and these scholars differed about their meaning. ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Zayd ibn Aslam said: "They are only the names of the chapters." [The scholar Abū al-Qāsim Maḥmūd ibn ʿUmar al-Zamakhsharī said in his tafsir: "Most scholars agree on this, and he transmitted it from Sībawayh, who stated it explicitly."] [[Addition from manuscripts J, T, A, and W.]] This is supported by what is reported in the two Ṣaḥīḥs (Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī and Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim) from Abū Hurayrah (may Allah be pleased with him): that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) used to recite in the Dawn prayer on Friday ﴿Alif Lām Mīm. The Revelation of the Book﴾ (Surah al-Sajdah) and ﴿Has there come upon man a period of time?﴾ (Surah al-Insān). [[Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī, no. 891, and Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim, no. 880.]]

Sufyān al-Thawrī related from Ibn Abī Najīḥ, from Mujāhid, that he said: "Alif Lām Mīm, Ḥā Mīm, Ṭā Sīn Mīm, Ṣād are openings with which Allah began the Qur'an."

Others also said the same thing from Mujāhid. And Mujāhid, in the narration of Abū Ḥudhayfah Mūsā ibn Masʿūd, from Shibl, from Ibn Abī Najīḥ, from him, said: "Alif Lām Mīm is a name of the Qur'an."

Qatādah and Zayd ibn Aslam also said likewise. Perhaps this returns to the meaning of ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Zayd's statement that it is a name of the chapters [[In manuscripts T, B, A, and W: "the surah"]], since every chapter may be called by the name of the Qur'an. But it is far-fetched that "Al-Mīm Ṣād" should be a name for the whole Qur'an, because what immediately comes to the mind of the listener when someone says "I recited Al-Mīm Ṣād" is that it refers to Surah al-Aʿrāf, not to the entire Qur'an. And Allah knows best.

It was also said that they are a name of one of the names of Allah, the Exalted. Al-Shaʿbī said: "The openings of the chapters are among the names of Allah, the Exalted." Likewise Sālim ibn ʿAbd Allāh and Ismāʿīl ibn ʿAbd al-Raḥmān al-Suddī al-Kabīr said. Shuʿbah reported from al-Suddī: "It reached me that Ibn ʿAbbās said: 'Alif Lām Mīm is one of the names of Allah, the Greatest.'" Thus Ibn Abī Ḥātim narrated it from the hadith of Shuʿbah.

Ibn Jarīr narrated from Bundār, from Ibn Mahdī, from Shuʿbah, who said: "I asked al-Suddī about Ḥā Mīm, Ṭā Sīn, and Alif Lām Mīm, and he said: 'Ibn ʿAbbās said: they are the Greatest Name of Allah.'"

Ibn Jarīr also said: Muḥammad ibn al-Muthannā narrated to us, Abū al-Nuʿmān narrated to us, Shuʿbah narrated to us, from Ismāʿīl al-Suddī, from Murrah al-Hamdānī, who said: "ʿAbd Allāh (Ibn Masʿūd) said," and he mentioned something similar. [And something similar is related from ʿAlī and Ibn ʿAbbās.] [[Addition from manuscripts J, T, B, A, and W.]]

ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭalḥah said, from Ibn ʿAbbās: "It is an oath which Allah swore by, and it is one of the names of Allah, the Exalted."

Ibn Abī Ḥātim and Ibn Jarīr narrated from the hadith of Ibn ʿUlayyah, from Khālid al-Ḥadhdhāʾ, from ʿIkrimah, that he said: "Alif Lām Mīm is an oath."

They also both narrated from the hadith of Sharīk ibn ʿAbd Allāh, from ʿAṭāʾ ibn al-Sāʾib, from Abū al-Ḍuḥā, from Ibn ʿAbbās: "Alif Lām Mīm," he said: "I am Allah, the All-Knowing."

Likewise Saʿīd ibn Jubayr said. Al-Suddī said, from Abū Mālik, and from Abū Ṣāliḥ, from Ibn ʿAbbās, and from Murrah al-Hamdānī, from Ibn Masʿūd, and from some companions of the Prophet (ﷺ): "Alif Lām Mīm." He said: "As for Alif Lām Mīm, they are letters taken from the letters of the names of Allah, the Exalted."

Abū Jaʿfar al-Rāzī said, from al-Rabīʿ ibn Anas, from Abū al-ʿĀliyah, regarding the words of the Exalted ﴿Alif Lām Mīm﴾: "These three letters are from the twenty-nine letters around which all tongues revolve. There is no letter among them but that it is the key to one of His names, and there is no letter among them but that it is from His bounties and His trials, and there is no letter among them but that it is within the term and appointed times of peoples. ʿĪsā ibn Maryam (peace be upon him) said, and wondered, and said: 'And more wondrous is that they utter His names and live on His provision, so how do they disbelieve in Him? So the Alif is the key to the name Allah, the Lām is the key to His name al-Laṭīf [[In manuscript J: "His name al-Laṭīf"; in A: "name Laṭīf"]], and the Mīm is the key to His name al-Majīd [[In manuscript J: "al-Majīd"]]. So the Alif is the blessings of Allah, the Lām is the gentleness of Allah, and the Mīm is the glory of Allah. And the Alif is a year, the Lām is thirty years, and the Mīm is forty years [year]." [[Addition from manuscripts J, T, and B.]] This is the wording of Ibn Abī Ḥātim, and Ibn Jarīr narrated something similar. Then he began to explain each of these statements and to reconcile them, and he held that there is no contradiction between each one of them and the others, and that the combination is possible. So they are names of the chapters, and with the names of Allah, the Exalted, the chapters are opened; so each letter among them indicates one of His names and one of His attributes, just as He opened many chapters with His praise, His glorification, and His magnification. He said: "There is no barrier to a letter among them indicating a name of Allah, and an attribute of His, and a term, and other things, as al-Rabīʿ ibn Anas mentioned from Abū al-ʿĀliyah, because a single word is applied to many meanings, such as the word 'ummah.' It is used to mean the religion, as in the words of the Exalted: ﴿Indeed, we found our fathers upon a religion﴾ [Al-Zukhruf: 22–23]. It is also used to mean a man obedient to Allah, as in His saying: ﴿Indeed, Abraham was a leader, devoutly obedient to Allah, inclining toward truth, and he was not of those who associate others with Allah﴾ [Al-Naḥl: 120]. It is also used to mean a group, as in His saying: ﴿He found upon it a community of people watering [their flocks]﴾ [Al-Qaṣaṣ: 23], and His saying: ﴿And We certainly sent into every community a messenger﴾ [Al-Naḥl: 36]. And it is used to mean a period of time, as in His saying: ﴿And the one who was saved of them two said, having remembered after a period [ummah]﴾ [Yūsuf: 45], meaning after a while, according to the more correct of the two opinions." He said: "So likewise is this."

This is the essence of his statement, explained. However, this is not as Abū al-ʿĀliyah stated, for Abū al-ʿĀliyah claimed that the letter indicates this, and this, and this all together. The word "ummah" and what resembles it of the shared terms in usage [[Addition from manuscripts J, T, B, A, and W: "and what resembles it"]], indicates in the Qur'an in every place only one meaning indicated by the context of the speech. As for taking it to mean all its possible meanings when that is possible, this is a matter disputed among the scholars of usul al-fiqh (the foundations of jurisprudence), and this is not the place to examine it. And Allah knows best. Then, the word "ummah" indicates every one of its meanings in the context of speech by the indication of its established usage. But as for a single letter indicating a name, which could indicate another name without one of them being preferable to the other in estimation or implication, neither by convention nor otherwise, this is something that cannot be understood except through divine tawqif (authoritative revelation), and the matter is disputed, and there is no consensus on it to be judged by.

As for the poetic evidences they cited to validate the use of a single letter to refer to the rest of the word, in the context there is something that indicates what was omitted, unlike this case, as the poet said:

"We said, 'Stop for us,' and she said, 'Qāf (stop),'
Do not think we have forgotten the haste."

meaning: "I stopped." And another said:

"What is wrong with the ostrich, how is it that it does not... (yā)
Its skin is torn from it when... (yā)."

Ibn Jarīr said: It seems he wanted to say: "When it does such and such," so he suffices with the yā from yafʿalu. Another said:

"With good, good things, and if evil, then fa...
And I do not want evil except that you wish (tā)."

He means: "And if evil, then it is evil, and I do not want evil except that you will (tashāʾ)." So he suffices with the fāʾ and the tāʾ from the two words for the rest of them. But this is evident from the context of the speech. And Allah knows best.

[Al-Qurṭubī said: And in the hadith: "Whoever helps in killing a Muslim even with half a word" [[Tafsir al-Qurṭubī (1/156). The hadith was narrated by Ibn Mājah in al-Sunan, no. 2620, through Yazīd ibn Abī Ziyād, from al-Zuhrī, from Saʿīd, from Abū Hurayrah (may Allah be pleased with him), as a marfūʿ hadith. Al-Būṣīrī said in al-Zawāʾid (2/334): "This chain is weak; Yazīd ibn Abī Ziyād al-Dimashqī, about whom al-Bukhārī and Abū Ḥātim said: 'munkar al-ḥadīth' (rejected in narration)."
Note: In some copies the word "al-musāʿadah" appears, "Qāla Sufyān," instead of "Shaqīq." What is in Tafsir al-Qurṭubī agrees with what is here. This statement is also related from Sufyān al-Iṣbahānī in al-Targhīb wa al-Tarhīb, no. 2329.]] the hadith... Shaqīq said: "It is that he says in 'uqtul (kill): 'Iq'" [[Addition from manuscripts J, T, A, and W.]].

Khaṣīf said, from Mujāhid, that he said: "The openings of all the chapters: 'Qāf, Ṣād, Ḥā Mīm, Ṭā Sīn Mīm, and Nūn,' and other than that is a fabricated spelling (hijāʾ mawḍūʿ)." Some of the people of Arabic grammar said: "They are letters from the letters of the alphabet. The mention of some of them in the openings of the chapters suffices instead of mentioning their remainder, which are the completion of the twenty-eight letters, just as a speaker says: 'My son writes in: Alif Bā Tā Thā,' meaning in the twenty-eight letters of the alphabet, so the mention of some of them suffices instead of the whole." This was narrated by Ibn Jarīr.

I say: The total of the letters mentioned in the openings of the chapters, after removing the repeated ones, is fourteen letters, and they are: Alif, Lām, Mīm, Ṣād, Rāʾ, Kāf, Yāʾ, ʿAyn, Ṭāʾ, Sīn, Ḥāʾ, Qāf, and Nūn. Your saying gathers them: "Naṣṣun ḥakīmun qāṭiʿun lahu sirr" (a decisive text, wise, with a secret). They are half of the letters in number, and what is mentioned of them is more honorable than what is left out, and the explanation of that belongs to the science of morphology (ṣarf).

[Al-Zamakhsharī said: These fourteen letters comprise half of the types of letters, meaning of the voiceless and voiced, of the soft and hard, of the emphatic and open, of the elevated and the lowered, and of the letters of qalqalah (echoing). He listed them in detail, then said: "Glory be to Him, in whose every thing His wisdom is exact. These counted types are thirty, with those mentioned among them, and you know that the majority of a thing and most of it takes the place of all of it."] [[Addition from manuscripts J, T, B, A, and W.]]

From here some of them noted a discussion on this matter, and said: "There is no doubt that these letters were not sent down by Him, the Glorified and Exalted, in vain or without purpose. Whoever among the ignorant says that in the Qur'an there is what is purely devotional with no meaning at all has erred a great error. So it is established that they have a meaning in reality. If anything from the Infallible (the Prophet) about them is authentic to us, we will speak by it; otherwise we will stop where we stop, and say: ﴿We believe in it; all of it is from our Lord﴾ [Āl ʿImrān: 7]."

The scholars did not agree on any specific thing concerning them, but they differed. Whoever a view has become clear to, with evidence, must follow it; otherwise he should suspend judgment until it is clarified. This is one position.

The other position concerns the wisdom which required the mention of these letters at the beginnings of the chapters, what is it? Apart from their meanings in themselves. Some of them said: "They were mentioned so that we would know by them the beginnings of the chapters." Ibn Jarīr narrated this, and it is weak, because the separation is achieved without them in the places where they are not mentioned, and in the places where they are mentioned, it is achieved by the basmalah in recitation and writing.

Others said: "Rather, they were introduced to open the ears of the polytheists to listen to them, since they had agreed with one another to turn away from the Qur'an, so that when they listened to it, the composition of it would be recited to them." Ibn Jarīr also narrated this, and it is also weak, because if it were so, it would be in all the chapters and not in some of them; rather, most of them are not like that. And if it were so, it would also be fitting to begin with them in opening speech with them, whether at the opening of a chapter or otherwise. Furthermore, this chapter and the one that follows it, namely al-Baqarah and Āl ʿImrān, are Madinan, and are not addressed to the polytheists, so what they mentioned is refuted by these aspects.

And others said: Rather, these letters were mentioned at the beginnings of the surahs in which they occur only as a demonstration of the inimitability (i'jaz) of the Qur'an, and that creation is incapable of producing its like in opposition to it, despite the fact that it is [composed] [[addition from manuscripts ج, ط, ب.]] of these disjoined letters with which they converse.

For this reason, every surah that opens with the letters, it is necessary that there be mentioned in it the defence of the Qur'an and the demonstration of its inimitability and greatness. This is known by induction (istiqra'), and it is what occurs in twenty-nine surahs. Thus the Exalted says: ﴿Alif, Lam, Mim. That is the Book, there is no doubt in it﴾ [al-Baqarah: 1, 2]. ﴿Alif, Lam, Mim. Allah, there is no god but Him, the Living, the Self-Subsisting. He has sent down to you the Book in truth, confirming what is before it﴾ [Al 'Imran: 1-3]. ﴿Alif, Lam, Mim, Sad. A Book revealed to you, so let there be no discomfort in your breast concerning it﴾ [al-A'raf: 1, 2]. ﴿Alif, Lam, Ra. A Book which We have sent down to you that you may bring mankind out of darknesses into the light by the permission of their Lord﴾ [Ibrahim: 1]. ﴿Alif, Lam, Mim. The revelation of the Book, there is no doubt in it, from the Lord of the worlds﴾ [al-Sajdah: 1, 2]. ﴿Ha, Mim. A revelation from the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate﴾ [Fussilat: 1, 2]. ﴿Ha, Mim. 'Ain, Sin, Qaf. Thus does He reveal to you and to those before you, Allah, the Mighty, the Wise﴾ [al-Shura: 1-3], and other verses that indicate the soundness of what these scholars held, for one who looks carefully. And Allah knows best.

As for one who claims that they indicate knowledge of the duration (al-madad), and that from them are extracted the times of events, trials and great battles (al-malahim), he has claimed what is not his, and has flown beyond his own field. A weak hadith has been narrated concerning this, and it is, moreover, more indicative of the invalidity of this path than of its validity. It is what Muhammad ibn Ishaq ibn Yasar, the author of the Maghazi, narrated: al-Kalbi narrated to me, from Abu Salih, from Ibn 'Abbas, from Jabir ibn 'Abd Allah ibn Ri'ab, who said: Abu Yasir [in another copy: Abu Iyas] ibn Akhtab passed by the Messenger of Allah ﷺ with men of the Jews, while he was reciting the opening of Surat al-Baqarah: ﴿Alif, Lam, Mim. That is the Book, there is no doubt in it [guidance for the God-fearing]﴾ [al-Baqarah: 1, 2]. So he came to his brother Huyayy ibn Akhtab with men of the Jews and said: Do you know, by Allah, I heard Muhammad reciting in what Allah has sent down to him: ﴿Alif, Lam, Mim. That is the Book, there is no doubt in it﴾. He said: Did you hear it yourself? He said: Yes. He said: So Huyayy ibn Akhtab walked with those men of the Jews to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, and they said: O Muhammad, has it not been mentioned that you recite in what Allah has sent down to you: ﴿Alif, Lam, Mim. That is the Book, there is no doubt [in it]﴾? The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Yes." They said: Did Jibril bring you this from Allah? He said: "Yes." They said: Allah sent prophets before you, and we do not know that He explained to any of them the duration of his kingdom and the term of his community other than you. Then Huyayy ibn Akhtab stood up, turned to those who were with him, and said to them: The Alif is one, the Lam is thirty, and the Mim is forty; these are seventy-one years. Will you enter the religion of a prophet whose kingdom and community's term is only seventy-one years? Then he turned to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and said: O Muhammad, is there anything beyond this? He said: "Yes." He said: What is it? He said: "Alif Lam Mim Sad." He said: This is heavier and longer: the Alif is one, the Lam is thirty, the Mim is forty, and the Sad is seventy [in another copy: ninety; in others: sixty]; these are one hundred and thirty-one years. Is there anything beyond this, O Muhammad? He said: "Yes." He said: What is it? He said: "Alif Lam Ra." He said: This is heavier and longer: the Alif is one, the Lam is thirty, and the Ra is two hundred. These are two hundred and thirty-one years. Is there anything beyond this, O Muhammad? He said: "Yes." He said: What is it? He said: "Alif Lam Mim Ra." He said: This is heavier and longer: the Alif is one, the Lam is thirty, the Mim is forty, and the Ra is two hundred; these are two hundred and seventy-one years. Then he said: Your affair has been confused for us, O Muhammad, so that we do not know whether you have been given little or much. Then he said: Leave him. Then Abu Yasir said to his brother Huyayy ibn Akhtab and to those of the rabbis with him: What do you know? Perhaps all of this has been gathered for Muhammad: seventy-one, and one hundred and thirty-one, and two hundred and thirty-one, and two hundred and seventy-one; that makes seven hundred and [four] years. They said: His affair has become confused for us. They claim that these verses were revealed concerning them: ﴿It is He who has sent down to you the Book, in it are clear verses, they are the foundation of the Book, and others are ambiguous﴾ [Al 'Imran: 7] [[Al-Bukhari narrated it in al-Tarikh al-Kabir (2/208) and al-Tabari in his tafsir (1/217) through the chain of Ibn Ishaq; the scholar Ahmad Shakir expanded on its discussion in his notes to the tafsir of al-Tabari.]].

This report revolves around Muhammad ibn al-Sa'ib al-Kalbi, and he is among those whose solitary reports are not used as proof. Moreover, if this path were sound, it would require that the numerical value of each of the fourteen letters we have mentioned be calculated, and that would reach a large total; and if it were counted with repetition, it would be even greater and more magnificent. And Allah knows best.

Ibn Jurayj said: Ibn 'Abbas said, regarding "Dhalika al-Kitab" (That is the Book): "This Book." Mujahid, 'Ikrimah, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, al-Suddi, Muqatil ibn Hayyan, Zayd ibn Aslam and Ibn Jurayj likewise said that "dhalika" carries the meaning of "hadha" (this). The Arabs interchange these two demonstrative nouns, using each in place of the other, and this is well known in their speech.

"Al-Kitab" (the Book) is the Qur'an. As for those who said that "al-Kitab" in this verse refers to the Torah and the Gospel, as related by Ibn Jarir and others, they have gone too far in their interpretation (ab'ada al-najʿah wa-aghraqa fi al-nazʿ), and have burdened themselves with what they have no knowledge of.[[In manuscript J: "aghrab" (more strange).]]

"Al-Rayb" means doubt. Al-Suddi related from Abu Malik, and from Abu Salih from Ibn 'Abbas, and from Murrah al-Hamdani from Ibn Mas'ud, and from some of the Companions of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, regarding ﴿la rayba fihi﴾ (there is no doubt in it): "There is no doubt in it."[[In manuscripts J and T: "naas" (people).]]

Abu al-Darda', Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, Abu Malik, Nafi' the client of Ibn 'Umar, 'Ata', Abu al-'Aliyah, al-Rabi' ibn Anas, Muqatil ibn Hayyan, al-Suddi, Qatadah and Isma'il ibn Abi Khalid all said the same. Ibn Abi Hatim said: "I know of no disagreement on this."

[Al-rayb may also be used to mean accusation (tuhmah). Jamil said:

Buthaynah said: "O Jamil, you have made me doubt,"
So I said: "Both of us, O Buthaynah, are suspect."

It is also used to mean need (hajah), as one of them said:[[It is the verse of Ka'b ibn Malik; it is in Lisan al-Arab, under the root "r-y-b".]]

"We have fulfilled from Tihamah every need, and from Khaybar, then we gathered the swords."]

The meaning of the statement is: this Book, which is the Qur'an, there is no doubt that it was sent down from Allah, as Allah the Exalted said in Surat al-Sajdah: ﴿Alif-Lam-Mim. The revelation of the Book, there is no doubt in it, is from the Lord of the worlds﴾ [al-Sajdah: 1, 2]. [Some said: this is a statement in the form of a report, but its meaning is a prohibition, i.e., do not doubt in it.][[Added from manuscripts J and T.]]

Some reciters pause at His saying ﴿la rayb﴾ and begin with His saying ﴿fihi hudan lil-muttaqin﴾ (in it is guidance for the God-fearing). Pausing at His saying ﴿la rayba fihi﴾ is preferable, because of the verse we mentioned, and because the word ﴿hudan﴾ then becomes a description of the Qur'an, and that is more eloquent than ﴿fihi hudan﴾.

﴿Hudan﴾ (guidance) may grammatically be in the nominative case as an adjective (na't), or in the accusative case as a circumstantial state (hal).

Guidance is specified for the God-fearing, as He said: ﴿Say: It is for those who believe a guidance and a healing. And as for those who do not believe, in their ears is deafness, and it is blindness for them. Those are called from a far place﴾ [Fussilat: 44]. ﴿And We send down of the Qur'an that which is a healing and a mercy for the believers, and it does not increase the wrongdoers except in loss﴾ [al-Isra': 82], and other verses indicating that the believers alone benefit from the Qur'an. This is because it is in itself a guidance, but only the righteous attain it, as He said: ﴿O mankind, there has come to you an admonition from your Lord and a healing for what is in the breasts, and a guidance and a mercy for the believers﴾ [Yunus: 57].

Al-Suddi related from Abu Malik, and from Abu Salih from Ibn 'Abbas, and from Murrah al-Hamdani from Ibn Mas'ud, and from some of the Companions of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, regarding ﴿hudan lil-muttaqin﴾: he said it means "a light (nur) for the God-fearing."[[In manuscripts J and B: "nur" (light).]]

Al-Sha'bi said: "guidance from misguidance." Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: "a clarification (tibyan) for the God-fearing." All of these are correct.

Al-Suddi said, from Abu Malik, and from Abu Salih, from Ibn 'Abbas, and from Murrah al-Hamdani, from Ibn Mas'ud, and from some people of the Companions of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, regarding ﴿hudan lil-muttaqin﴾: he said, "They are the believers."[[In manuscript J: "a light for the believers."]]

Muhammad ibn Ishaq related from Muhammad ibn Abi Muhammad, client of Zayd ibn Thabit, from 'Ikrimah or Sa'id ibn Jubayr, from Ibn 'Abbas, regarding ﴿lil-muttaqin﴾: that is, those who guard against Allah's punishment by abandoning what they know of guidance, and hope for His mercy by affirming what was brought.

Abu Rawq related from al-Dahhak, from Ibn 'Abbas, regarding ﴿lil-muttaqin﴾: he said, "The believers who guard against associating partners with Me (al-shirk bi), and who act in obedience to Me."[[In manuscript J: "those who seek refuge from".]]

Sufyan al-Thawri said, from a man, from al-Hasan al-Basri, regarding His saying ﴿lil-muttaqin﴾: he said, "They guard against what Allah has forbidden for them, and they fulfill what He has made obligatory upon them."

Abu Bakr ibn 'Ayyash said: "Al-A'mash asked me about the God-fearing (al-muttaqin), and I answered him. He said: 'Ask al-Kalbi about them.' So I asked him, and he said: 'Those who avoid the major sins (kaba'ir al-ithm).'" He said: "So I returned to al-A'mash, and he said: 'We think it is like that,' and he did not deny it."[[Added from manuscripts J, T and B.]]

Qatadah said: ﴿lil-muttaqin﴾ are those whom Allah described with His saying: ﴿who believe in the unseen and establish prayer﴾ [al-Baqarah: 3], and the verse after it [al-Baqarah: 4].

Ibn Jarir chose that the verse encompasses all of that, and that is as he said.

Al-Tirmidhi and Ibn Majah narrated, through the chain of Abu 'Aqil 'Abd Allah ibn 'Aqil, from 'Abd Allah ibn Yazid, from Rabi'ah ibn Yazid and 'Atiyyah ibn Qays, from 'Atiyyah al-Sa'di, who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "The servant does not reach the level of being among the God-fearing until he abandons what is not harmful to him, out of caution about what is harmful." Then al-Tirmidhi said: "Hasan gharib."[[Sunan al-Tirmidhi, no. 2451; Sunan Ibn Majah, no. 4215.]]

Ibn Abi Hatim said: Narrated to us my father, narrated to us 'Abd Allah ibn 'Imran, narrated to us Ishaq ibn Sulayman al-Razi, from al-Mughirah ibn Muslim, from Maymun Abu Hamzah, who said: "I was sitting with Abu Wa'il when a man called Abu 'Afif, one of the companions of Mu'adh, entered upon us. Shaqiq ibn Salamah said to him: 'O Abu 'Afif, will you not narrate to us from Mu'adh ibn Jabal?' He said: 'Yes, I heard him say: People will be held on the Day of Resurrection in one plain, and a caller will call out: Where are the God-fearing? They will stand in a shelter of the Most Merciful, where Allah will not veil Himself from them nor conceal Himself.' I said: 'Who are the God-fearing?' He said: 'A people who guarded against shirk and the worship of idols, and made their worship sincerely for Allah, and they will pass on to Paradise.'"[[Tafsir Ibn Abi Hatim (1/33); its chain contains Maymun al-Qassab, who is weak.]]

The root of taqwa (God-consciousness, piety) is to guard oneself against what is disliked, for its origin is "wqy," from al-wiqayah (protection). Al-Nabighah said:

"The veil fell, and she did not intend to drop it,
So she took hold of it, and shielded us with her hand."

Another said:

"She cast off a veil, behind which the sun was shielded,
With the most beautiful of two joined things: a palm and a wrist."

It is said that 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him, asked Ubayy ibn Ka'b about taqwa, and he said to him: "Have you not walked a path full of thorns?" He said: "Yes." He said: "What did you do?" He said: "I girded up and strove." He said: "That is taqwa."

Ibn al-Mu'tazz took up this meaning and said:

"Leave sins, both small and great,
That is taqwa.
And act like one who walks over a land of thorns, wary of what he sees.
Do not belittle any small sin,
For mountains are made of pebbles."

Abu al-Darda' once recited:

"A man wishes to attain his aims,
But Allah refuses except what He wills.
A man says: 'My gain and my wealth,'
But the fear of Allah is the best gain."

In Sunan Ibn Majah, from Abu Umamah, who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "After the fear of Allah, a man gains nothing better than a righteous wife: if he looks at her, she pleases him; if he commands her, she obeys him; if he swears an oath concerning her, she fulfills it for him; and if he is absent from her, she guards herself and his property."[[Sunan Ibn Majah, no. 1857, through the chain of 'Uthman ibn Abi al-'Atikah, from 'Ali ibn Zayd, from al-Qasim, from Abu Umamah, may Allah be pleased with him. Al-Busiri said in al-Zawa'id (2/70): "This chain contains 'Ali ibn Zayd ibn Jud'an, who is weak, and 'Uthman ibn Abi al-'Atikah, about whom there is difference of opinion."]]

Commentary of Ibn Kathir (Tafsir al-Quran al-'Azim) on surah 2, verse 3 (part 1 of 2):

Abu Ja'far al-Razi related from al-'Ala' ibn al-Musayyib ibn Rafi', from Abu Ishaq, from Abu al-Ahwas, from 'Abd Allah (ibn Mas'ud), who said: "Iman (faith) is tasdiq (affirmation of truth)."

'Ali ibn Abi Talhah and others related from Ibn 'Abbas regarding ﴿yu'minun﴾ (they believe): "yusaddiqun" (they affirm).

Ma'mar related from al-Zuhri: "Iman is action."

Abu Ja'far al-Razi related from al-Rabi' ibn Anas regarding ﴿yu'minun﴾: "yakhsha'un" (they fear).

Ibn Jarir and others said: "The more preferable view is that they are described as having faith in the unseen, in speech, belief and action." He said: "The fear of Allah may enter into the meaning of iman, which is the affirmation of speech by action. Iman is a comprehensive term encompassing the acknowledgment of Allah, His books and His messengers, and the affirmation of that acknowledgment through deeds."

I (Ibn Kathir) say: Linguistically, iman is applied to mere tasdiq (affirmation), and it may be used in the Qur'an with that meaning, as Allah the Exalted says: ﴿yu'minu billahi wa yu'minu lil-mu'minin﴾ [al-Tawbah: 61], and as the brothers of Yusuf said to their father: ﴿wa ma anta bi-mu'minin lana wa law kunna sadiqin﴾ [Yusuf: 17]. Likewise, when it is used together with deeds, as in His saying: ﴿illa alladhina amanu wa 'amilu al-salihat﴾ [al-Inshiqaq: 25; al-Tin: 6]. But when it is used absolutely, the legally required iman is nothing other than belief, speech and action.

This is the view taken by the majority of the imams. Indeed, al-Shafi'i, Ahmad ibn Hanbal, Abu 'Ubayd and many others have related it as a consensus that iman is speech and action, which increases and decreases. Many reports and hadiths have been transmitted concerning this, and we have treated them at length at the beginning of our commentary on al-Bukhari, and all praise and blessings are due to Allah.

Some interpreted it as khashyah (fear), based on His saying: ﴿inna alladhina yakhshawna rabbahum bil-ghayb﴾ [al-Mulk: 12], and His saying: ﴿man khashiya al-Rahman bil-ghayb wa ja'a bi-qalbin muni b﴾ [Qaf: 33]. Khashyah is the essence of iman and knowledge, as Allah the Exalted says: ﴿innama yakhsha Allaha min 'ibadihi al-'ulama'﴾ [Fatir: 28].

As for the meaning of al-ghayb (the unseen) intended here, the expressions of the early scholars differ concerning it, and all of them are correct, returning to the point that all of them are intended.

Abu Ja'far al-Razi related from al-Rabi' ibn Anas, from Abu al-'Aliyah, regarding His saying: ﴿yu'minuna bil-ghayb﴾, that he said: "They believe in Allah, His angels, His books, His messengers, the Last Day, His Paradise, His Fire and His meeting, and they believe in life after death and in resurrection. All of this is the unseen."

Qatadah ibn Di'amah said likewise.

al-Suddi related from Abu Malik, and from Abu Salih, from Ibn 'Abbas, and from Murrah al-Hamdani, from Ibn Mas'ud, and from some of the companions of the Prophet ﷺ: "As for al-ghayb, it is what is hidden from the servants: matters of Paradise and Hell, and what is mentioned in the Qur'an."

Muhammad ibn Ishaq related from Muhammad ibn Abi Muhammad, from 'Ikrimah, or from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, from Ibn 'Abbas regarding ﴿bil-ghayb﴾: "by what has come from it, meaning from Allah the Exalted."

Sufyan al-Thawri related from 'Asim, from Zirr, who said: "al-Ghayb is the Qur'an."

'Ata' ibn Abi Rabah said: "Whoever believes in Allah has believed in the unseen."

Isma'il ibn Abi Khalid said regarding ﴿yu'minuna bil-ghayb﴾: "in the unseen of Islam."

Zayd ibn Aslam said regarding ﴿alladhina yu'minuna bil-ghayb﴾: "in the decree (qadar)." All of these are close in one meaning, because all of the things mentioned are part of the unseen that must be believed in.

Sa'id ibn Mansur said: Abu Mu'awiyah related to us from al-A'mash, from 'Imarah ibn 'Umayr, from 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Yazid, who said: "We were sitting with 'Abd Allah ibn Mas'ud, and we mentioned the companions of the Prophet ﷺ and what they had preceded in. 'Abd Allah said: 'The matter of Muhammad ﷺ was clear to whoever saw him. By the One besides whom there is no god, no one has ever believed with a faith better than faith in the unseen.' Then he recited: ﴿Alif Lam Mim. Dhalika al-Kitabu la rayba fihi hudan lil-muttaqin. Alladhina yu'minuna bil-ghayb﴾ up to His saying: ﴿al-muflihun﴾ [al-Baqarah: 1-5]."

This was also related by Ibn Abi Hatim, Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Hakim in his Mustadrak, through several chains, from al-A'mash, with the same wording.

al-Hakim said: "Sahih according to the condition of the two Shaykhs (al-Bukhari and Muslim), though they did not record it."

In the meaning of this hadith, Imam Ahmad related: Abu al-Mughirah related to us, al-Awza'i informed us, Usayd ibn 'Abd al-Rahman related to me, from Khalid ibn Duraik, from Ibn Muhayriz, who said: "I said to Abu Jum'ah: 'Narrate to us a hadith you heard from the Messenger of Allah ﷺ.' He said: 'Yes, I will narrate to you an excellent hadith: We had lunch with the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, and with us was Abu 'Ubaydah ibn al-Jarrah. He said: "O Messenger of Allah, is there anyone better than us? We embraced Islam with you and we struggled with you." He said: "Yes, a people after you who will believe in me though they have not seen me."'"

Another chain: Abu Bakr ibn Mardawayh said in his tafsir: 'Abd Allah ibn Ja'far related to us, Isma'il related to us from 'Abd Allah ibn Mas'ud, 'Abd Allah ibn Salih related to us, Mu'awiyah ibn Salih related to us, from Salih ibn Jubayr, who said: "Abu Jum'ah al-Ansari, companion of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, came to us in Bayt al-Maqdis to pray there, and with us that day was Raja' ibn Haywah. When he finished, we went out to see him off. When he wished to leave, he said: 'For you is a reward and a right; I will narrate to you a hadith I heard from the Messenger of Allah ﷺ.' We said: 'Speak, may Allah have mercy on you.' He said: 'We were with the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, and with us was Mu'adh ibn Jabal, the tenth of ten.
