Mention of a hadith on the meaning of this noble verse:

Imam Ahmad said: Affan narrated to us; Abu Khalaf Musa ibn Khalaf, who was counted among the abdal (a class of righteous saints), narrated to us; Yahya ibn Abi Kathir narrated to us, from Zayd ibn Sallam, from his grandfather Mamtur, from al-Harith al-Ash'ari, that the Prophet of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, commanded Yahya ibn Zakariyya, peace be upon him, with five words to act upon, and to command the Children of Israel to act upon them. He was slow to convey them, so Isa, peace be upon him, said to him: 'You have been commanded with five words to act upon and to command the Children of Israel to act upon them. Either you convey them, or I will convey them.' He said: 'O my brother, I fear that if you precede me, I will be punished or swallowed up by the earth.'" He said: "So Yahya ibn Zakariyya gathered the Children of Israel in Bayt al-Maqdis until the mosque was filled. He sat upon the elevated place, praised Allah and extolled Him, and then said: 'Indeed Allah has commanded me with five words to act upon, and I command you to act upon them. The first of them: worship Allah [alone], and do not associate anything with Him. For the example of this is that of a man who bought a slave with pure wealth, with silver or gold, and the slave began to work and pay his earnings to someone other than his master. Which of you would be pleased that his slave should be like this? Allah created you and provided for you, so worship Him and do not associate anything with Him. He also commanded you to pray, for Allah turns His face toward the face of His servant as long as he does not turn aside; so when you pray, do not turn aside. He commanded you to fast, for the example of this is that of a man who had a purse of musk in a bag, and everyone smelled its fragrance; and indeed the odour of a fasting person's mouth is more fragrant to Allah than the scent of musk. He commanded you to give charity, for the example of this is that of a man whom the enemy captured, bound his hands to his neck, and brought him forward to strike off his neck; so he said to them: "Will you accept that I ransom myself?" and he began to ransom himself from them with little and much until he freed himself. He commanded you to remember Allah much, for the example of this is that of a man whom the enemy pursued swiftly on his trail; he came to a strong fortress and took refuge in it. Likewise, the servant is most protected from Satan when he is engaged in the remembrance of Allah.'"

He said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) also said: "And I command you with five which Allah has commanded me: the community (al-jama'ah), listening (al-sam'), obedience (al-ta'ah), emigration (al-hijrah), and striving in the way of Allah (al-jihad). For whoever leaves the community by a span has indeed removed the bond of Islam from his neck, unless he returns. And whoever calls to a call of the Jahiliyyah (pre-Islamic ignorance), he is among the kneeling ones of Hell." They said: "O Messenger of Allah, even if he fasts and prays?" He said: "Even if he prays and fasts and claims that he is a Muslim. So call the Muslims by the names Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, has named them: the Muslims, the believers, the servants of Allah" [al-Musnad, 4/130].

This is a good (hasan) hadith, and its relevance to this verse is his saying: "Indeed Allah created you and provided for you, so worship Him and do not associate anything with Him."

This verse indicates the oneness of God in worship, that He alone has no partner. Many exegetes, such as al-Razi and others, cited it as evidence for the existence of the Creator, saying: it indicates this by way of a stronger inference, for whoever reflects on these existing things, the lower and the higher, and the variety of their forms, colours, natures and benefits, and their placement in positions where their benefit is firmly established, knows the power, wisdom, knowledge, perfection and great authority of their Creator. As one of the Bedouins said when he was asked: "What is the proof of the existence of the Lord, exalted is He?" He said: "Glory be to Allah! Indeed, a single dropping points to a camel, and the trace of footprints points to the path. So does a sky with constellations, an earth with pathways, and seas with waves not indicate the existence of the Subtle, the All-Aware?"

Fakhr al-Din (al-Razi) relates from Imam Malik that al-Rashid asked him about this, and he argued from the difference of languages, voices and melodies. And from Abu Hanifa: some of the zindiqs (heretics) asked him about the existence of the Creator, the Exalted, and he said to them: "Leave me, for I am reflecting on a matter about which I have been informed. They told me that there is a ship on the sea, laden with all kinds of merchandise, with no one in it to guard it or steer it, and yet it goes and comes, moves on its own, cuts through the great waves until it escapes them, and travels wherever it wills by itself, without anyone driving it." They said: "This is something no sane person would say." He said: "Woe to you! These existing things, with what they contain of the upper and lower world and the firmly-made things they comprise, have no maker!" The people were confounded, returned to the truth, and embraced Islam at his hands.

From al-Shafi'i: he was asked about the existence of the Maker, and he said: "This mulberry leaf has one taste. The silkworm eats it and silk comes out of it; the bee eats it and honey comes out of it; the sheep, the camel and the cattle eat it and expel it as dung and droppings; the gazelle eats it and musk comes out of it. Yet it is one thing."

From Imam Ahmad ibn Hanbal: he was asked about this and said: "Here is a strong, smooth fortress, with no door and no opening. Its outside is like white silver and its inside like pure gold. While it is in this state, its wall splits open and there emerges from it a living being that hears and sees, of fine form and pleasant voice." He meant by this the egg, when the chick comes out of it.

Abu Nuwas was asked about this and recited:
Reflect upon the plants of the earth and look
at the traces of what the King has made...
Eyes of silver, gazing,
with pupils that are refined gold...
standing upon stems of emerald,
bearing witness that God has no partner.

Ibn al-Mu'tazz said:
How strange it is that the God is disobeyed,
or how the denier can deny Him...
And in everything there is a sign for Him
that shows that He is One.

Others said: Whoever reflects upon these heavens in their height and vastness, and upon the great and small shining stars among them, the wandering planets and the fixed stars, and observes how they revolve with the great sphere every day and night, and yet have in themselves a movement peculiar to them; and who looks at the seas surrounding the earth on every side, and at the mountains placed upon the earth so that it may be steady and its inhabitants may dwell in peace, with their differing shapes and colours, as He said: ﴿And among the mountains are streaks, white and red, of varying hues, and jet-black ones. And among men and beasts and cattle are those of varying hues likewise. Only those of His servants who have knowledge truly fear God﴾ [Fatir: 27-28]; and likewise these rivers flowing from region to region for the benefit of His servants, and what is scattered on the earth of diverse creatures and plants of differing tastes, scents, forms and colours, while the nature of the soil and the water is one: he knows the existence of the Maker, His great power, His wisdom, His mercy toward His creation, His gentleness and kindness toward them, His goodness and beneficence to them. There is no god but Him and no lord besides Him. In Him I place my trust, and to Him I turn in repentance. The verses in the Qur'an indicating this station are very numerous indeed.

From al-Shafi'i: he was asked about the existence of the Maker, and he said: "This mulberry leaf has one taste. The silkworm eats it and silk comes out of it; the bee eats it and honey comes out of it; the sheep, the camel and the cattle eat it and expel it as dung and droppings; the gazelle eats it and musk comes out of it. Yet it is one thing."

From Imam Ahmad ibn Hanbal: he was asked about this and said: "Here is a strong, smooth fortress, with no door and no opening. Its outside is like white silver and its inside like pure gold. While it is in this state, its wall splits open and there emerges from it a living being that hears and sees, of fine form and pleasant voice." He meant by this the egg, when the chick comes out of it.

Abu Nuwas was asked about this and recited:
Reflect upon the plants of the earth and look
at the traces of what the King has made...
Eyes of silver, gazing,
with pupils that are refined gold...
standing upon stems of emerald,
bearing witness that God has no partner.

Ibn al-Mu'tazz said:
How strange it is that the God is disobeyed,
or how the denier can deny Him...
And in everything there is a sign for Him
that shows that He is One.

Others said: Whoever reflects upon these heavens in their height and vastness, and upon the great and small shining stars among them, the wandering planets and the fixed stars, and observes how they revolve with the great sphere every day and night, and yet have in themselves a movement peculiar to them; and who looks at the seas surrounding the earth on every side, and at the mountains placed upon the earth so that it may be steady and its inhabitants may dwell in peace, with their differing shapes and colours, as He said: ﴿And among the mountains are streaks, white and red, of varying hues, and jet-black ones. And among men and beasts and cattle are those of varying hues likewise. Only those of His servants who have knowledge truly fear God﴾ [Fatir: 27-28]; and likewise these rivers flowing from region to region for the benefit of His servants, and what is scattered on the earth of diverse creatures and plants of differing tastes, scents, forms and colours, while the nature of the soil and the water is one: he knows the existence of the Maker, His great power, His wisdom, His mercy toward His creation, His gentleness and kindness toward them, His goodness and beneficence to them. There is no god but Him and no lord besides Him. In Him I place my trust, and to Him I turn in repentance. The verses in the Qur'an indicating this station are very numerous indeed.

Then Allah, exalted is He, began to establish prophethood after establishing that there is no god but Him. He addressed the disbelievers, saying: ﴿And if you are in doubt about what We have sent down upon Our servant﴾, meaning Muhammad (ﷺ), ﴿then produce a surah⁠﻿ like it﴾, i.e., of the same kind as what he has brought, if you claim that it is from other than Allah. So contend with it by bringing something like it, and seek help in that from whomever you wish besides Allah, ﴿for you will not be able to do so﴾.

Ibn ʿAbbas said: ﴿your witnesses﴾ means your helpers [i.e., other people who would assist you in this].

As-Suddi said, from Abu Malik: "your partners" [i.e., seek help from your gods in this; they will aid you and support you].

Mujahid said: ﴿and call your witnesses﴾ — he said: people who will testify to it [meaning: the eloquent judges].

Allah challenged them with this in more than one place in the Qur'an. He said in Surat al-Qasas: ﴿Say: "Then bring a book from Allah which is better guided than both of them, that I may follow it, if you are truthful."﴾ [al-Qasas: 49]. He said in Surat al-Isra': ﴿Say: "If mankind and the jinn gathered to produce the like of this Qur'an, they would not produce its like, even if they were to one another assistants."﴾ [al-Isra': 88]. He said in Surat Hud: ﴿Or do they say, "He has invented it." Say: "Then bring ten surahs like it, invented, and call upon whomever you can besides Allah, if you are truthful."﴾ [Hud: 13]. He said in Surat Yunus: ﴿And it is not [possible] for this Qur'an to be produced by other than Allah, but it is a confirmation of what was before it and a detailed explanation of the Book, about which there is no doubt, from the Lord of the worlds. Or do they say, "He has invented it"? Say: "Then bring a surah like it and call upon whomever you can besides Allah, if you are truthful."﴾ [Yunus: 37-38]. All of these verses are Meccan.

Then He challenged them with this again in Medina, saying in this verse: ﴿And if you are in doubt⁠﻿﻿ — i.e., in ⁠﻿﻿ uncertainty — about what We have sent down upon Our servant﴾, meaning Muhammad (ﷺ). ﴿Then produce a surah of the like of it﴾, meaning of the like of [this] Qur'an. This was said by Mujahid and Qatadah, and Ibn Jarir chose it, as evidenced by His saying: ﴿Then bring ten surahs like it﴾ [Hud: 13] and His saying: ﴿They will not produce its like﴾ [al-Isra': 88]. Some of them said: "of the like of Muhammad (ﷺ)", meaning: a man unlettered like him. The correct view is the first, because the challenge is general to all of them, together with the fact that they were the most eloquent of nations. He challenged them with this in Mecca and Medina many times, despite their intense enmity towards him and their hatred for his religion, and yet they were unable to do it. Therefore Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿But if you do not, and you will never do it﴾. "Lan" is for negating perpetuity, i.e., "and you will never do that ever." This is another miracle: He informed that this Qur'an will never be opposed by its like, ever, and so it has been. It has not been opposed from its revelation until our present time, nor is it possible. How could that be possible for anyone, when the Qur'an is the speech of Allah, the Creator of all things? How could the speech of the Creator resemble the speech of created beings?

Whoever reflects upon the Qur'an finds in it aspects of inimitability, manifest and hidden, in terms of wording and in terms of meaning. Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿Alif, Lam, Ra. A Book whose verses have been perfected and then elaborated from One who is Wise and Acquainted﴾ [Hud: 1]. So its wording is made perfect and its meanings are elaborated, or the reverse, according to the differing views. Each of its wording and meaning is eloquent, unmatched and unapproachable. It informs of unseen matters, past and future, which occurred exactly as it reported, precisely as stated. It commands every good and forbids every evil, as He said: ﴿And the word of your Lord has been fulfilled in truth and justice﴾ [al-An'am: 115], i.e., truthful in its reports and just in its rulings. All of it is truth, truthfulness, justice and guidance, with no rashness, no lying and no fabrication. This is unlike the poetry of the Arabs and others, which contains lies and exaggerations without which their poetry would not be beautiful; as it is said of poetry: "its sweetest part is its most false." You find a long, extended qasidah mostly employed in describing women, horses or wine, or in praising a specific person, a horse, a she-camel, a war, an event, a fear, or a beast, or some other specific observed matter that yields nothing except the speaker's ability to express the hidden or subtle thing or to make it manifest as something clear. Then you find in it one, two or more verses which are the "heads of the poem," while the rest is idle talk with no benefit in it.

As for the Qur'an, all of it is eloquent to the utmost extent of eloquence for one who knows this in detail and in summary, from among those who understand the speech of the Arabs and the variations of expression. If you reflect upon its reports, you find them in the utmost sweetness, whether they are expanded or concise, and whether they are repeated or not. Each time it is repeated, it grows sweeter and loftier; it does not wear out through frequent recitation, and scholars do not tire of it. When it addresses warning and threat, there comes from it what makes the solid, firm mountains tremble; so what do you think of understanding hearts? When it promises, it brings what opens hearts and ears and yearns for the Abode of Peace and proximity to the Throne of the Most Merciful. As He said in encouragement: ﴿No soul knows what has been hidden for them of comfort for the eyes, as a reward for what they used to do﴾ [as-Sajdah: 17]. And He said: ﴿Therein is what the souls desire and what the eyes delight in, and you therein will abide eternally﴾ [az-Zukhruf: 71]. In warning, He said: ﴿Then are you secure that He will not cause the earth to swallow you on the side of the land?﴾ [al-Isra': 68]; ﴿Are you secure from He who is in the heaven that He will cause the earth to swallow you and then it will sway? Or are you secure from He who is in the heaven that He will send upon you a storm of stones, and you will know how My warning was?﴾ [al-Mulk: 16-17]. In rebuke, He said: ﴿So We seized each one for his sin﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 40]. In admonition, He said: ﴿Have you seen if We let them enjoy for years, then there comes to them what they were promised, will not avail them what they were enjoying?﴾ [ash-Shu'ara': 205-207]. And beyond these are other kinds of eloquence, rhetoric and sweetness. When the verses come concerning rulings, commands and prohibitions, they include the command to every good that is beneficial, pure and beloved, and the prohibition of every ugly, base and vile thing. As Ibn Mas'ud and other early scholars said: "When you hear Allah say in the Qur'an, ﴿O you who have believed﴾, then give it your attentive hearing, for it is either something good you are commanded to do or something evil you are forbidden from." For this reason He said: ﴿He enjoins upon them what is right and forbids them what is wrong and makes lawful for them good things and prohibits for them evil things and relieves them of their burden and the shackles that were upon them﴾ [al-A'raf: 157]. When the verses come describing the Return and its terrors, and describing Paradise and Hellfire and what Allah has prepared therein for His allies and His enemies of bliss, torment, pleasure and painful punishment, they give glad tidings, warn and admonish; they call to good deeds and avoiding evil deeds, they make one ascetic regarding this world and eager for the Hereafter, they keep one firm upon the most excellent path, they guide to the straight path of Allah and His upright law, and they remove from hearts the filth of the accursed Satan.

For this reason it is established in the two Sahihs from Abu Hurairah, may Allah be pleased with him, that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "There is no prophet among the prophets except that he was given signs such that people believed because of them. What I was given was a revelation which Allah revealed to me, so I hope that I will have the most followers on the Day of Resurrection." This is the wording of Muslim. His saying "What I was given was a revelation" means: what I was singled out with among them is this Qur'an, which is inimitable for mankind to oppose, unlike other divine books, for they are not considered miraculous by many scholars. And Allah knows best. He, peace and blessings be upon him, has many signs that indicate his prophethood and the truth of what he brought, which cannot be counted. And to Allah belong praise and favor.

[Some scholars established inimitability by a method that encompasses the view of the People of the Sunnah and the view of the Mu'tazilah concerning the Sufis. He said: If this Qur'an is inimitable in itself, such that humans cannot produce its like and are not capable of opposing it, then the claim and the objective are achieved. If it were within their power to oppose it with its like and they did not do so despite their intense enmity towards him, that would be evidence that it is from Allah, because He diverted them from opposing it while they were capable of it. This method, although it is not the preferred one, because the Qur'an in itself is inimitable and humans cannot oppose it, as we have established, is still suitable as an approach for argument, debate and defending the truth. By this method Fakhr al-Din answered his question concerning the short surahs such as al-'Asr and ﴿Indeed, We have granted you al-Kawthar﴾.]

As for His saying: ﴿So fear the Fire whose fuel is men and stones, prepared for the disbelievers﴾. As for "waqud" with a fatha on the waw, it is that which is thrown into the fire to kindle it, such as firewood and the like, as He said: ﴿And as for the deviators, they will be fuel for Hell﴾ [al-Jinn: 15]. And Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿Indeed, you and what you worship besides Allah are the fuel of Hell; you will be arriving thereto﴾ [al-Anbiya': 98].

What is meant by "stones" here is the great black, hard, foul-smelling stones of sulfur, which are among the most intensely hot of stones when heated. May Allah protect us from them.

ʿAbd al-Malik ibn Maysarah az-Zarrad related from ʿAbd ar-Rahman ibn Sabit, from ʿAmr ibn Maymun, from ʿAbdullah ibn Mas'ud, regarding His saying: ﴿Its fuel is men and stones﴾: he said: "They are stones of sulfur which Allah created on the day He created the heavens and the earth, in the lowest heaven, preparing them for the disbelievers." Narrated by Ibn Jarir, and this is his wording; and Ibn Abi Hatim; and al-Hakim in his Mustadrak, who said: "according to the conditions of the two Shaykhs" [Tafsir al-Tabari (1/381), Tafsir Ibn Abi Hatim (1/85), al-Mustadrak (2/61)].

As-Suddi said in his tafsir, from Abu Malik, and from Abu Salih, from Ibn ʿAbbas, and from Murrah from Ibn Mas'ud, and from a number of Companions: ﴿So fear the Fire whose fuel is men and stones﴾. As for the stones, they are stones in the Fire of black sulfur, with which they are tormented alongside the Fire.

Mujahid said: stones of sulfur more foul-smelling than carrion. Abu Ja'far Muhammad ibn 'Ali said: they are stones of sulfur. Ibn Jurayj said: stones of black sulfur in the Fire. And 'Amr ibn Dinar said to me: "harder than these stones and greater."

Some say that by "the stones" is meant the stones of the idols and rivals that were worshipped besides God, as He said: ﴿Indeed, you and what you worship besides God are fuel for Hell﴾ [al-Anbiya: 98]. Al-Qurtubi and Fakhr al-Din reported this view and preferred it over the first. He said: "Because kindling fire in sulphur stones is not strange, so making these the stones is more fitting." But what he said is not strong. That is because when fire is kindled with sulphur stones, its heat is greater and its blaze more intense, especially according to what the early scholars (al-salaf) mentioned, that they are stones of sulphur prepared for this purpose. Moreover, kindling fire in such stones is also observed, and this plaster (al-jis) becomes stones, and fire acts upon it until it becomes like that. Likewise, fire swells and burns all kinds of stones. This was only mentioned regarding the heat of that Fire which they were promised, the intensity of its flames and the strength of its blaze, as He said: ﴿Whenever it dies down, We increase them in blaze﴾ [al-Isra: 97]. In the same way, al-Qurtubi preferred that by them is meant the stones with which the Fire is kindled so that it becomes hot and its flame intensifies. He said: "So that this will be a greater punishment for its people." He said: "It has come in a hadith from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: 'Every harmer is in the Fire.'" But this hadith is neither preserved (mahfuz) nor well known.[[Reported by al-Khatib in Tarikh Baghdad (11/299) through al-Mufid, from al-Ashajj, from Ali (may Allah be pleased with him), as a marfu' report.]] Then al-Qurtubi said: "It has been explained in two meanings: one, that everyone who harms people enters the Fire;[[In A: "punished in the Fire".]] and the other, that everything that harms is in the Fire, and its people are harmed by it, from predatory animals, vermin and other things."[[Addition from J, T, B, A, and W.]]

* *

As for His saying: ﴿It has been prepared for the disbelievers﴾, the more apparent view is that the pronoun in ﴿prepared﴾ refers to the Fire whose fuel is people and stones. It may also refer to the stones, as Ibn Mas'ud said. There is no contradiction between the two views in meaning, because they are mutually implicated.

And ﴿prepared﴾ means: made ready and established for the disbelievers in God and His Messenger. As Muhammad ibn Ishaq said, from Muhammad, from Ikrimah or Sa'id ibn Jubayr, from Ibn Abbas: ﴿prepared for the disbelievers﴾ means: for whoever is upon the same disbelief as you are upon.

Many of the imams of the Sunnah (a'immat al-sunnah) have used this verse as evidence that the Fire already exists now, because of His saying ﴿prepared﴾, i.e., readied and made ready. Many hadiths have been transmitted on this, among them: "The Garden and the Fire disputed," and among them: "The Fire asked its Lord, saying: 'My Lord, some of me has consumed others of me,' so He permitted it two breaths: a breath in winter and a breath in summer." And the hadith of Ibn Mas'ud: "We heard a crash, and we said: 'What is this?' The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'This is a stone that was thrown into the edge of Hell seventy years ago, and now it has reached its bottom.'" It is in Muslim.[[Sahih Muslim, no. (2844).]] And the hadith of the eclipse prayer, the Night Journey, and other hadiths that are widely transmitted (mutawatirah) in this meaning. The Mu'tazila (a rationalist theological school) opposed this out of their ignorance, and the judge Mundhir ibn Sa'id al-Ballluti, judge of al-Andalus, agreed with them.

A point that must be noted:

His saying: ﴿then produce a surah like it﴾, and His saying in Surah Yunus: ﴿a surah like it﴾ [Yunus: 38], includes every surah in the Qur'an, whether long or short, because it is indefinite in the context of a condition, so it is general, just as it is in the context of negation according to the verifying scholars of legal theory (al-usuliyyun), as is established in its place. So the inimitability (i'jaz) is present in long surahs and short ones alike. I know of no dispute among people on this, earlier or later. The eminent imam Fakhr al-Din al-Razi said in his tafsir: "If it is said: His saying ﴿then produce a surah like it﴾ encompasses Surah al-Kawthar and Surah al-Asr, and ﴿Say: O disbelievers﴾, and we know by necessity that producing its like, or something close to it, is possible. If you say that producing the like of these surahs is beyond human capacity, that would be obstinacy, and persisting in such obstinacy casts suspicion upon the religion: we say: For this reason we have chosen the second way, and we said: If this surah reaches the limit of inimitability in eloquence, the purpose has been achieved. If it is not so, then their refraining from contending, despite their strong motives to belittle its matter, is itself a miracle. So in either case the miracle is attained." This is his wording exactly. The correct view is that every surah of the Qur'an is a miracle which people cannot contend against, whether it is long or short.

Al-Shafi'i, may Allah have mercy on him, said: "If people reflected upon this surah alone, it would suffice them: ﴿By time, indeed mankind is in loss, except for those who have believed and done righteous deeds and advised each other to truth and advised each other to patience﴾ [Surah al-Asr]." We have also narrated from Amr ibn al-As that he went as a delegate to Musaylima the Liar before he embraced Islam. Musaylima said to him: "What has been revealed to your companion in Mecca in this time?" Amr said to him: "A short, eloquent surah has been revealed to him." He said: "And what is it?" He said: "﴿By time, indeed mankind is in loss﴾." Musaylima thought for a while, then raised his head and said: "Indeed, something like it has been revealed to me." He said: "And what is it?" He said: "O Wabr, O Wabr, you are only two ears and a chest, and the rest of you is a contemptible, wretched thing." Then he said: "How do you see it, O Amr?" Amr said to him: "By Allah, you know that I know you are lying."[[The account of this story will come under the tafsir of Surah al-Asr.]]

Then Allah, exalted is He, began to establish prophethood after establishing that there is no god but Him. He addressed the disbelievers, saying: ﴿And if you are in doubt about what We have sent down upon Our servant﴾, meaning Muhammad (ﷺ), ﴿then produce a surah⁠﻿ like it﴾, i.e., of the same kind as what he has brought, if you claim that it is from other than Allah. So contend with it by bringing something like it, and seek help in that from whomever you wish besides Allah, ﴿for you will not be able to do so﴾.

Ibn ʿAbbas said: ﴿your witnesses﴾ means your helpers [i.e., other people who would assist you in this].

As-Suddi said, from Abu Malik: "your partners" [i.e., seek help from your gods in this; they will aid you and support you].

Mujahid said: ﴿and call your witnesses﴾ — he said: people who will testify to it [meaning: the eloquent judges].

Allah challenged them with this in more than one place in the Qur'an. He said in Surat al-Qasas: ﴿Say: "Then bring a book from Allah which is better guided than both of them, that I may follow it, if you are truthful."﴾ [al-Qasas: 49]. Or do they say, "He has invented it"? Say: "Then bring a surah like it and call upon whomever you can besides Allah, if you are truthful."﴾ [Yunus: 37-38]. All of these verses are Meccan.

Then He challenged them with this again in Medina, saying in this verse: ﴿And if you are in doubt⁠﻿﻿ — i.e., in ⁠﻿﻿ uncertainty — about what We have sent down upon Our servant﴾, meaning Muhammad (ﷺ). ﴿Then produce a surah of the like of it﴾, meaning of the like of [this] Qur'an. This was said by Mujahid and Qatadah, and Ibn Jarir chose it, as evidenced by His saying: ﴿Then bring ten surahs like it﴾ [Hud: 13] and His saying: ﴿They will not produce its like﴾ [al-Isra': 88]. Some of them said: "of the like of Muhammad (ﷺ)", meaning: a man unlettered like him. The correct view is the first, because the challenge is general to all of them, together with the fact that they were the most eloquent of nations. He challenged them with this in Mecca and Medina many times, despite their intense enmity towards him and their hatred for his religion, and yet they were unable to do it. Therefore Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿But if you do not, and you will never do it﴾. "Lan" is for negating perpetuity, i.e., "and you will never do that ever." This is another miracle: He informed that this Qur'an will never be opposed by its like, ever, and so it has been. It has not been opposed from its revelation until our present time, nor is it possible. How could that be possible for anyone, when the Qur'an is the speech of Allah, the Creator of all things? How could the speech of the Creator resemble the speech of created beings?

If it were within their power to oppose it with its like and they did not do so despite their intense enmity towards him, that would be evidence that it is from Allah, because He diverted them from opposing it while they were capable of it. This method, although it is not the preferred one, because the Qur'an in itself is inimitable and humans cannot oppose it, as we have established, is still suitable as an approach for argument, debate and defending the truth. By this method Fakhr al-Din answered his question concerning the short surahs such as al-'Asr and ﴿Indeed, We have granted you al-Kawthar﴾.]

As for His saying: ﴿So fear the Fire whose fuel is men and stones, prepared for the disbelievers﴾. As for "waqud" with a fatha on the waw, it is that which is thrown into the fire to kindle it, such as firewood and the like, as He said: ﴿And as for the deviators, they will be fuel for Hell﴾ [al-Jinn: 15]. And Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿Indeed, you and what you worship besides Allah are the fuel of Hell; you will be arriving thereto﴾ [al-Anbiya': 98].

What is meant by "stones" here is the great black, hard, foul-smelling stones of sulfur, which are among the most intensely hot of stones when heated. May Allah protect us from them.

ʿAbd al-Malik ibn Maysarah az-Zarrad related from ʿAbd ar-Rahman ibn Sabit, from ʿAmr ibn Maymun, from ʿAbdullah ibn Mas'ud, regarding His saying: ﴿Its fuel is men and stones﴾: he said: "They are stones of sulfur which Allah created on the day He created the heavens and the earth, in the lowest heaven, preparing them for the disbelievers." Narrated by Ibn Jarir, and this is his wording; and Ibn Abi Hatim; and al-Hakim in his Mustadrak, who said: "according to the conditions of the two Shaykhs" [Tafsir al-Tabari (1/381), Tafsir Ibn Abi Hatim (1/85), al-Mustadrak (2/61)].

As-Suddi said in his tafsir, from Abu Malik, and from Abu Salih, from Ibn ʿAbbas, and from Murrah from Ibn Mas'ud, and from a number of Companions: ﴿So fear the Fire whose fuel is men and stones﴾. As for the stones, they are stones in the Fire of black sulfur, with which they are tormented alongside the Fire.

Mujahid said: stones of sulfur more foul-smelling than carrion. Abu Ja'far Muhammad ibn 'Ali said: they are stones of sulfur. Ibn Jurayj said: stones of black sulfur in the Fire. And 'Amr ibn Dinar said to me: "harder than these stones and greater."

Some say that by "the stones" is meant the stones of the idols and rivals that were worshipped besides God, as He said: ﴿Indeed, you and what you worship besides God are fuel for Hell﴾ [al-Anbiya: 98]. Al-Qurtubi and Fakhr al-Din reported this view and preferred it over the first. He said: "Because kindling fire in sulphur stones is not strange, so making these the stones is more fitting." But what he said is not strong. That is because when fire is kindled with sulphur stones, its heat is greater and its blaze more intense, especially according to what the early scholars (al-salaf) mentioned, that they are stones of sulphur prepared for this purpose. Moreover, kindling fire in such stones is also observed, and this plaster (al-jis) becomes stones, and fire acts upon it until it becomes like that. Likewise, fire swells and burns all kinds of stones. This was only mentioned regarding the heat of that Fire which they were promised, the intensity of its flames and the strength of its blaze, as He said: ﴿Whenever it dies down, We increase them in blaze﴾ [al-Isra: 97]. In the same way, al-Qurtubi preferred that by them is meant the stones with which the Fire is kindled so that it becomes hot and its flame intensifies. He said: "So that this will be a greater punishment for its people." He said: "It has come in a hadith from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: 'Every harmer is in the Fire.'" But this hadith is neither preserved (mahfuz) nor well known.[[Reported by al-Khatib in Tarikh Baghdad (11/299) through al-Mufid, from al-Ashajj, from Ali (may Allah be pleased with him), as a marfu' report.]] Then al-Qurtubi said: "It has been explained in two meanings: one, that everyone who harms people enters the Fire;[[In A: "punished in the Fire".]] and the other, that everything that harms is in the Fire, and its people are harmed by it, from predatory animals, vermin and other things."[[Addition from J, T, B, A, and W.]]

* *

As for His saying: ﴿It has been prepared for the disbelievers﴾, the more apparent view is that the pronoun in ﴿prepared﴾ refers to the Fire whose fuel is people and stones. It may also refer to the stones, as Ibn Mas'ud said. There is no contradiction between the two views in meaning, because they are mutually implicated.

And ﴿prepared﴾ means: made ready and established for the disbelievers in God and His Messenger. As Muhammad ibn Ishaq said, from Muhammad, from Ikrimah or Sa'id ibn Jubayr, from Ibn Abbas: ﴿prepared for the disbelievers﴾ means: for whoever is upon the same disbelief as you are upon.

Many of the imams of the Sunnah (a'immat al-sunnah) have used this verse as evidence that the Fire already exists now, because of His saying ﴿prepared﴾, i.e., readied and made ready. Many hadiths have been transmitted on this, among them: "The Garden and the Fire disputed," and among them: "The Fire asked its Lord, saying: 'My Lord, some of me has consumed others of me,' so He permitted it two breaths: a breath in winter and a breath in summer." And the hadith of Ibn Mas'ud: "We heard a crash, and we said: 'What is this?' The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'This is a stone that was thrown into the edge of Hell seventy years ago, and now it has reached its bottom.'" It is in Muslim.[[Sahih Muslim, no. (2844).]] And the hadith of the eclipse prayer, the Night Journey, and other hadiths that are widely transmitted (mutawatirah) in this meaning. The Mu'tazila (a rationalist theological school) opposed this out of their ignorance, and the judge Mundhir ibn Sa'id al-Ballluti, judge of al-Andalus, agreed with them.

A point that must be noted:

His saying: ﴿then produce a surah like it﴾, and His saying in Surah Yunus: ﴿a surah like it﴾ [Yunus: 38], includes every surah in the Qur'an, whether long or short, because it is indefinite in the context of a condition, so it is general, just as it is in the context of negation according to the verifying scholars of legal theory (al-usuliyyun), as is established in its place. So the inimitability (i'jaz) is present in long surahs and short ones alike. I know of no dispute among people on this, earlier or later. The eminent imam Fakhr al-Din al-Razi said in his tafsir: "If it is said: His saying ﴿then produce a surah like it﴾ encompasses Surah al-Kawthar and Surah al-Asr, and ﴿Say: O disbelievers﴾, and we know by necessity that producing its like, or something close to it, is possible. If you say that producing the like of these surahs is beyond human capacity, that would be obstinacy, and persisting in such obstinacy casts suspicion upon the religion: we say: For this reason we have chosen the second way, and we said: If this surah reaches the limit of inimitability in eloquence, the purpose has been achieved. If it is not so, then their refraining from contending, despite their strong motives to belittle its matter, is itself a miracle. So in either case the miracle is attained." This is his wording exactly. The correct view is that every surah of the Qur'an is a miracle which people cannot contend against, whether it is long or short.

Al-Shafi'i, may Allah have mercy on him, said: "If people reflected upon this surah alone, it would suffice them: ﴿By time, indeed mankind is in loss, except for those who have believed and done righteous deeds and advised each other to truth and advised each other to patience﴾ [Surah al-Asr]." We have also narrated from Amr ibn al-As that he went as a delegate to Musaylima the Liar before he embraced Islam. Musaylima said to him: "What has been revealed to your companion in Mecca in this time?" Amr said to him: "A short, eloquent surah has been revealed to him." He said: "And what is it?" He said: "﴿By time, indeed mankind is in loss﴾." Musaylima thought for a while, then raised his head and said: "Indeed, something like it has been revealed to me." He said: "And what is it?" He said: "O Wabr, O Wabr, you are only two ears and a chest, and the rest of you is a contemptible, wretched thing." Then he said: "How do you see it, O Amr?" Amr said to him: "By Allah, you know that I know you are lying."[[The account of this story will come under the tafsir of Surah al-Asr.]]

He, exalted is He, having mentioned what He has prepared for His enemies, the wretched disbelievers in Him and in His messengers, of punishment and torment, follows it with mention of the condition of His friends, the happy believers in Him and in His messengers, who confirmed their faith with their righteous deeds. This is the meaning of naming the Qur'an "mathani" (the oft-repeated, paired) according to the most correct of the scholars' opinions, as we will expound in its proper place. It means mentioning a thing together with its opposite: faith followed by mention of disbelief, or the reverse, or the condition of the happy followed by the wretched, or the reverse. Its essence is the mention of a thing and its counterpart. As for mentioning a thing together with its like, that is "tashabuh" (resemblance), as we will clarify, God willing. Therefore He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And give good tidings to those who believe and do righteous deeds, that for them are gardens beneath which rivers flow﴾. He described them as having rivers flowing beneath them, just as He described the Fire as having people and stones as its fuel. The meaning of ﴿beneath which rivers flow﴾ is: beneath their trees and their chambers. It has come in a hadith that its rivers flow without a trench (ukhdud). It has also come concerning al-Kawthar that its banks are domes of hollow pearl, and there is no contradiction between them. Its clay is pure musk, and its pebbles are pearls and gems. We ask God for His bounty [and His generosity] (added from MSS. ج, ط, ب), indeed He is the Most Kind, the Most Merciful.

Ibn Abi Hatim said: It was recited to al-Rabi' ibn Sulayman: Asad ibn Musa narrated to us: Ibn Thawban narrated to us, from 'Ata' ibn Qurrah, from 'Abdullah ibn Damrah, from Abu Hurayrah, who said: The Messenger of God ﷺ said: "The rivers of Paradise gush forth from beneath the hills (or from beneath the mountains) of musk." [Ibn Abi Hatim, Tafsir (1/87). Abu Nu'aym narrated it in Sifat al-Jannah, no. (313), through al-Rabi' ibn Sulayman with the same chain. Ibn Hibban narrated it in his Sahih, no. (2622) "Mawarid," through al-Qurtasi, from Asad ibn Musa, from Ibn Thawban with the same chain.]

He also said: Abu Sa'id narrated to us: Waki' narrated to us, from al-A'mash, from 'Abdullah ibn Murrah, from Masruq, who said: 'Abdullah (ibn Mas'ud) said: "The rivers of Paradise gush forth from a mountain of musk."

* *

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Whenever they are provided with fruit therefrom as provision, they say: "This is what we were provided with before."﴾ As-Suddi said in his tafsir, from Abu Malik, and from Abu Salih, from Ibn 'Abbas, and from Murrah, from Ibn Mas'ud, and from some of the Companions, regarding ﴿They say: "This is what we were provided with before"﴾: they were brought fruit in Paradise, and when they looked at it they said: "This is what we were provided with before, in [the abode of] (added from MS. ج) the world."

Qatadah said likewise, as did 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Zayd ibn Aslam, and Ibn Jarir supported this view.

'Ikrimah said regarding ﴿They say: "This is what we were provided with before"﴾: its meaning is: "Like what we had yesterday." Al-Rabi' ibn Anas said likewise. Mujahid said: They say: "How much it resembles it!"

Ibn Jarir said: Others said: Rather, the interpretation of this is: "This is what we were provided with of the fruits of Paradise before this," because of the great resemblance of some of it to other parts of it, based on His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And they will be brought it in semblance﴾. Sunayd ibn Dawud said: a shaykh from the people of al-Massisah narrated to us, from al-Awza'i, from Yahya ibn Abi Kathir, who said: One of them is brought a dish of something, he eats from it, then another is brought, and he says: "This is what we were brought before." The angels say: "Eat, for the color is one, but the taste differs."

Ibn Abi Hatim said: My father narrated to us: Sa'id ibn Sulayman narrated to us: 'Amir ibn Yasaf narrated to us, from Yahya ibn Abi Kathir, who said: "The grass of Paradise is saffron, its sand dunes are musk, and the youths go around among them with fruits, and they eat them. Then they are brought the like of them, and the people of Paradise say to them: 'This is what you brought us just now.' The youths say to them: 'Eat, for the color is one, but the taste differs.'" This is the saying of God, exalted is He: ﴿And they will be brought it in semblance﴾.

Abu Ja'far al-Razi narrated from al-Rabi' ibn Anas, from Abu al-'Aliyah, regarding ﴿And they will be brought it in semblance﴾: "Some of it resembles other parts of it, and it differs in taste."

Ibn Abi Hatim said: It has been related from Mujahid, al-Rabi' ibn Anas, and al-Suddi something similar to this.

Ibn Jarir, with his chain, narrated from al-Suddi in his tafsir, from Abu Malik, and from Abu Salih, from Ibn 'Abbas, and from Murrah, from Ibn Mas'ud, and from some of the Companions, regarding His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And they will be brought it in semblance﴾: meaning in color and appearance, but it does not resemble in taste.

This is the view chosen by Ibn Jarir.

'Ikrimah said regarding ﴿And they will be brought it in semblance﴾: it resembles the fruits of the world, except that the fruits of Paradise are more delicious.

Sufyan al-Thawri narrated, from al-A'mash, from Abu Zabyan, from Ibn 'Abbas: "Nothing in Paradise resembles what is in the world except in names." In another narration: "There is nothing in the world of what is in Paradise except the names." Ibn Jarir related it through al-Thawri's narration, and Ibn Abi Hatim through the hadith of Abu Mu'awiyah; both of them from al-A'mash, with the same wording.

'Abd al-Rahman ibn Zayd ibn Aslam said regarding His saying: ﴿And they will be brought it in semblance﴾: "They recognize its names as they did in the world: apple is called apple, and pomegranate is called pomegranate. They say in Paradise: 'This is what we were provided with before in the world,' and they are brought it in semblance; they recognize it, but it is not the same in taste."

* *

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And for them therein are purified spouses﴾. Ibn Abi Talhah narrated from Ibn 'Abbas: "Purified from filth and harm."

Mujahid said: "From menstruation, excrement, urine, phlegm, spittle, semen, and childbirth."

Qatadah said: "Purified from harm and sin." In another narration from him: "No menstruation and no impurity." Similar to this was related from 'Ata', al-Hasan, al-Dahhak, Abu Salih, 'Atiyyah, and al-Suddi.

Ibn Jarir said: Yunus ibn 'Abd al-A'la narrated to me: Ibn Wahb informed us, from 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Zayd ibn Aslam, who said: "The purified one is she who does not menstruate." He said: "And thus was Eve, upon her be peace, created, until she disobeyed; when she disobeyed, God, exalted is He, said: 'I created you purified, and I will make you bleed as you made this tree bleed.'" This is strange.

The hafiz Abu Bakr ibn Mardawayh said: Ibrahim ibn Muhammad narrated to us: Ja'far ibn Muhammad ibn Harb narrated to me, and Ahmad ibn Muhammad al-Juwari [in MSS. ج, ط, ب: al-Jawari] both said: Muhammad ibn 'Ubayd al-Kindi narrated to us: 'Abd al-Razzaq ibn 'Umar al-Bazi'i narrated to us: 'Abdullah ibn al-Mubarak narrated to us, from Shu'bah, from Qatadah, from Abu Nadrah, from Abu Sa'id, from the Prophet ﷺ regarding His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And for them therein are purified spouses﴾, he said: "From menstruation, excrement, phlegm, and spittle." [Abu Nu'aym narrated it in Sifat al-Jannah, no. (363), through 'Abdullah ibn Muhammad ibn Ya'qub, from Muhammad ibn 'Ubayd with the same chain.]

This is a strange hadith. Al-Hakim narrated it in his Mustadrak, from Muhammad ibn Ya'qub, from al-Hasan ibn 'Ali ibn 'Affan, from Muhammad ibn 'Ubayd, with the same chain, and said: "Sahih according to the conditions of the two shaykhs (al-Bukhari and Muslim)."

But this claim of his is open to scrutiny, for 'Abd al-Razzaq ibn 'Umar al-Bazi'i (in MS. أ: al-Rab'i) was described by Abu Hatim ibn Hibban al-Busti, who said: "It is not permissible to argue with him."

I say: The more evident view is that this is from the words of Qatadah, as has preceded, and God knows best.

* *

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And they therein are abiding forever﴾. This is the completion of happiness, for they, with this bliss, are in a secure station, free from death and cessation; there is no end to it and no termination. Rather, they are in everlasting, perpetual bliss, enduring forever. And God is the one asked to gather us in their company; indeed He is Generous, Noble, Righteous, and Merciful.

Commentary of Ibn Kathir (Tafsir al-Quran al-'Azim) on surah 2, verses 26–27 (part 1 of 2):

Al-Suddi said in his tafsir (exegesis), from Abu Malik, and from Abu Salih, from Ibn Abbas, and from Murrah, from Ibn Mas'ud, and from some of the Companions: When Allah struck these two parables for the hypocrites, meaning His saying ﴿Their likeness is that of one who kindled a fire﴾ [al-Baqarah: 17] and His saying ﴿or like a rainstorm from the sky﴾ [al-Baqarah: 19], the three verses, the hypocrites said: "Allah is too exalted and too majestic to strike such parables." So Allah revealed this verse up to His saying: ﴿they are the losers﴾.

Abd al-Razzaq said, from Ma'mar, from Qatadah: When Allah mentioned the spider and the fly, the polytheists said: "What is the matter with the spider and the fly that they are mentioned?" So Allah revealed [[Addition from manuscript Ṭ.]] ﴿Indeed, Allah is not ashamed to present an example, [even] of a mosquito or what is smaller than it﴾.

Sa'id said, from Qatadah: That is, Allah is not ashamed of the truth to mention anything, be it small or great. When Allah mentioned the fly and the spider in His Book, the people of misguidance said: "What did Allah intend by mentioning this?" So Allah revealed: ﴿Indeed, Allah is not ashamed to present an example, [even] of a mosquito or what is smaller than it﴾.

I say: The first wording from Qatadah implies that this verse is Meccan, and that is not the case. The wording of Sa'id's narration from Qatadah is closer, and Allah knows best. Ibn Jurayj narrated from Mujahid something similar to this second report from Qatadah.

Ibn Abi Hatim said: It was narrated from al-Hasan and Isma'il ibn Abi Khalid something similar to the saying of al-Suddi and Qatadah.

Abu Ja'far al-Razi said, from al-Rabi' ibn Anas, concerning this verse: "This is a parable that Allah struck for the worldly life, for the mosquito lives as long as it is hungry, and when it becomes fat, it dies. Likewise is the likeness of these people [[In manuscript A: "this"]] for whom this parable was struck in the Qur'an: when they are filled with the world and content, Allah seizes them at that moment," and then he recited ﴿Then when they forgot what they had been reminded of, We opened for them the doors of everything﴾ [al-An'am: 44].

Thus Ibn Jarir narrated it. Ibn Abi Hatim narrated it from the hadith of Abu Ja'far, from al-Rabi', from Abu al-Aliyah, with similar wording. And Allah knows best.

This is their difference regarding the occasion of revelation (asbab al-nuzul). Ibn Jarir chose what al-Suddi related, because it is closer to the context of the surah and is more appropriate. The meaning of the verse is that He, the Exalted, informed that He is not ashamed, that is, He does not disdain, and it was said: He does not fear to strike any parable, that is, whatever parable it may be, with whatever thing it may be, whether small or great.

And "mā" here is for diminution [[In manuscripts J, T, B, A, and W: "for diminution, additional"]], and ﴿baʿūḍatan﴾ (a mosquito) is in the accusative as a substitute (badal), as you say: "I will strike a strike of some kind," so it is fulfilled by the least thing. [Or "mā" is an indefinite noun described by ﹛baʿūḍatin﹜ (a mosquito) [[Addition from manuscripts J, T, B, A, and W.]]]. Ibn Jarir chose that "mā" is a relative pronoun (mawsulah), and ﴿baʿūḍatan﴾ takes its case according to its own i'rab (grammatical case-marking). He said: This is permissible [[In manuscripts J, A, and W: "common"]] in the speech of the Arabs, that they give the complement of "mā" and "man" the same i'rab as them, because they are sometimes definite and sometimes indefinite, as Hassan ibn Thabit said:

"And it suffices us as a virtue over others [that] the Prophet Muhammad loves us."

He said: It is also possible that ﴿baʿūḍatan﴾ is in the accusative by deleting the preposition, and the sense of the sentence is: Indeed, Allah is not ashamed to strike a parable of any kind, from a mosquito up to what is above it.

This is what al-Kisa'i and al-Farra' chose. Al-Dahhak and Ibrahim ibn Abi Ablah recited it, and it was also related as ﴿baʿūḍatun﴾ with the nominative. Ibn Jinni said: It would then be a complement of "mā," and the returning pronoun has been deleted, as in His saying ﴿completion upon the one who did well﴾ [al-An'am: 154], meaning: upon the one who did well, he is good. Sibawayh related: "I am not the one who will say anything to you," meaning: "by the one who is saying anything to you" [[Addition from manuscripts J, T, B.]].

* *

As for His saying ﴿so what is above it﴾, there are two opinions. The first: so what is below it in smallness and insignificance, as when a man is described as base and miserly, and the listener says: "Yes, and he is beyond that," meaning in what you have described. This is the saying of al-Kisa'i and Abu Ubaydah. Al-Razi said: It is the view of most of the scholars who verify matters. In a hadith: "If the world weighed in the sight of Allah the wing of a mosquito, He would not give a disbelieving man a sip of water from it" [[Narrated by al-Tirmidhi in his Sunan, no. 2320, through the route of Abd al-Hamid ibn Sulayman, from Abu Hazim, from Sahl ibn Sa'd (may Allah be pleased with him), traced to the Prophet. In its chain is Abd al-Hamid ibn Sulayman, who is weak.]].

The second: "so what is above it" means: that which is larger than it, because there is nothing more contemptible or smaller than the mosquito. This is the saying of Qatadah ibn Di'amah [[Addition from manuscripts J and Ṭ.]] and the choice of Ibn Jarir.

This is supported by what Muslim narrated from Aishah, may Allah be pleased with her, that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "No Muslim is pricked by a thorn or anything above it, except that a degree is recorded for him by it and a sin is erased from him by it" [[Sahih Muslim, no. 2572.]] [[Addition from manuscripts J, Ṭ, A, and W.]].

So He informed that He does not disdain to strike as a parable anything, even if it is as contemptible and small as the mosquito, just as He did not disdain to create it. Likewise, He does not disdain to strike the parable of the fly and the spider in His saying: ﴿O mankind, a parable has been presented, so listen to it. Indeed, those you invoke other than Allah will never create a fly, even if they gathered together for it. And if the fly should steal from them a thing, they could not recover it from it. Weak are the seeker and the sought﴾ [al-Hajj: 73]. He also said: ﴿The example of those who take protectors other than Allah is like the spider that takes a house. And indeed, the frailest of houses is the spider's house, if only they knew﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 41]. And the Exalted said: ﴿Have you not considered how Allah presents an example: a good word is like a good tree, its root firmly fixed and its branches in the sky, giving its produce every time by the permission of its Lord. And Allah presents parables for the people that perhaps they may remember. And the example of an evil word is like an evil tree, uprooted from the surface of the earth, having no stability. Allah gives firmness to those who believe with the firm word in the worldly life and in the Hereafter, and Allah sends astray the wrongdoers, and Allah does what He wills﴾ [Ibrahim: 24–27]. He also said: ﴿Allah presents an example: a slave owned, unable to do anything [and one We have provided with good provision from Us]﴾ [al-Nahl: 75], up to the end of the verse. Then He said: ﴿And Allah presents an example of two men, one of them mute, unable to do anything, a burden upon his master; wherever he directs him, he brings no good. Is he equal to one who commands justice [and is upon a straight path]?﴾ [al-Nahl: 76], up to the end of the verse. As He said: ﴿He presents to you an example from yourselves: do you have among those whom your right hands possess any partners in what We have provided you?﴾ [al-Rum: 28], up to the end of the verse. And He said: ﴿Allah presents an example: a man in which are partners disputing, and a man belonging wholly to one man﴾ [al-Zumar: 29], up to the end of the verse. And Allah the Exalted has said: ﴿And these parables We present to the people, but none will understand them except the knowledgeable﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 43]. And there are many parables in the Qur'an.

One of the early scholars (salaf) said: When I hear a parable in the Qur'an and do not understand it, I weep over myself, because Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And these parables We present to the people, but none will understand them except the knowledgeable﴾.

Mujahid said concerning His saying ﴿Indeed, Allah is not ashamed to present an example, [even] of a mosquito or what is smaller than it﴾: The parables, small and great, the believers believe in them, and they know that they are the truth from their Lord, and Allah guides them by them.

Qatadah said: ﴿As for those who believe, they know that it is the truth from their Lord﴾: that is, they know that it is the speech of the Most Merciful, and that it is from Allah.

Something similar was related from Mujahid, al-Hasan, and al-Rabi' ibn Anas.

Abu al-Aliyah said: ﴿As for those who believe, they know that it is the truth from their Lord﴾ means: this parable. ﴿But as for those who disbelieve, they say: "What did Allah intend by this as a parable?"﴾ As He said in Surat al-Muddaththir: ﴿And We have not made the keepers of the Fire except angels, and We have not made their number except as a trial for those who disbelieve, that those who were given the Scripture may be certain and those who believe may increase in faith, and those who were given the Scripture and the believers will not doubt, and that those in whose hearts is disease and the disbelievers may say, "What did Allah intend by this as an example?" Thus Allah leaves astray whom He wills and guides whom He wills. And none knows the soldiers of your Lord except Him﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 31]. And likewise He said here: ﴿By it He causes many to go astray and by it He guides many, and He causes none to go astray except the defiantly disobedient﴾.

Al-Suddi said in his tafsir, from Abu Malik and from Abu Salih, from Ibn Abbas, and from Murrah, from Ibn Mas'ud, and from some of the Companions: ﴿By it He causes many to go astray﴾ means the hypocrites, and ﴿and by it He guides many﴾ means the believers. So these increase in misguidance upon their misguidance, because they deny what they had known with certainty to be true, of the parable that Allah struck for them, and that it agrees with what He struck as a parable for them. That is Allah's leading them astray by it. ﴿And by it He guides﴾, meaning by the parable, many of the people of faith and affirmation, so He increases them in guidance upon their guidance and in faith upon their faith, because of their affirmation of what they had known with certainty to be true, that it agrees with what Allah struck as a parable for it, and their acknowledgment of it. That is guidance from Allah for them through it. ﴿And He causes none to go astray except the defiantly disobedient﴾. He said: They are the hypocrites [[In manuscript A: "the people of hypocrisy."]].

Abu al-Aliyah said: ﴿And He causes none to go astray except the defiantly disobedient﴾: He said: They are the people of hypocrisy. Al-Rabi' ibn Anas said likewise.

Ibn Jurayj said, from Mujahid, from Ibn Abbas: ﴿And He causes none to go astray except the defiantly disobedient﴾: He says: The disbelievers recognize it, and so they disbelieve in it.

Qatadah said: ﴿And He causes none to go astray except the defiantly disobedient﴾: They defied, so Allah misguided them for their defiance.

Ibn Abi Hatim said: I was told, from Ishaq ibn Sulayman, from Abu Sinan, from Amr ibn Murrah, from Mus'ab ibn Sa'd, from Sa'd: ﴿By it He causes many to go astray﴾ means the Khawarij (Kharijites).

Shu'bah said, from Amr ibn Murrah, from Mus'ab ibn Sa'd, who said: I asked my father about His saying the Exalted: ﴿Those who break the covenant of Allah after its confirmation﴾ up to the end of the verse, and he said: They are the Harurites (Khawarij). If this chain is authentic from Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas, may Allah be pleased with him, then it is an interpretation according to meaning, not that the verse intended specifically the Khawarij who rebelled against Ali at Nahrawan. Those people were not present at the time of the revelation of the verse, but they enter it by their attribute along with whoever else enters it, because they were named Khawarij for their rebellion against the obedience of the Imam and their abandonment of the duties of Islam's laws.

In language, the fasiq is also one who goes out of obedience. The Arabs say: "The date-fruit fasaqat" when it comes out of its skin. For this reason the mouse is called fuwaysiqah (the little transgressor), because it comes out of its hole for corruption. It is established in the two Sahihs, from Aishah, that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Five transgressors are to be killed in the sacred and non-sacred areas: the crow, the kite, the scorpion, the mouse, and the rabid dog" [[Sahih al-Bukhari, no. 3314, and Sahih Muslim, no. 1198.]].

Among the scholars of exegesis (tafsir), the phrase *fasiq* (ungodly, defiant) includes both the disbeliever (kafir) and the disobedient (ʿasi), but the ungodliness of the disbeliever is more severe and more shameful. The intended meaning of the verse is the disbelieving *fasiq*, and God knows best, as shown by His description of them in His words: ﴿Those who break the covenant of God after its ratification, and sever what God has commanded to be joined, and cause corruption on the earth. Those are the losers.﴾

These are the attributes of disbelievers, which contrast with the attributes of the believers, as God the Exalted said in Surat al-Ra'd: ﴿Is he who knows that what has been sent down to you from your Lord is the truth like one who is blind? Only the people of understanding are reminded. Those who fulfil the covenant of God and do not break the pact. And those who join what God has commanded to be joined, and fear their Lord and dread the terrible reckoning.﴾ (The verses continue until He says:) ﴿And those who break the covenant of God after its ratification, and sever what God has commanded to be joined, and cause corruption on the earth; for them is the curse, and for them is the evil abode.﴾ [al-Ra'd: 19–25]

The exegetes have differed over the meaning of the covenant (ʿahd) by which these ungodly ones are described as breaking it. Some said: it is God's injunction to His creation and His command to them to obey Him, and His prohibition to them of what He forbade them of disobedience to Him, in His Books and through the tongues of His messengers. Their breaking of it is their abandoning of acting upon it.

Others said: rather, it refers to the disbelieving People of the Book and the hypocrites among them. The covenant of God that they broke is what God took from them in the Torah: to act by what is in it, to follow Muhammad ﷺ when he is sent, and to believe in him and in what he brought from their Lord. Their breaking of it is their denial of him after they recognised his reality, their rejection of that, and their concealing of the knowledge of it from the people, after they had given God a covenant from themselves that they would make it clear to the people and not conceal it. So God informed that they cast it behind their backs and sold it for a small price. This is the view chosen by Ibn Jarir (al-Tabari), may God have mercy on him, and the opinion of Muqatil ibn Hayyan.

Others said: this verse means all of the disbelievers, polytheists and hypocrites. His covenant to all of them concerning His oneness is the proofs He established for them indicating His lordship, and His covenant to them concerning His commands and prohibitions is the miracles with which He supported His messengers, which none of mankind other than they can produce a like of, bearing witness to their truthfulness. They said: their breaking of that is their abandoning of acknowledging what has been established as sound for them by the proofs, and their denying of the messengers and the Books while knowing that what they brought is true. This was also narrated from Muqatil ibn Hayyan, something similar to this, and it is good. [Al-Zamakhshari also inclined to this, for he said: If you say, what is meant by the covenant of God? I say: what He fixed in their minds of the proof for the oneness of God, as if it were a command He enjoined upon them and bound them to. This is the meaning of His words: ﴿And He made them testify concerning themselves: "Am I not your Lord?" They said: "Yes"﴾ [al-A'raf: 172], when He took the covenant from them in the Books sent down to them. As His words say: ﴿And fulfil My covenant, I will fulfil your covenant﴾ [al-Baqarah: 40].]

Others said: the covenant mentioned by God the Exalted is the covenant He took from them when He brought them out from the loins of Adam, which is described in His words: ﴿And when your Lord took from the children of Adam, from their loins, their descendants, and made them testify concerning themselves: "Am I not your Lord?" They said: "Yes, we testify"﴾ [al-A'raf: 172–173]. Their breaking of it is their failure to fulfil it. This too was narrated from Muqatil ibn Hayyan. Ibn Jarir related these opinions in his tafsir.

Abu Ja'far al-Razi related, from al-Rabi' ibn Anas, from Abu al-'Aliyah, concerning His words: ﴿Those who break the covenant of God after its ratification﴾ up to His words: ﴿the losers﴾, he said: these are six characteristics of the hypocrites. When they hold power over the people, they display these characteristics: when they speak they lie, when they promise they break it, when they are entrusted they betray, and they break the covenant of God after its ratification, and sever what God commanded to be joined, and cause corruption on the earth. And when the power is against them, they conceal these characteristics, and display only the three: when they speak they lie, when they promise they break it, and when they are entrusted they betray.

Al-Rabi' ibn Anas also said likewise. Al-Suddi, in his tafsir with his chain of narration, concerning the words of God the Exalted: ﴿Those who break the covenant of God after its ratification﴾, said: it is what was enjoined upon them in the Qur'an, so they acknowledged it, then disbelieved and broke it.

* *

As for His words: ﴿and sever what God has commanded to be joined﴾, it has been said: what is meant by it is the joining of the ties of kinship and relatives, as Qatadah explained, like His words: ﴿Would you, if you turned away, cause corruption on the earth and sever your ties of kinship?﴾ [Muhammad: 22]. Ibn Jarir preferred this view. It has also been said: what is meant is more general than that, so everything God commanded to be joined and done, they severed and abandoned.

Muqatil ibn Hayyan, concerning His words: ﴿Those are the losers﴾, said: [it means] in the Hereafter. This is like His words: ﴿For them is the curse, and for them is the evil abode﴾ [al-Ra'd: 25].

Al-Dahhak related from Ibn 'Abbas: every name God attributed to people other than the people of Islam, such as "losers," He means by it disbelief, and what He attributed to the people of Islam He means by it sin.

Ibn Jarir said concerning His words: ﴿Those are the losers﴾: al-khasirun is the plural of khasir, and they are those who diminish their own selves and their shares by their disobedience to God, of His mercy. It is like a man who loses in his trade by having something deducted from his capital in his sale. Likewise the disbeliever and the hypocrite lose by God's depriving them of His mercy, which He created for His servants, on the Day of Resurrection, when they are most in need of His mercy. It is said of this: khasira al-rajulu yakhsaru khasran wa khusranan wa khasaran, as Jarir ibn 'Atiyyah said:

Indeed Sulayt is in loss, indeed he is
a son of a people who were created as slaves.

Commentary of Ibn Kathir (Tafsir al-Quran al-'Azim) on surah 2, verses 26–27 (part 1 of 2):

Al-Suddi said in his tafsir (exegesis), from Abu Malik, and from Abu Salih, from Ibn Abbas, and from Murrah, from Ibn Mas'ud, and from some of the Companions: When Allah struck these two parables for the hypocrites, meaning His saying ﴿Their likeness is that of one who kindled a fire﴾ [al-Baqarah: 17] and His saying ﴿or like a rainstorm from the sky﴾ [al-Baqarah: 19], the three verses, the hypocrites said: "Allah is too exalted and too majestic to strike such parables." So Allah revealed this verse up to His saying: ﴿they are the losers﴾.

Abd al-Razzaq said, from Ma'mar, from Qatadah: When Allah mentioned the spider and the fly, the polytheists said: "What is the matter with the spider and the fly that they are mentioned?" So Allah revealed [[Addition from manuscript Ṭ.]] ﴿Indeed, Allah is not ashamed to present an example, [even] of a mosquito or what is smaller than it﴾.

Sa'id said, from Qatadah: That is, Allah is not ashamed of the truth to mention anything, be it small or great. When Allah mentioned the fly and the spider in His Book, the people of misguidance said: "What did Allah intend by mentioning this?" So Allah revealed: ﴿Indeed, Allah is not ashamed to present an example, [even] of a mosquito or what is smaller than it﴾.

I say: The first wording from Qatadah implies that this verse is Meccan, and that is not the case. The wording of Sa'id's narration from Qatadah is closer, and Allah knows best. Ibn Jurayj narrated from Mujahid something similar to this second report from Qatadah.

Ibn Abi Hatim said: It was narrated from al-Hasan and Isma'il ibn Abi Khalid something similar to the saying of al-Suddi and Qatadah.

Abu Ja'far al-Razi said, from al-Rabi' ibn Anas, concerning this verse: "This is a parable that Allah struck for the worldly life, for the mosquito lives as long as it is hungry, and when it becomes fat, it dies. Likewise is the likeness of these people [[In manuscript A: "this"]] for whom this parable was struck in the Qur'an: when they are filled with the world and content, Allah seizes them at that moment," and then he recited ﴿Then when they forgot what they had been reminded of, We opened for them the doors of everything﴾ [al-An'am: 44].

Thus Ibn Jarir narrated it. Ibn Abi Hatim narrated it from the hadith of Abu Ja'far, from al-Rabi', from Abu al-Aliyah, with similar wording. And Allah knows best.

This is their difference regarding the occasion of revelation (asbab al-nuzul). Ibn Jarir chose what al-Suddi related, because it is closer to the context of the surah and is more appropriate. The meaning of the verse is that He, the Exalted, informed that He is not ashamed, that is, He does not disdain, and it was said: He does not fear to strike any parable, that is, whatever parable it may be, with whatever thing it may be, whether small or great.

And "mā" here is for diminution [[In manuscripts J, T, B, A, and W: "for diminution, additional"]], and ﴿baʿūḍatan﴾ (a mosquito) is in the accusative as a substitute (badal), as you say: "I will strike a strike of some kind," so it is fulfilled by the least thing. [Or "mā" is an indefinite noun described by ﹛baʿūḍatin﹜ (a mosquito) [[Addition from manuscripts J, T, B, A, and W.]]]. Ibn Jarir chose that "mā" is a relative pronoun (mawsulah), and ﴿baʿūḍatan﴾ takes its case according to its own i'rab (grammatical case-marking). He said: This is permissible [[In manuscripts J, A, and W: "common"]] in the speech of the Arabs, that they give the complement of "mā" and "man" the same i'rab as them, because they are sometimes definite and sometimes indefinite, as Hassan ibn Thabit said:

"And it suffices us as a virtue over others [that] the Prophet Muhammad loves us."

He said: It is also possible that ﴿baʿūḍatan﴾ is in the accusative by deleting the preposition, and the sense of the sentence is: Indeed, Allah is not ashamed to strike a parable of any kind, from a mosquito up to what is above it.

This is what al-Kisa'i and al-Farra' chose. Al-Dahhak and Ibrahim ibn Abi Ablah recited it, and it was also related as ﴿baʿūḍatun﴾ with the nominative. Ibn Jinni said: It would then be a complement of "mā," and the returning pronoun has been deleted, as in His saying ﴿completion upon the one who did well﴾ [al-An'am: 154], meaning: upon the one who did well, he is good. Sibawayh related: "I am not the one who will say anything to you," meaning: "by the one who is saying anything to you" [[Addition from manuscripts J, T, B.]].

* *

As for His saying ﴿so what is above it﴾, there are two opinions. The first: so what is below it in smallness and insignificance, as when a man is described as base and miserly, and the listener says: "Yes, and he is beyond that," meaning in what you have described. This is the saying of al-Kisa'i and Abu Ubaydah. Al-Razi said: It is the view of most of the scholars who verify matters. In a hadith: "If the world weighed in the sight of Allah the wing of a mosquito, He would not give a disbelieving man a sip of water from it" [[Narrated by al-Tirmidhi in his Sunan, no. 2320, through the route of Abd al-Hamid ibn Sulayman, from Abu Hazim, from Sahl ibn Sa'd (may Allah be pleased with him), traced to the Prophet. In its chain is Abd al-Hamid ibn Sulayman, who is weak.]].

The second: "so what is above it" means: that which is larger than it, because there is nothing more contemptible or smaller than the mosquito. This is the saying of Qatadah ibn Di'amah [[Addition from manuscripts J and Ṭ.]] and the choice of Ibn Jarir.

This is supported by what Muslim narrated from Aishah, may Allah be pleased with her, that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "No Muslim is pricked by a thorn or anything above it, except that a degree is recorded for him by it and a sin is erased from him by it" [[Sahih Muslim, no. 2572.]] [[Addition from manuscripts J, Ṭ, A, and W.]].

So He informed that He does not disdain to strike as a parable anything, even if it is as contemptible and small as the mosquito, just as He did not disdain to create it. Likewise, He does not disdain to strike the parable of the fly and the spider in His saying: ﴿O mankind, a parable has been presented, so listen to it. Indeed, those you invoke other than Allah will never create a fly, even if they gathered together for it. And if the fly should steal from them a thing, they could not recover it from it. Weak are the seeker and the sought﴾ [al-Hajj: 73]. He also said: ﴿The example of those who take protectors other than Allah is like the spider that takes a house. And indeed, the frailest of houses is the spider's house, if only they knew﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 41]. And the Exalted said: ﴿Have you not considered how Allah presents an example: a good word is like a good tree, its root firmly fixed and its branches in the sky, giving its produce every time by the permission of its Lord. And Allah presents parables for the people that perhaps they may remember. And the example of an evil word is like an evil tree, uprooted from the surface of the earth, having no stability. Allah gives firmness to those who believe with the firm word in the worldly life and in the Hereafter, and Allah sends astray the wrongdoers, and Allah does what He wills﴾ [Ibrahim: 24–27]. He also said: ﴿Allah presents an example: a slave owned, unable to do anything [and one We have provided with good provision from Us]﴾ [al-Nahl: 75], up to the end of the verse. Then He said: ﴿And Allah presents an example of two men, one of them mute, unable to do anything, a burden upon his master; wherever he directs him, he brings no good. Is he equal to one who commands justice [and is upon a straight path]?﴾ [al-Nahl: 76], up to the end of the verse. As He said: ﴿He presents to you an example from yourselves: do you have among those whom your right hands possess any partners in what We have provided you?﴾ [al-Rum: 28], up to the end of the verse. And He said: ﴿Allah presents an example: a man in which are partners disputing, and a man belonging wholly to one man﴾ [al-Zumar: 29], up to the end of the verse. And Allah the Exalted has said: ﴿And these parables We present to the people, but none will understand them except the knowledgeable﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 43]. And there are many parables in the Qur'an.

One of the early scholars (salaf) said: When I hear a parable in the Qur'an and do not understand it, I weep over myself, because Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And these parables We present to the people, but none will understand them except the knowledgeable﴾.

Qatadah said: ﴿As for those who believe, they know that it is the truth from their Lord﴾: that is, they know that it is the speech of the Most Merciful, and that it is from Allah.

Something similar was related from Mujahid, al-Hasan, and al-Rabi' ibn Anas.

Thus Allah leaves astray whom He wills and guides whom He wills. And none knows the soldiers of your Lord except Him﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 31]. And likewise He said here: ﴿By it He causes many to go astray and by it He guides many, and He causes none to go astray except the defiantly disobedient﴾.
