He said: Then an anger came from Allah, and a thunderbolt came upon them after the repentance, and it struck them and they all died. He said: Then Allah brought them to life after their death, and he recited the words of Allah: ﴿Then We raised you up after your death, that you might be grateful﴾. Then Musa said to them: "Take the Book of Allah." They said: "No." He said: "What has befallen you?" They said: "What has befallen us is that we died and then were brought to life." He said: "Take the Book of Allah." They said: "No." So Allah sent angels who lifted up the mountain over them.

[This narration indicates that they were charged with obligations after they were brought back to life. Al-Mawardi related two opinions regarding this: one of them is that the obligation (taklif) was lifted from them because they had witnessed the matter openly, until they became compelled to affirm it. The second is that they remained obligated, so that no sane person would be free of obligation. Al-Qurtubi said: This is the correct view, because their witnessing of dreadful matters does not prevent their being obligated, since the Children of Israel had witnessed great extraordinary events (khawariq al-'adat), and they were nonetheless obligated. This is clear, and Allah knows best.]

God, exalted is He, says: Remember My favour upon you in raising you up for you after the thunderbolt (al-sa'q), when you asked to see Me openly and directly (jahratan 'iyanan), something that is not possible for you or for those like you, as Ibn Jurayj said. Ibn 'Abbas said regarding this verse: ﴿And when you said, "O Musa, we will never believe you until we see Allah openly"﴾ He said: "Openly" ( 'alaniyatan).[[In ج: "yatatallaʿ".]]

Similarly, Ibrahim ibn Tahman narrated from 'Abbad ibn Ishaq, from Abu al-Huwayrith, from Ibn 'Abbas, that he said regarding the words of Allah, exalted is He: ﴿We will never believe you until we see Allah openly﴾: "That is, openly, that is, until we see Allah."

Qatadah and al-Rabi' ibn Anas said: ﴿Until we see Allah openly﴾ means directly ('iyanan).

Abu Ja'far narrated from al-Rabi' ibn Anas: They were the seventy whom Musa chose, and they went with him. He said: They heard speech, and they said: ﴿We will never believe you until we see Allah openly.﴾ He said: Then they heard a voice and were struck down (fasu'iqu), meaning they died.

Marwan ibn al-Hakam, in a sermon he delivered on the pulpit of Makkah, said: The thunderbolt (al-sa'iqah) is a cry from the sky.

Al-Suddi said regarding His words: ﴿So the thunderbolt seized you﴾: The thunderbolt is fire.

'Urwah ibn Ruwaym said regarding His words: ﴿while you were looking on﴾: He said: Some of them were struck down while others were looking on. Then these were raised up and those were struck down.

Al-Suddi also said: ﴿So the thunderbolt seized you﴾ means they died. Musa stood up weeping and calling upon Allah, saying: "My Lord, what shall I say to the Children of Israel when I come to them, after You have destroyed their best men? ﴿If You had willed, You would have destroyed them before, and me too. Would You destroy us for what the foolish among us did?﴾" [Al-A'raf: 155]. Then Allah revealed to Musa that these seventy were among those who had taken the calf. Then Allah brought them back to life, and they stood up and lived, man by man, looking at one another, asking: "How are we living?" He said: That is His statement, exalted is He: ﴿Then We raised you up after your death, that you might be grateful.﴾

Al-Rabi' ibn Anas said: Their death was a punishment for them, and they were raised after death so that they might complete their appointed terms (ajal). Qatadah said the same.

Ibn Jarir said: Muhammad ibn Humayd narrated to us, Salamah ibn al-Fadl narrated to us, from Muhammad ibn Ishaq, who said: When Musa returned to his people and saw what they were doing in worshipping the calf, and said what he said to his brother and to al-Samiri, and burned the calf and scattered it into the sea, Musa chose from among them seventy men, the best of the best, and said: "Go to Allah, repent to Allah for what you have done, and ask Him to accept your repentance on behalf of those whom you left behind among your people. Fast, purify yourselves, and purify your garments." He set out with them toward Mount Sinai (Tur Sina') for an appointed time that his Lord had set for him. He would not come to it except with His permission and knowledge. The seventy said to him, as has been related to me, when they had done what they were commanded and went out to meet Allah: "O Musa, ask your Lord on our behalf that we may hear the speech of our Lord." He said: "I will do so." When Musa drew near the mountain, the cloud covered it entirely. Musa drew near and entered it, and said to the people: "Come near." Whenever Allah spoke to him, a bright light would fall upon his forehead, so that no one of the children of Adam could look at it. A veil was placed between him and them. The people drew near until, when they entered the cloud, they fell down in prostration, and they heard Him speaking to Musa, commanding him and forbidding him: "Do, and do not do." When He had finished His command to him, the cloud withdrew from Musa and he came to them. They said to Musa: ﴿We will never believe you until we see Allah openly﴾, so the quake (al-rajfah) seized them, which is the thunderbolt, and they all died. Musa stood up, pleading with his Lord, calling upon Him, and begging Him, saying: ﴿My Lord, if You had willed, You would have destroyed them before and me [too]﴾ [Al-A'raf: 155]. "They have acted foolishly. Will You destroy those who are behind me of the Children of Israel for what the foolish among us have done?" That is: this would be their destruction. "I chose from them seventy men, the best of the best. I will return to them, and not one man from them is with me! What then will they believe me about, and trust me in, after this?" ﴿We have turned back to You﴾ [Al-A'raf: 156]. Musa continued pleading with his Lord, mighty and majestic, and asking Him, until He returned their souls to them. He asked Him to accept the repentance of the Children of Israel from worshipping the calf. He said: "No, unless they kill themselves."[[Tafsir al-Tabari (2/77).]]

This is the narration of Muhammad ibn Ishaq.

Ismail ibn 'Abd al-Rahman al-Suddi al-Kabir said: When the Children of Israel repented from worshipping the calf, and Allah accepted their repentance by having some of them kill others, as He had commanded them, Allah commanded Musa to come to Him with a group of people from the Children of Israel, who would apologise to Him for worshipping the calf. Musa had promised them, so Musa chose seventy men from his people, by his own choice, then went with them so that they could make their apology. He related the rest.

[This narration implies that the address was directed to the Children of Israel in His words: ﴿And when you said, "O Musa, we will never believe you until we see Allah openly"﴾, and the intended meaning is the seventy chosen from among them. Most of the commentators did not relate anything other than this. Fakhr al-Din al-Razi was strange in his commentary when he related, concerning the story of these seventy, that after they were brought back to life they said: "O Musa, you do not ask Allah for anything without Him giving it to you. So ask Him to make us prophets." He prayed for that and Allah answered his supplication. This is extremely strange, since no prophet is known in the time of Musa besides Harun and then Yusha' ibn Nun. The People of the Book (Ahl al-Kitab) also erred in their claim that these people saw Allah, mighty and majestic, for Musa the Interlocutor (al-Kalim), peace be upon him, asked for that and was refused. How then could these seventy attain it?]

The second opinion regarding the verse: 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Zayd ibn Aslam said, in explaining this verse: When Musa returned from his Lord with the tablets, on which he had written the Torah (al-Tawrat, the Torah), he found them worshipping the calf. He commanded them to kill themselves, and they did so, and Allah accepted their repentance. He said: "These tablets contain the Book of Allah, in which is your command, which He commanded you, and your prohibition, which He forbade you." They said: "And who will take it on the basis of your word? No, by Allah, not until we see Allah openly, until Allah looks upon us and says: 'This is My Book, so take it.' Why does He not speak to us as He speaks to you, O Musa!" He recited the words of Allah: ﴿We will never believe you until we see Allah openly﴾. He said: Then an anger came from Allah, and a thunderbolt came upon them after the repentance, and it struck them and they all died. He said: Then Allah brought them to life after their death, and he recited the words of Allah: ﴿Then We raised you up after your death, that you might be grateful﴾. Then Musa said to them: "Take the Book of Allah." They said: "No." He said: "What has befallen you?" They said: "What has befallen us is that we died and then were brought to life." He said: "Take the Book of Allah." They said: "No." So Allah sent angels who lifted up the mountain over them.

[This narration indicates that they were charged with obligations after they were brought back to life. Al-Mawardi related two opinions regarding this: one of them is that the obligation (taklif) was lifted from them because they had witnessed the matter openly, until they became compelled to affirm it. The second is that they remained obligated, so that no sane person would be free of obligation. Al-Qurtubi said: This is the correct view, because their witnessing of dreadful matters does not prevent their being obligated, since the Children of Israel had witnessed great extraordinary events (khawariq al-'adat), and they were nonetheless obligated. This is clear, and Allah knows best.]

Commentary of Ibn Kathir (Tafsir al-Quran al-'Azim) on surah 2, verse 57 (part 1 of 2):

When Allah mentioned the calamities He had warded off from them, He began to remind them, again, of the blessings He had bestowed upon them, so He said: ﴿And We shaded you with the clouds﴾. Al-Ghamam is the plural of ghamamah, and it was so named because it covers (yaghummu) the sky, meaning it conceals and veils it. It is the white cloud, and they were shaded by it in the wilderness of al-Tih (the wandering) to protect them from the heat of the sun. This is as al-Nasa'i and others narrated from Ibn 'Abbas in the hadith of al-Futun (the trials), who said: "Then He shaded them with the clouds in al-Tih."

Ibn Abi Hatim said: It was also narrated from Ibn 'Umar, al-Rabi' ibn Anas, Abu Mijlaz, al-Dahhak, and al-Suddi, something similar to the saying of Ibn 'Abbas.

Al-Hasan and Qatadah said: ﴿And We shaded you with the clouds﴾ [He said:] This was in the desert [in A: "in the wandering"]. He shaded them with the clouds from the sun.

Ibn Jarir [in B and T: "Ibn Jurayj"] said: Others said: It was a cloud cooler than this and more pleasant.

Ibn Abi Hatim said: My father narrated to us, Abu Hudhayfah narrated to us, Shibl narrated to us, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid: ﴿And We shaded you with the clouds﴾ [in B and T: "upon them", which is an error.] He said: It is not the ordinary cloud; it is the cloud in which Allah will come on the Day of Resurrection, and it was not granted except to them.

Ibn Jarir narrated it likewise from al-Muthanna ibn Ibrahim, from Abu Hudhayfah.

al-Thawri and others also narrated it from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, and it seems that he intends, and Allah knows best, that it is not of the same form as this cloud, but better than it, more pleasant and more beautiful in appearance. This is as Sunayd said in his tafsir, from Hajjaj ibn Muhammad, from Ibn Jurayj, who said: Ibn 'Abbas said: ﴿And We shaded you with the clouds﴾. He said: A cloud cooler than this and more pleasant, and it is the one in which Allah will come, in His saying: ﴿Do they await only that Allah should come to them in canopies of clouds, and the angels?﴾ [al-Baqarah: 210], and it is the one in which the angels came on the day of Badr. Ibn 'Abbas said: It was with them in the wandering.

* *

As for His saying: ﴿And We sent down to you the manna﴾, the expressions of the commentators differed regarding what the manna is. 'Ali ibn Abi Talhah narrated from Ibn 'Abbas: The manna used to descend upon them on the trees, and they would go out to it and eat from it whatever they wished.

Mujahid said: The manna is a gum (samghah). 'Ikrimah said: The manna is something Allah sent down upon them like dew, resembling thick rain.

Al-Suddi said: They said: "O Musa, how shall we manage with what is here? Where is the food?" So Allah sent down the manna upon them, and it used to fall upon the trees of al-Zanjabil (ginger).

Qatadah said: The manna used to descend upon them in their settlement like the falling of snow, whiter than milk and sweeter than honey. It would fall upon them from the break of dawn until sunrise, and a man would take from it what sufficed him for that day; if he exceeded that, it spoiled and did not remain. But when it was the sixth day, the day of their Friday, he would take what sufficed him for the sixth day and the seventh day, because it was a day of festivity on which he would not set out for the affairs of his livelihood nor seek anything. All of this was in the desert.

Al-Rabi' ibn Anas said: The manna is a drink that used to descend upon them like honey, and they would mix it with water and then drink it.

Wahb ibn Munabbih, when asked about the manna, said: It is bread of ruqaq, like corn or like clean flour.

Abu Ja'far ibn Jarir said: Ahmad ibn Ishaq narrated to me, Abu Ahmad narrated to us, Isra'il narrated to us, from Jabir, from 'Amir, namely al-Sha'bi, who said: Your honey here is a part of seventy parts of the manna.

Likewise 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Zayd ibn Aslam said: It is honey.

And it occurs in the poetry of Umayyah ibn Abi al-Salt, where he said:

"So Allah saw that they were in a barren place,
neither with cultivated fields nor with produce.
So He sent down upon them in the mornings (clouds),
and their clouds were seen as heavy and abundant.
Honey flowing, and sweet water,
and milk of pleasing, pure quality."

[The verses are in Tafsir al-Tabari (2/94, 95).] Al-nati (flowing) is what is poured out, and milk al-marmur is the pure part of it.

The point is that the expressions of the commentators are close in explaining the manna: some of them explained it as food, and some explained it as drink. The apparent meaning, and Allah knows best, is that it is everything Allah bestowed upon them as a favour of food and drink, and other things, in which they had no labour or toil. The well-known manna, if eaten alone, was food and sweetness; if mixed with water, it became a good drink; and if combined with other things, it became another kind. But it is not the sole meaning of the verse. The evidence for this is the saying of al-Bukhari:

Abu Nu'aym narrated to us, Sufyan narrated to us, from 'Abd al-Malik, from 'Umar ibn Huraith [in B: "Hawshab"] from Sa'id [in B: "Sufyan"] ibn Zayd, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "The mushroom is of the manna, and its water is a cure for the eye."

This hadith was narrated by Imam Ahmad from Sufyan ibn 'Uyaynah, from 'Abd al-Malik, who is Ibn 'Umayr, with it [Sahih al-Bukhari no. (4478) and al-Musnad (1/187)].

The group (of compilers) narrated it in their books, except Abu Dawud, by several routes from 'Abd al-Malik, who is Ibn 'Umayr, with it [Sahih al-Bukhari no. (4639), Sahih Muslim no. (2049), Sunan al-Tirmidhi no. (2067), Sunan al-Nasa'i al-Kubra no. (6667)]. al-Tirmidhi said: Hasan sahih. al-Bukhari, Muslim and al-Nasa'i narrated it through the route of al-Hakam, from al-Hasan al-'Uranī, from 'Amr ibn Huraith, with it [Sahih al-Bukhari no. (5708), Sahih Muslim no. (2049), Sunan al-Nasa'i al-Kubra no. (10988)].

al-Tirmidhi said: Abu 'Ubaydah ibn Abi al-Safar and Mahmud ibn Ghaylan narrated to us, both saying: Sa'id ibn 'Amir narrated to us, from Muhammad ibn 'Amr, from Abu Salamah, from Abu Hurayrah, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "The 'ajwah is from Paradise, and in it is a cure from poison, and the mushroom is of the manna and its water is a cure for the eye" [Sunan al-Tirmidhi no. (3013)].

al-Tirmidhi alone narrated it, then said: This is a hasan gharib hadith; we do not know it except from the hadith of Muhammad ibn 'Amr, and from the hadith of Sa'id [in B: "Muhammad"] ibn 'Amir from him. In the chapter there is also (narration) from Sa'id ibn Zayd, Abu Sa'id and Jabir.

Thus he said. But al-Hafiz Abu Bakr ibn Mardawayh narrated it in his tafsir by another route, from Abu Hurayrah, saying: Ahmad ibn al-Hasan [in B, A, and W: "al-Husayn"] ibn Ahmad al-Basri narrated to us, Aslam ibn Sahl narrated to us, al-Qasim ibn 'Isa narrated to us, Talhah ibn 'Abd al-Rahman narrated to us, from Qatadah [in B: "'Ubadah"], from Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab, from Abu Hurayrah, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "The mushroom is of the manna, and its water is a cure for the eye."

This hadith is gharib from this route. Talhah ibn 'Abd al-Rahman here is a Sulami Wasiti, kunyah Abu Muhammad, and it was said: Abu Sulayman al-Mu'addib. The hafiz Abu Ahmad ibn 'Adi said about him: He narrated from Qatadah things that have no corroboration [al-Kamil of Ibn 'Adi (4/114)].

Then al-Tirmidhi said: Muhammad ibn Bashshar narrated to us, Mu'adh ibn Hisham narrated to us, my father narrated to us, from Qatadah, from Shahr ibn Hawshab, from Abu Hurayrah: that some people from the companions of the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "The mushroom is the smallpox of the earth." The Prophet of Allah (ﷺ) said: "The mushroom is of the manna, and its water is a cure for the eye, and the 'ajwah is from Paradise and it is a cure from poison."

This hadith was narrated by al-Nasa'i from Muhammad ibn Bashshar with it [it is in Sunan al-Nasa'i al-Kubra no. (6671) from Nasir ibn al-Faraj, from Mu'adh ibn Hisham with it, and I have not found it from Muhammad ibn Bashshar; al-Mizzi mentioned it from Muhammad ibn Bashshar in Tuhfat al-Ashraf (10/112)]. And from him, from Ghundar, from Shu'bah, from Abu Bishr Ja'far ibn Iyas, from Shahr ibn Hawshab, from Abu Hurayrah, with it [Sunan al-Nasa'i al-Kubra no. (6673)]. And from Muhammad ibn Bashshar, from 'Abd al-A'la, from Khalid al-Hadhdha', from Shahr ibn Hawshab, with the story of the mushroom only [Sunan al-Nasa'i al-Kubra no. (6672)].

al-Nasa'i also narrated, and Ibn Majah, from the hadith of Muhammad ibn Bashshar, from Abu 'Abd al-Samad 'Abd al-'Aziz ibn 'Abd al-Samad, from Matar al-Warraq, from Shahr: with the story of the 'ajwah according to al-Nasa'i, and with both stories according to Ibn Majah [Sunan Ibn Majah no. (3400)].

This route is interrupted between Shahr ibn Hawshab and Abu Hurayrah, for he did not hear it from him, as evidenced by what al-Nasa'i narrated in the Book of Walimah in his Sunan, from 'Ali ibn al-Husayn al-Darhami [in B: "al-Dahrami"], from 'Abd al-A'la, from Sa'id ibn Abi 'Arubah, from Qatadah, from Shahr ibn Hawshab, from 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Ghanm, from Abu Hurayrah, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) went out while they were mentioning the mushroom, and some of them were saying it is the smallpox of the earth, so he said: "The mushroom is of the manna, and its water is a cure for the eye" [Sunan al-Nasa'i al-Kubra no. (6670)].

It was also narrated from Shahr ibn Hawshab, from Abu Sa'id and Jabir, as Imam Ahmad said: Asbat ibn Muhammad narrated to us, al-A'mash narrated to us, from Ja'far ibn Iyas, from Shahr ibn Hawshab, from Jabir ibn 'Abd Allah and Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, both of whom said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "The mushroom is of the manna, and its water is a cure for the eye, and the 'ajwah is from Paradise and it is a cure from poison" [al-Musnad (3/48)].

al-Nasa'i said in the Book of Walimah also: Muhammad ibn Bashshar narrated to us, Muhammad ibn Ja'far narrated to us, Shu'bah narrated to us, from Abu Bishr Ja'far ibn Iyas, from Shahr ibn Hawshab, from Abu Sa'id and Jabir, may Allah be pleased with them both, that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "The mushroom is of the manna, and its water is a cure for the eye" [I have not found it in the printed Sunan al-Nasa'i al-Kubra]. Then he narrated it also, and Ibn Majah, through routes from al-A'mash, from Abu Bishr, from Shahr, from them both, with it [Sunan Ibn Majah no. (3453), and I have not found it in the printed Sunan al-Nasa'i al-Kubra].

Both of them (al-Nasa'i and Ibn Majah) narrated it through the hadith of Sa'id ibn Muslim [in B: "Muslimah"], both from al-A'mash, from Ja'far ibn Iyas, from Abu Nadrah, from Abu Sa'id, and al-Nasa'i added: [and the hadith of] Jabir, from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "The mushroom is of the manna, and its water is a cure for the eye" [Sunan al-Nasa'i al-Kubra nos. (6676, 6677) and Sunan Ibn Majah no. (3453), but in al-Nasa'i it occurs from Jarir from al-A'mash, and Allah knows best].

Ibn Mardawayh narrated it from Ahmad ibn 'Uthman, from 'Abbas al-Duri, from Lahiq ibn Sawab [in B: "Sawan"], from 'Ammar ibn Ruzayq [in B: "Zurayq"], from al-A'mash, like Ibn Majah.

Ibn Mardawayh also said: Ahmad ibn 'Uthman narrated to us, 'Abbas al-Duri narrated to us, al-Hasan [in B: "al-Husayn"] ibn al-Rabi' narrated to us, Abu al-Ahwas narrated to us, from al-A'mash, from al-Minhal ibn 'Amr, from 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Abi Layla, from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) came out to us with mushrooms in his hand, and said: "The mushroom is of the manna, and its water is a cure for the eye."

Commentary of Ibn Kathir (Tafsir al-Quran al-'Azim) on surah 2, verse 57 (part 2 of 2):

Al-Nasa'i also narrated it from 'Amr ibn Mansur, from al-Hasan ibn al-Rabi' [[I have not found it in the printed edition of Sunan al-Nasa'i al-Kubra.]] Then [he narrated it] [[Addition from manuscripts J, T, A, W.]] Ibn Mardawayh. He also narrated it from 'Abdullah ibn Ishaq, from al-Hasan ibn Salam, from 'Ubaydullah ibn Musa, from Shayban [[In manuscript J: "Sufyan".]] from al-A'mash, with the same wording. Likewise, al-Nasa'i narrated it from Ahmad ibn 'Uthman ibn Hakim, from 'Ubaydullah ibn Musa [with the same wording] [[Addition from manuscripts J, T, A.]] [[Sunan al-Nasa'i al-Kubra, no. (6678).]].

It has also been narrated from the hadith of Anas ibn Malik, may Allah be pleased with him, as Ibn Mardawayh said:

Muhammad ibn 'Abdullah ibn Ibrahim narrated to us, Hamdun ibn Ahmad narrated to us, Hawthara ibn Ashras narrated to us, Hammad narrated to us, from Shu'ayb ibn al-Habhab [[In J: "Ibn al-Hujjab", and in A: "Ibn al-Hajjaj".]], from Anas: that the Companions of the Messenger of Allah [[In J: "the Companions of the Prophet".]] ﷺ disputed [[In J: "discussed".]] concerning the tree that was uprooted from the surface of the earth, having no stability (Qur'an 14:26), and some of them said: "We think it is the kam'ah (truffle)." The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "The kam'ah is from al-manna, and its water is a cure for the eye, and the 'ajwah is from Paradise, and in it is a cure for poison." [[Ibn 'Adi narrated it in al-Kamil (2/370) through the chain of Hassan ibn Sayyah, from Thabit, from Anas, with similar wording.]]

This hadith is preserved, its origin being the narration of Hammad ibn Salamah. al-Tirmidhi and al-Nasa'i narrated some of this through his chain, and Allah knows best [[In J: "and Allah, blessed is He, knows best".]] [[Sunan al-Tirmidhi, no. (3119), and Sunan al-Nasa'i al-Kubra, no. (11262).]].

[It] [[Addition from manuscript T.]] has been narrated from Shahr, from Ibn 'Abbas, as al-Nasa'i also narrated in (the book of) al-Walima, from Abu Bakr Ahmad ibn 'Ali ibn Sa'id, from 'Abdullah ibn 'Awn al-Kharraz, from Abu 'Ubaydah al-Haddad, from 'Abd al-Jalil ibn 'Atiyyah, from Shahr, from 'Abdullah ibn 'Abbas, from the Prophet ﷺ, who said: "The kam'ah is from al-manna, and its water is a cure for the eye." [[Sunan al-Nasa'i al-Kubra, no. (6669).]].

As you see, it has been reported with variations from Shahr ibn Hawshab. In my view it is possible that he memorised it and narrated it through all these routes, and that he heard it from some of the Companions and conveyed it on the authority of some of them, for the chains leading to him are sound, and he does not deliberately lie. The origin of the hadith is preserved from the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, as has already been mentioned through the narration of Sa'id ibn Zayd.

As for the quail (salwa), 'Ali ibn Abi Talhah said, from Ibn 'Abbas: "The salwa is a bird similar to the summani (quail), which they used to eat."

al-Suddi said, in a report he mentioned from Abu Malik and from Abu Salih, from Ibn 'Abbas, and from Murrah, from Ibn Mas'ud, and from some Companions: "The salwa is a bird resembling the summani."

Ibn Abi Hatim said: al-Hasan ibn Muhammad ibn al-Sabbah narrated to us, 'Abd al-Samad ibn 'Abd al-Warith narrated to us, Qurrah ibn Khalid narrated to us, from Jahdam, from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "The salwa is the summani."

Likewise said Mujahid, al-Sha'bi, al-Dahhak, al-Hasan, 'Ikrimah, and al-Rabi' ibn Anas, may Allah have mercy on them.

And from 'Ikrimah: "As for the salwa, it is a bird like a bird that exists in Paradise, larger than a sparrow, or thereabouts."

Qatadah said: "The salwa is from a bird of reddish colour, which the south wind brings to them. Each man would slaughter from it what sufficed him for that day, and if he exceeded that, it spoiled and nothing remained with him. But on the sixth day, which precedes their Friday, he would take what sufficed him for the sixth and seventh days, because it was a day of worship in which he did not travel for anything or seek it."

Wahb ibn Munabbih said: "The salwa is a fat bird like a pigeon, which would come to them, and they would take from it from Sabbath to Sabbath." In another report from Wahb, he said: "The Children of Israel asked Musa, peace be upon him, for meat, and Allah said: 'I shall feed them from the least meat known on earth.' So He sent a wind upon them, and it scattered the salwa, which is the summan, near their dwellings, a mile by a mile, a spear's length high towards the sky. They stored some for the morrow, and the meat rotted and the bread turned sour."

al-Suddi said: "When the Children of Israel entered the wilderness (al-tih), they said to Musa, peace be upon him: 'How shall we manage with what is here? Where is the food?' So Allah sent down upon them the manna, which would fall upon the ginger tree (al-zanjabil) and the salwa, which is a bird resembling the summan but larger than it. One of them would come and look at the bird, and if it was fat he would slaughter it, and if not he would release it, and when it grew fat he would come to it. They said: 'This is food, but where is the drink?' So Musa was commanded, and he struck the rock with his staff, and there gushed forth from it twelve springs, and each tribe drank from its spring. They said: 'This is drink, but where is the shade?' So the cloud overshadowed them. They said: 'This is shade, but where is the clothing?' So their garments would grow longer with them as children's do, and no garment of theirs would tear." This is the saying of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿And We shaded you with the cloud and sent down upon you the manna and the quail﴾ and His saying ﴿And when Musa asked for water for his people, We said: Strike the rock with your staff; and there gushed forth from it twelve springs. Every people knew its drinking place﴾ (Qur'an 2:60).

It has also been narrated from Wahb ibn Munabbih and 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Zayd ibn Aslam something similar to what al-Suddi said.

Sunayd said, from Hajjaj, from Ibn Jurayj, who said: Ibn 'Abbas said: "Garments were created for them in the wilderness that would not tear nor become soiled." Ibn Jurayj said: "When a man took from the manna and the salwa more than a day's food, it spoiled, except that on Friday they would take the food for Saturday, and it would not become spoiled in the morning."

[Ibn 'Atiyyah said: "The salwa is a bird, by the consensus (ijma') of the exegetes (mufassirun). al-Hudhali erred in his saying that it is honey, and he recited in support of that:

And he swore to her by Allah, earnestly, that you are sweeter than the salwa when it is roasted..."

He said: "So he thought that the salwa was honey." al-Qurtubi said: "The claim of consensus is not valid, because the historian, one of the scholars of language and tafsir, said that it is honey, and he cited this verse of al-Hudhali as evidence, and mentioned that it is so in the dialect of Kinanah, because one is consoled (yusla) by it, and from it comes the 'Spring of Salwan' (ayn Sulwan)." al-Jawhari said: "al-Salwa is honey," and he also cited the verse of al-Hudhali. "Al-sulwanah," with a damma, is a bead (kharazah); they used to say that when rainwater is poured over it and the lovesick person drinks it, he is consoled (salā). The poet said:

I drank over a sulwanah water of a cloud,
So by the new life, O Mayy, I do not console myself...

The name of that water is al-sulwan. Some of them said: "al-Sulwan is a medicine that cures the grieving so that he is consoled, and physicians call it (mufarrih, the exhilarator)." They said: "al-Salwa is also a collective noun with the form of the singular, as one says 'summani' for the singular and the plural, and 'diflā' likewise." al-Khalil said: "Its singular is salwah," and he recited:

And indeed, at the remembrance of you a trembling overtakes me,
As the salwah shakes off the wetness of the rain...

al-Kisa'i said: "al-Salwa is singular, and its plural is salawi." al-Qurtubi transmitted all of this.] [[Addition from manuscripts J, T, B, A, W.]].

* *

The saying of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿Eat of the good things with which We have provided you﴾ is an imperative of permission, guidance, and favour. And His saying: ﴿and they did not wrong Us, but they were wronging themselves﴾ (Qur'an 2:57) means: We commanded them to eat of what We had provided them and to worship, as He said: ﴿Eat of the provision of your Lord and be grateful to Him﴾ (Qur'an 34:15). But they disobeyed and disbelieved, and so they wronged themselves, and this despite the clear signs and the decisive miracles and the extraordinary acts of custom they witnessed. And from here becomes clear the excellence of the Companions of Muhammad ﷺ, and may Allah be pleased with them, over all the companions of the prophets, in their patience, steadfastness, and their lack of obstinacy. Just as they were with him on his journeys and campaigns, among them the year of Tabuk, in that intense heat, scorching hardship and exertion, they did not ask for the breaking of custom nor the bringing about of a matter, although that would have been easy for the Messenger ﷺ. But when hunger afflicted them, they asked him to increase their food, so they gathered what they had, and it came to the amount of a sheep's kneeling place (mabrak al-shah). He invoked Allah over it, and commanded them, and they filled every vessel they had. Likewise, when they needed water, he asked Allah, the Exalted, and a cloud came and rained upon them, and they drank, watered the camels, and filled their water-skins. Then they looked, and behold, it had not gone beyond the camp. This is the most perfect form of following: walking with the decree of Allah, together with following the Messenger, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him.

Allah, exalted is He, rebukes them for their reluctance to fight in jihad and to enter the Holy Land (ٱلْأَرْضُ ٱلْمُقَدَّسَة, al-ard al-muqaddasah), when they came out of the land of Egypt in the company of Musa, peace be upon him. They were commanded to enter the Holy Land, which was an inheritance for them from their father Israel, and to fight those in it of the disbelieving Amalekites. But they shrank back from fighting them, grew weak, and lost heart. So Allah made them wander in the wilderness (al-tih) as a punishment for them, as He mentioned in Surah al-Ma'idah. For this reason, the more correct of the two opinions is that this town is Bayt al-Maqdis (Jerusalem), as stated by al-Suddi, al-Rabi' ibn Anas, Qatadah, [Abu Muslim al-Isfahani and others. Allah the Exalted has said: ﴿O my people, enter the Holy Land which Allah has prescribed for you﴾ and the verses that follow] [Al-Ma'idah: 21-24].

And others said: it is Ariha (Jericho), [and this is related from Ibn Abbas and Abd al-Rahman ibn Zayd]. But this is far-fetched, because it is not on their route, for they were heading to Bayt al-Maqdis, not Ariha. [Even further from this is the view of those who held that it is Egypt, related by Fakhr al-Din in his tafsir. The correct view is the first, because it is Bayt al-Maqdis.] This happened when they came out of the wilderness after forty years with Yusha' ibn Nun, peace be upon him, and Allah granted them the conquest on a Friday evening, and the sun was held back for them that day briefly until the conquest was achieved. As for Ariha, it was a town not targeted by the Children of Israel. When they conquered it, they were commanded to enter the gate, the gate of the town, ﴿prostrating﴾, meaning in gratitude to Allah the Exalted for what He had bestowed upon them of conquest and victory, the return of their land to them, and their rescue from wandering and misguidance.

Al-Awfi related in his tafsir, from Ibn Abbas, that he used to say concerning His words ﴿And enter the gate prostrating﴾: it means bowing (rukka').

Ibn Jarir said: Muhammad ibn Bashshar narrated to us, Abu Ahmad al-Zubayri narrated to us, Sufyan narrated to us, from al-A'mash, from al-Minhal ibn Amr, and from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, from Ibn Abbas concerning His words ﴿And enter the gate prostrating﴾, he said: bowing (ruka'an), from a small gate.

Al-Hakim narrated it from the hadith of Sufyan, with this chain. Ibn Abi Hatim narrated it from the hadith of Sufyan, who is al-Thawri, with this chain. And he added: so they entered from their backsides.

[Al-Hasan al-Basri said: they were commanded to prostrate upon their faces while entering. Al-Razi considered this unlikely, and related from some of them that the meaning of prostration here is humility, since it cannot be taken literally.]

Khusayf said: Ikrimah said, Ibn Abbas said: the gate was facing the qiblah.

Mujahid, al-Suddi, Qatadah, and al-Dahhak [and Ibn Abbas] said: it is the gate of al-Hittah, from the gate of Iliya' in Bayt al-Maqdis. [Al-Razi related from some of them that it was the gate of one of the quarters of the town.]

Khusayf said: Ikrimah said: Ibn Abbas said: they entered sideways. Al-Suddi said, from Abu Sa'id al-Azdi, from Abu al-Kunud, from Abdullah ibn Mas'ud: It was said to them, "Enter the gate prostrating," so they entered with their heads raised (muqni'i ru'usihim), that is, lifting their heads, contrary to what they were commanded.

* *

As for His words ﴿And say: Hittah﴾, al-Thawri narrated from al-A'mash, from al-Minhal, from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, from Ibn Abbas: ﴿And say: Hittah﴾, he said: forgiveness; seek forgiveness.

It is related from Ata', al-Hasan, Qatadah, and al-Rabi' ibn Anas, something similar.

Al-Dahhak said, from Ibn Abbas: ﴿And say: Hittah﴾, he said: say, "This matter is true, as you were told."

Ikrimah said: say, "There is no god but Allah."

Al-Awza'i said: Ibn Abbas wrote to a man whom he named, asking him about the words of the Exalted: ﴿And say: Hittah﴾. He wrote back to him: acknowledge your sin.

Al-Hasan and Qatadah said: that is, "Remove from us our sins."

﴿We will forgive you your sins, and We will increase the doers of good﴾. This is the response to the command: that is, if you do what We have commanded you, We will forgive you your misdeeds and multiply your good deeds.

The summary of the matter: they were commanded to humble themselves before Allah the Exalted at the conquest, by action and by speech, to acknowledge their sins and seek forgiveness for them, and to be grateful for the blessing at that time, and to hasten to that, which is beloved to Allah the Exalted, as He said: ﴿When the help of Allah comes and the conquest, and you see the people entering the religion of Allah in multitudes, then glorify the praise of your Lord and seek His forgiveness; indeed, He is ever Accepting of repentance﴾ [Surah al-Nasr]. Some of the Companions explained it as increasing in remembrance and seeking forgiveness at the time of conquest and victory. Ibn Abbas explained it as meaning that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was informed that his death was near at that time, and Umar [ibn al-Khattab] (may Allah be pleased with him) confirmed this interpretation. There is no contradiction between his being commanded to do this at that time and his noble soul being informed of his passing. For this reason, he, peace be upon him, would show great humility at the time of victory, as it is related that on the day of the conquest of Makkah, entering it from the upper pass (al-Thaniyyah al-'Ulya), he was deeply humble before his Lord, such that his beard touched the saddle-front of his mount, thanking Allah for that. Then when he entered the city, he performed ghusl and prayed eight rak'ahs, and that was in the forenoon. Some said: this is the Duha prayer; others said: rather, it is the prayer of the Conquest. Therefore, scholars recommended that an imam or commander, upon conquering a town, pray eight rak'ahs at the moment of his first entering, as Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas (may Allah be pleased with him) did when he entered the Iwan of Khosrow and prayed eight rak'ahs there. The correct view is that he separates every two rak'ahs with a salam; it was also said that he prays them all with one salam. And Allah knows best.

* *

As for His words the Exalted: ﴿But those who did wrong substituted a saying other than that which had been said to them﴾, al-Bukhari said: Muhammad narrated to me, Abd al-Rahman ibn Mahdi narrated to us, from Ibn al-Mubarak, from Ma'mar, from Hammam ibn Munabbih, from Abu Hurayrah (may Allah be pleased with him), from the Prophet (ﷺ) who said: "It was said to the Children of Israel: ﴿Enter the gate prostrating and say: Hittah﴾, but they entered crawling on their backsides, and they changed it and said: 'Hittah': a grain in a hair" [Sahih al-Bukhari, no. 4479].

It was narrated by al-Nasa'i from Muhammad ibn Isma'il ibn Ibrahim, from Abd al-Rahman ibn Mahdi, with it as a mawquf (ending with a Companion), and from Muhammad ibn Ubayd ibn Muhammad, from Ibn al-Mubarak, with part of it musnad (traced to the Prophet), concerning His words ﴿Hittah﴾: he said: they changed it, and said: "Habbah" [Sunan al-Nasa'i al-Kubra, no. 10990]. [In one version: "Hintah".]

Abd al-Razzaq said: Ma'mar informed us, from Hammam ibn Munabbih, that he heard Abu Hurayrah say: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Allah said to the Children of Israel: ﴿And enter the gate prostrating and say: Hittah, We will forgive you your sins﴾, but they changed it, and entered the gate crawling on their backsides, and said: 'A grain in a hair [or barley-corn]'."

This is a sahih hadith, narrated by al-Bukhari from Ishaq ibn Nasr, by Muslim from Muhammad ibn Rafi', and by al-Tirmidhi from Abd ibn Humayd, all of them from Abd al-Razzaq, with this chain [Sahih al-Bukhari no. 4641; Sahih Muslim no. 3015; Sunan al-Tirmidhi no. 2956]. Al-Tirmidhi said: hasan sahih.

Muhammad ibn Ishaq said: Their change was as Salih ibn Kaysan narrated to me, from Salih, mawla of al-Tawama, from Abu Hurayrah, and from one whom I do not accuse, from Ibn Abbas, that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "They entered the gate, which they were commanded to enter prostrating, crawling on their backsides, and they were saying: 'Hintah fi Shu'ayrah (wheat in barley)'" [It was related by al-Tabarani in his tafsir (2/112) from Muhammad ibn Ishaq, from Salih ibn Kaysan, from Abu Hurayrah; from Muhammad ibn Abi Muhammad, from Sa'id or Ikrimah, from Ibn Abbas].

Abu Dawud said: Ahmad ibn Salih narrated to us, and Sulayman ibn Dawud narrated to us, Abd Allah ibn Wahb narrated to us, Hisham ibn Sa'd narrated to us, from Zayd ibn Aslam, from Ata' ibn Yasar, from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri (may Allah be pleased with him), from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "Allah said to the Children of Israel: ﴿Enter the gate prostrating and say: Hittah, We will forgive you your sins﴾." Then Abu Dawud said: Ja'far ibn Musafir narrated to us, Ibn Abi Fudayk narrated to us, from Hisham ibn Sa'd, the like of it [Sunan Abi Dawud no. 4006].

Thus he narrated it alone in the Book of Letters (Kitab al-Huruf), in abridged form.

Ibn Mardawayh said: Abd Allah ibn Ja'far narrated to us, Ibrahim ibn Mahdi narrated to us, Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn al-Mundhir al-Qazzaz narrated to us, Muhammad ibn Isma'il ibn Abi Fudayk narrated to us, from Hisham ibn Sa'd, from Zayd ibn Aslam, from Ata' ibn Yasar, from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, who said: We travelled with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) until, at the end of the night, we passed through a mountain pass called Dhat al-Handhal. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "The likeness of this pass tonight is only like the likeness of the gate about which Allah said to the Children of Israel: ﴿Enter the gate prostrating and say: Hittah, We will forgive you your sins﴾" [It was related by al-Bazzar in his Musnad (no. 1812) from Ishaq ibn Bahlul, from Muhammad ibn Isma'il ibn Abi Fudayk with something similar; al-Haythami said in al-Majma' (6/144): "its narrators are trustworthy"].

Al-Thawri said, from Abu Ishaq, from al-Bara': ﴿The foolish among the people will say﴾ [al-Baqarah: 142]: the Jews said: It was said to them, "Enter the gate prostrating," and he said: "bowing," and "say: Hittah," that is, forgiveness, so they entered on their backsides, and began saying: "Hintah hamra' fiha shu'ayrah (red wheat with a barley-grain in it)." That is the saying of Allah the Exalted: ﴿But those who did wrong substituted a saying other than that which had been said to them﴾.

Al-Thawri said, from al-Suddi, from Abu Sa'd al-Azdi, from Abu al-Kunud, from Ibn Mas'ud: ﴿And say: Hittah﴾, so they said: "Hintah habbah hamra' fiha shu'ayrah (a red grain of wheat with a barley-grain in it)," and Allah revealed: ﴿But those who did wrong substituted a saying other than that which had been said to them﴾.

Asbat said, from al-Suddi, from Murrah, from Ibn Mas'ud, that he said: they said: "Huththi sim'ata azbah mazba," which in Arabic means: a red grain of wheat, pierced, with a black hair in it. That is His saying: ﴿But those who did wrong substituted a saying other than that which had been said to them﴾.

Al-Thawri said, from al-A'mash, from al-Minhal, from Sa'id, from Ibn Abbas concerning His words ﴿Enter the gate prostrating﴾: bowing, from a small gate; they entered from their backsides, and said: "Hintah," and that is His saying: ﴿But those who did wrong substituted a saying other than that which had been said to them﴾.

Similarly it is related from Ata', Mujahid, Ikrimah, al-Dahhak, al-Hasan, Qatadah, al-Rabi' ibn Anas, and Yahya ibn Rafi'.

The summary of what the commentators have mentioned, and what the context indicates, is that they changed the command of Allah to them concerning humility in word and deed. They were commanded to enter prostrating, but they entered crawling on their buttocks, dragging themselves from their rear while raising their heads. They were commanded to say "ḥiṭṭah" (remove [our sins]), meaning "Lord, remove our sins from us," but they mocked and said "ḥinṭah fī sha'rah" (wheat in a hair). This is the utmost of opposition and defiance. For this reason Allah sent down upon them His might and His punishment because of their *fisq* (defiant disobedience), meaning their departure from His obedience. For this reason He said: ﴿So We sent down upon those who wronged a punishment from the sky because they used to defy Allah's command﴾.

Al-Ḍaḥḥāk narrated from Ibn ʿAbbās: Everything in the Book of Allah that is called *rijz* means punishment.

It was narrated similarly from Mujāhid, Abū Mālik, al-Suddī, al-Ḥasan and Qatādah that it means punishment. Abū al-ʿĀliyah said: *al-rijz* is anger. al-Shaʿbī said: *al-rijz* is either the plague (*ṭāʿūn*) or hail. Saʿīd ibn Jubayr said: it is the plague.

Ibn Abī Ḥātim said: Abū Saʿīd al-Ashajj narrated to us, Wakīʿ narrated to us, from Sufyān, from Ḥabīb ibn Abī Thābit, from Ibrāhīm ibn Saʿd (meaning Ibn Abī Waqqāṣ), from Saʿd ibn Mālik, Usāmah ibn Zayd and Khuzaymah ibn Thābit, may Allah be pleased with them, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "The plague is a *rijz* (affliction) and a punishment with which those before you were punished."¹

Al-Nasāʾī narrated it similarly from the ḥadīth of Sufyān al-Thawrī with the same chain.² The origin of the ḥadīth is in the two Ṣaḥīḥs (Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī and Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim), from the ḥadīth of Ḥabīb ibn Abī Thābit: "If you hear of the plague in a land, do not enter it," and so on.³

Ibn Jarīr said: Yūnus ibn ʿAbd al-Aʿlā narrated to me, from Ibn Wahb, from Yūnus, from al-Zuhrī, who said: ʿĀmir ibn Saʿd ibn Abī Waqqāṣ informed me, from Usāmah ibn Zayd, from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), who said: "This pain and sickness is a *rijz* with which some nations before you were punished."⁴ This ḥadīth is originally recorded in the two Ṣaḥīḥs, from the ḥadīth of al-Zuhrī, and from the ḥadīth of Mālik, from Muḥammad ibn al-Munkadir and Sālim Abū al-Naḍr, from ʿĀmir ibn Saʿd, in similar wording.⁵

[In one version: "Hintah".]

Abd al-Razzaq said: Ma'mar informed us, from Hammam ibn Munabbih, that he heard Abu Hurayrah say: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Allah said to the Children of Israel: ﴿And enter the gate prostrating and say: Hittah, We will forgive you your sins﴾, but they changed it, and entered the gate crawling on their backsides, and said: 'A grain in a hair [or barley-corn]'."

This is a sahih hadith, narrated by al-Bukhari from Ishaq ibn Nasr, by Muslim from Muhammad ibn Rafi', and by al-Tirmidhi from Abd ibn Humayd, all of them from Abd al-Razzaq, with this chain [Sahih al-Bukhari no. 4641; Sahih Muslim no. 3015; Sunan al-Tirmidhi no. 2956]. Al-Tirmidhi said: hasan sahih.

Muhammad ibn Ishaq said: Their change was as Salih ibn Kaysan narrated to me, from Salih, mawla of al-Tawama, from Abu Hurayrah, and from one whom I do not accuse, from Ibn Abbas, that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "They entered the gate, which they were commanded to enter prostrating, crawling on their backsides, and they were saying: 'Hintah fi Shu'ayrah (wheat in barley)'" [It was related by al-Tabarani in his tafsir (2/112) from Muhammad ibn Ishaq, from Salih ibn Kaysan, from Abu Hurayrah; from Muhammad ibn Abi Muhammad, from Sa'id or Ikrimah, from Ibn Abbas].

Abu Dawud said: Ahmad ibn Salih narrated to us, and Sulayman ibn Dawud narrated to us, Abd Allah ibn Wahb narrated to us, Hisham ibn Sa'd narrated to us, from Zayd ibn Aslam, from Ata' ibn Yasar, from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri (may Allah be pleased with him), from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "Allah said to the Children of Israel: ﴿Enter the gate prostrating and say: Hittah, We will forgive you your sins﴾." Then Abu Dawud said: Ja'far ibn Musafir narrated to us, Ibn Abi Fudayk narrated to us, from Hisham ibn Sa'd, the like of it [Sunan Abi Dawud no. 4006].

Thus he narrated it alone in the Book of Letters (Kitab al-Huruf), in abridged form.

Ibn Mardawayh said: Abd Allah ibn Ja'far narrated to us, Ibrahim ibn Mahdi narrated to us, Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn al-Mundhir al-Qazzaz narrated to us, Muhammad ibn Isma'il ibn Abi Fudayk narrated to us, from Hisham ibn Sa'd, from Zayd ibn Aslam, from Ata' ibn Yasar, from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, who said: We travelled with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) until, at the end of the night, we passed through a mountain pass called Dhat al-Handhal. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "The likeness of this pass tonight is only like the likeness of the gate about which Allah said to the Children of Israel: ﴿Enter the gate prostrating and say: Hittah, We will forgive you your sins﴾" [It was related by al-Bazzar in his Musnad (no. 1812) from Ishaq ibn Bahlul, from Muhammad ibn Isma'il ibn Abi Fudayk with something similar; al-Haythami said in al-Majma' (6/144): "its narrators are trustworthy"].

Al-Thawri said, from Abu Ishaq, from al-Bara': ﴿The foolish among the people will say﴾ [al-Baqarah: 142]: the Jews said: It was said to them, "Enter the gate prostrating," and he said: "bowing," and "say: Hittah," that is, forgiveness, so they entered on their backsides, and began saying: "Hintah hamra' fiha shu'ayrah (red wheat with a barley-grain in it)." That is the saying of Allah the Exalted: ﴿But those who did wrong substituted a saying other than that which had been said to them﴾.

Al-Thawri said, from al-Suddi, from Abu Sa'd al-Azdi, from Abu al-Kunud, from Ibn Mas'ud: ﴿And say: Hittah﴾, so they said: "Hintah habbah hamra' fiha shu'ayrah (a red grain of wheat with a barley-grain in it)," and Allah revealed: ﴿But those who did wrong substituted a saying other than that which had been said to them﴾.

Asbat said, from al-Suddi, from Murrah, from Ibn Mas'ud, that he said: they said: "Huththi sim'ata azbah mazba," which in Arabic means: a red grain of wheat, pierced, with a black hair in it. That is His saying: ﴿But those who did wrong substituted a saying other than that which had been said to them﴾.

Al-Thawri said, from al-A'mash, from al-Minhal, from Sa'id, from Ibn Abbas concerning His words ﴿Enter the gate prostrating﴾: bowing, from a small gate; they entered from their backsides, and said: "Hintah," and that is His saying: ﴿But those who did wrong substituted a saying other than that which had been said to them﴾.

Similarly it is related from Ata', Mujahid, Ikrimah, al-Dahhak, al-Hasan, Qatadah, al-Rabi' ibn Anas, and Yahya ibn Rafi'.

The summary of what the commentators have mentioned, and what the context indicates, is that they changed the command of Allah to them concerning humility in word and deed. They were commanded to enter prostrating, but they entered crawling on their buttocks, dragging themselves from their rear while raising their heads. They were commanded to say "ḥiṭṭah" (remove [our sins]), meaning "Lord, remove our sins from us," but they mocked and said "ḥinṭah fī sha'rah" (wheat in a hair). This is the utmost of opposition and defiance. For this reason Allah sent down upon them His might and His punishment because of their *fisq* (defiant disobedience), meaning their departure from His obedience. For this reason He said: ﴿So We sent down upon those who wronged a punishment from the sky because they used to defy Allah's command﴾.

Al-Ḍaḥḥāk narrated from Ibn ʿAbbās: Everything in the Book of Allah that is called *rijz* means punishment.

It was narrated similarly from Mujāhid, Abū Mālik, al-Suddī, al-Ḥasan and Qatādah that it means punishment. Abū al-ʿĀliyah said: *al-rijz* is anger. al-Shaʿbī said: *al-rijz* is either the plague (*ṭāʿūn*) or hail. Saʿīd ibn Jubayr said: it is the plague.

Ibn Abī Ḥātim said: Abū Saʿīd al-Ashajj narrated to us, Wakīʿ narrated to us, from Sufyān, from Ḥabīb ibn Abī Thābit, from Ibrāhīm ibn Saʿd (meaning Ibn Abī Waqqāṣ), from Saʿd ibn Mālik, Usāmah ibn Zayd and Khuzaymah ibn Thābit, may Allah be pleased with them, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "The plague is a *rijz* (affliction) and a punishment with which those before you were punished."¹

Al-Nasāʾī narrated it similarly from the ḥadīth of Sufyān al-Thawrī with the same chain.² The origin of the ḥadīth is in the two Ṣaḥīḥs (Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī and Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim), from the ḥadīth of Ḥabīb ibn Abī Thābit: "If you hear of the plague in a land, do not enter it," and so on.³

Ibn Jarīr said: Yūnus ibn ʿAbd al-Aʿlā narrated to me, from Ibn Wahb, from Yūnus, from al-Zuhrī, who said: ʿĀmir ibn Saʿd ibn Abī Waqqāṣ informed me, from Usāmah ibn Zayd, from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), who said: "This pain and sickness is a *rijz* with which some nations before you were punished."⁴ This ḥadīth is originally recorded in the two Ṣaḥīḥs, from the ḥadīth of al-Zuhrī, and from the ḥadīth of Mālik, from Muḥammad ibn al-Munkadir and Sālim Abū al-Naḍr, from ʿĀmir ibn Saʿd, in similar wording.⁵
