He, exalted is He, says: Remember My favour upon you in answering your Prophet Musa (peace be upon him) when he asked Me to give you water, and in My making water easy for you, bringing it forth for you from a rock that was carried with you, and in My causing water to gush forth for you from it, from twelve springs, one spring for each tribe (sibt) of yours, each one known to them. So eat of the manna and quail, and drink of this water which I caused to flow for you without any effort or toil on your part. And worship the One who subjected all of that to you. ﴿And do not commit corruption on the earth, causing mischief﴾, meaning: do not meet the blessings with disobedience, lest they be taken away from you.

The commentators have elaborated on this in their discourses, as Ibn 'Abbas said: A square rock was placed among them, and Musa (peace be upon him) was commanded to strike it with his staff, and twelve springs gushed forth from it, three springs on each side of it. He made known to each tribe its spring, from which they drank. Wherever they halted, they found the water with them in the place where it had been at the first stopping place.

This is part of the hadith that al-Nasa'i, Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated, which is the long hadith of al-Futun (the trials) [[It will come in full in the tafsir of Surat Ta-Ha.]].

'Atiyyah al-'Awfi said: A rock was made for them, like the head of a bull, which was carried on a bull. When they alighted at a stopping place, they set it down, and Musa struck it with his staff, and twelve springs gushed forth from it. When they journeyed, they loaded it onto a bull, and the water remained [with them].

'Uthman ibn 'Ata al-Khurasani said, on the authority of his father: Bani Isra'il had a rock. Harun would set it down, and Musa would strike it with the staff.

Qatadah said: It was a rock of Tur (Sinai), from the mountain, which they carried with them. When they alighted, Musa struck it with his staff.

[Al-Zamakhshari said: It was said: It was of marble, a cubit by a cubit. It was said: It was like a man's head. It was said: It was one of the foundations of Paradise, its length ten cubits by the height of Musa. It had two branches that shone in the darkness, and it was carried on a donkey. He said: It was said: Adam brought it down from Paradise, and they inherited it, until it came to Shu'ayb, who gave it to him along with the staff. It was also said: It is the rock on which he placed his garment when he bathed, and Jibril said to him: Lift this rock, for in it is power, and for you in it is a miracle, so he carried it in his bag. Al-Zamakhshari said: It is possible that the definite article (al-) is for the genus, not for a specific referent, meaning: strike the thing that is called a rock. It is related from al-Hasan that He did not command him to strike a particular rock. He said: This is more evident as a miracle and clearer as a proof of power. So he would strike the rock with his staff and it would gush forth, then he would strike it and it would dry up. They said: If Musa lost this rock, we would be thirsty. So Allah revealed to him that he should speak to the stones, and they would gush forth, without his touching them with the staff, so that they might acknowledge it.]

Yahya ibn al-Nadr said: I asked Juwaybir: How did every people know its drinking place? He said: Musa would set down the rock, and a man from each tribe would stand up, and Musa would strike the rock, and twelve springs would gush forth from it, and water would spring from each spring onto a man, and that man would call his tribe to that spring.

Al-Dahhak said: Ibn 'Abbas said: When the Children of Israel were in the wilderness (al-tih), He split rivers for them out of the rock.

Sufyan al-Thawri said, on the authority of Abu Sa'id, on the authority of Ikrimah, on the authority of Ibn 'Abbas, who said: That was in the wilderness. Musa struck the rock for them, and twelve springs of water came out of it, one spring for each tribe of them, from which they drank.

Mujahid said something similar to the saying of Ibn 'Abbas.

This story is similar to the story mentioned in Surat al-A'raf, but that surah is Meccan, which is why the reference to them is in the third person, because Allah, exalted is He, relates that to His Messenger (ﷺ) concerning what He did to them. As for this surah, al-Baqarah, it is Medinan, so the address in it is directed to them. In it He mentioned, in His words: ﴿So there gushed forth from it twelve springs﴾ [al-A'raf: 160], which is the beginning of the gushing forth, and here He mentions what the matter ultimately came to, which is the gushing forth. So the mention of the gushing forth fits here, and that [mention] fits there, and Allah knows best.

There are ten verbal and semantic differences between the two contexts, about which al-Razi asked in his tafsir, and he answered them with what he had. The matter in this is minor, and Allah, blessed and exalted is He, knows best the secrets of His Book.

Allah the Exalted says: "Remember My blessing upon you when I sent down to you the manna and the quails, a good, beneficial, wholesome and easy food. And remember your complaining and your impatience with what I provided for you, and your asking Moses to exchange that for lowly foods of herbs and the like, which you requested."

Al-Hasan al-Basri (may Allah have mercy on him) said: "They became insolent about this, did not endure it patiently, and remembered the life of ease they had been in. They were a people accustomed to lentils, onions, greens and garlic, and they said: ﴿O Moses, we will not endure one kind of food, so call upon your Lord to bring forth for us from what the earth grows: its greens, its cucumbers, its garlic, its lentils and its onions﴾ [while they were eating the manna and the quails, because it did not change or vary each day, so it was like one kind of food]. The greens, cucumbers, lentils and onions are all well known. As for "al-fum" (garlic/wheat), the early scholars differed about its meaning. In the reading of Ibn Mas'ud it appears as "wa-thumiha" with the letter thā', and Mujahid, in the narration of Layth ibn Abi Sulaym from him, likewise explained it as garlic. So too did al-Rabi' ibn Anas and Sa'id ibn Jubayr.

Ibn Abi Hatim said: My father narrated to us, 'Amr ibn Rafi' narrated to us, Abu 'Umara Ya'qub ibn Ishaq al-Basri narrated to us, from Yunus, from al-Hasan, regarding His words ﴿wa-fumiha﴾, he said: Ibn 'Abbas said: "It is garlic."

They said: In the ancient language, "fawwimu lana" means "bake for us." Ibn Jarir said: If that is correct, then it is among the interchanged letters, like their saying: "they fell into 'a'thur sharr' and 'a'fur sharr'," and "athafiyy" and "athathiyy," and "maghafir" and "maghathir," and similar words in which the fā' is changed to thā' and the thā' to fā', because their places of articulation are close. And Allah knows best.

Others said: al-Fum is wheat, which is the grain from which bread is made.

Ibn Abi Hatim said: Yunus ibn 'Abd al-A'la narrated to us by reading, Ibn Wahb informed us by reading, Nafi' ibn Abi Nu'aym narrated to me that Ibn 'Abbas was asked about the words of Allah ﴿wa-fumiha﴾: "What is its fum?" He said: "Wheat." Ibn 'Abbas said: "Have you not heard the saying of Uhayha ibn al-Julah when he said:

"I was indeed the richest of people, one person, who came to Medina without a crop of fum."

Ibn Jarir said: 'Ali ibn al-Hasan narrated to us, Muslim al-Jarmi narrated to us, 'Isa ibn Yunus narrated to us, from Rishdin ibn Kurayb, from his father, from Ibn 'Abbas, regarding the words of Allah Most High ﴿wa-fumiha﴾, he said: "al-Fum is wheat in the language of the Banu Hashim."

Likewise said 'Ali ibn Abi Talha, al-Dahhak and 'Ikrima, from Ibn 'Abbas, that al-Fum is wheat.

Sufyan al-Thawri said, from Ibn Juraij, from Mujahid and 'Ata': "﴿wa-fumiha﴾, they both said: and its bread."

Hushaym said, from Yunus, from al-Hasan, and Husayn, from Abu Malik: "﴿wa-fumiha﴾, he said: wheat."

This is also the view of 'Ikrima, al-Suddi, al-Hasan al-Basri, Qatada, 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Zayd ibn Aslam and others. And Allah knows best.

[Al-Jawhari said: al-Fum is wheat. Ibn Duraid said: al-Fum is the ear of grain. Al-Qurtubi related from 'Ata' and Qatada that al-Fum is every grain that is baked into bread. He said: Some said it is chickpeas, a Syrian dialect term, and from it the seller of it is called "fammi," altered from "fumi."]

Al-Bukhari said: "Some said: the grains that are eaten, all of them, are fum."

* *

His words: ﴿He said: Would you exchange what is lower for what is better?﴾ contain a rebuke and reproach to them for what they requested of these lowly foods, given the luxurious life and the wholesome, good, beneficial food they had.

* *

His words: ﴿Go down to a city﴾ are written thus, with tanwin and diptotic declension, with an alif in the Uthmanic mushafs, and this is the reading of the majority with declension.

Ibn Jarir said: I do not consider it permissible to recite otherwise, because the mushafs agree on this.

Ibn 'Abbas said regarding ﴿Go down to a city﴾: "A city among the cities." Ibn Abi Hatim related it from the narration of Abu Sa'id al-Baqqal, Sa'id ibn al-Marzuban, from 'Ikrima, from him.

He said: Something similar is related from al-Suddi, Qatada and al-Rabi' ibn Anas.

Ibn Jarir said: In the reading of Ubayy ibn Ka'b and Ibn Mas'ud, it occurs as "Ihbitu Misra" without idjra, meaning without declension. Then he related from Abu al-'Aliya and al-Rabi' ibn Anas that they explained it as "Misr of Pharaoh."

Likewise Ibn Abi Hatim related it from Abu al-'Aliya, and from al-A'mash as well.

Ibn Jarir said: It is possible that the intended meaning is the Misr of Pharaoh, even on the reading with idjra, and that this would be by way of following the writing of the mushaf, as in His words: ﴿qawarira, qawarira﴾ [al-Insan: 15-16]. Then he hesitated about what is intended: is it Pharaoh's Egypt or a city among the cities?

What he said in this is open to question. The truth is that what is intended is a city among the cities, as related from Ibn 'Abbas and others, and the meaning according to this is that Moses, peace be upon him, was saying to them: "What you have asked for is not a rare matter; rather it is abundant in any town you enter. Given its lowliness and abundance in the cities, it is not worth my asking Allah for it." For this reason He said: ﴿Would you exchange what is lower for what is better? Go down to a city, for you will have what you asked for﴾, that is, what you sought. Since their request was from insolence and arrogance and there was no necessity for it, they were not granted it. And Allah knows best.

﴿Humiliation and poverty were stamped upon them, and they returned with anger from Allah. That is because they used to disbelieve in the signs of Allah and kill the prophets without right. That is because they disobeyed and used to transgress﴾

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿Humiliation and poverty were stamped upon them﴾, that is, they were imposed upon them and they were bound to them by legislation and decree, meaning they will always be made abject: whoever finds them humbles and disgraces them, and He laid upon them lowliness, and they are, within themselves, abased and submissive.

Al-Dahhak related from Ibn 'Abbas regarding His words ﴿Humiliation and poverty were stamped upon them﴾, he said: "They are the people of the al-nihalat," meaning the people of the jizya.

'Abd al-Razzaq said, from Ma'mar, from al-Hasan and Qatada, regarding His words ﴿were stamped upon them﴾: "They pay the jizya willingly while they are humbled." Al-Dahhak said: ﴿Humiliation was stamped upon them﴾: "The humiliation." Al-Hasan said: "Allah humiliated them so they have no protection, and Allah placed them beneath the feet of the Muslims. This community even overtook them, and the Magians used to impose the jizya upon them."

Abu al-'Aliya, al-Rabi' ibn Anas and al-Suddi said: "Poverty (al-maskana) is destitution." 'Ata' al-'Awfi said: "The kharaj." Al-Dahhak said: "The jizya."

* *

His words: ﴿and they returned with anger from Allah﴾. Al-Dahhak said: "They deserved anger from Allah." Al-Rabi' ibn Anas said: "Anger from Allah settled upon them." Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: "﴿they returned with anger from Allah﴾ means: they incurred wrath." Ibn Jarir said: By His words ﴿they returned with anger from Allah﴾ is meant that they departed and returned; it is not said "ba'u" except connected either with good or with evil. It is said of someone: "ba'a fulan bi-dhanbihi, yabu'u bihi, bawan wa-bawa'an." From this is His words: ﴿I wish that you should bear my sin and your sin﴾ [al-Ma'ida: 29], meaning: you would depart bearing them and return with them, having become upon you rather than me. So the meaning of the statement is: they returned departing, bearing the anger of Allah; anger from Allah had come upon them, and wrath from Allah became due upon them.

* *

His words: ﴿That is because they used to disbelieve in the signs of Allah and kill the prophets without right﴾. He, the Exalted, says: This is what We requited them with of humiliation and poverty, and the descent of anger upon them, because of their arrogance in refusing to follow the truth, their disbelief in the signs of Allah, and their humiliation of the bearers of the law, who are the prophets and their followers. They belittled them to the point that their condition led them to kill them. There is no greater arrogance than this: they disbelieved in the signs of Allah and killed the prophets of Allah without right. For this reason it has come in the hadith agreed upon as authentic that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Pride is rejecting the truth and looking down upon people." [Related by Muslim in his Sahih, no. 91, from the hadith of 'Abd Allah ibn Mas'ud, may Allah be pleased with him.]

Imam Ahmad said: Isma'il narrated to us, from Ibn 'Awn, from 'Amr ibn Sa'id, from Humayd ibn 'Abd al-Rahman, who said: Ibn Mas'ud said: "I used not to be kept away from private conversations, nor from such and such," he said: "So I came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) while with him was Malik ibn Murara al-Rahawi, and I caught him at the end of his talk, and he was saying: 'O Messenger of Allah, I have been granted beauty such as you see, and I do not love that anyone among the people should surpass me by a pair of sandal-straps or more. Is that not transgression?' He said: 'No, that is not transgression; rather transgression is one who is insolent (or said: who despises the truth) and looks down on people.'" That is: rejecting the truth, belittling people, despising them and considering oneself great over them. For this reason, when the Children of Israel committed what they committed of disbelief in the signs of Allah and killing their prophets, Allah brought upon them His irresistible might, and clothed them in humiliation in this world, linked with the humiliation of the Hereafter, as a fitting recompense. [al-Musnad 1/385.]

Abu Dawud al-Tayalisi said: Shu'ba narrated to us, from al-A'mash, from Ibrahim, from Abu Ma'mar, from 'Abd Allah ibn Mas'ud, who said: "The Children of Israel would kill three hundred prophets in a single day, then they would set up their vegetable market at the end of the day."

Imam Ahmad also said: 'Abd al-Samad narrated to us, Aban narrated to us, 'Asim narrated to us, from Abu Wa'il, from 'Abd Allah (meaning Ibn Mas'ud), that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "The most severely punished people on the Day of Resurrection is a man who was killed by a prophet, or who killed a prophet, and a leader of misguidance, and a maker of images among the image-makers." [al-Musnad 1/407.]

* *

His words: ﴿That is because they disobeyed and used to transgress﴾. This is another cause for their recompense with what they were recompensed with: that they used to disobey and transgress. Disobedience is doing what is forbidden, and transgression (i'tida') is exceeding the limit of what is permitted or commanded. And Allah knows best.

When Allah, exalted is He, described the condition of those who opposed His commands, committed what He forbade, transgressed in doing what was not permitted, violated the sacred prohibitions, and the punishment He brought upon them, He then pointed out that whoever among the earlier nations was good and obeyed, for him is the reward of the best (al-husna). The same applies until the Hour is established: everyone who follows the Messenger, the unlettered Prophet, will have eternal happiness, and no fear will be upon them regarding what lies ahead, nor will they grieve over what they leave behind. As Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿Indeed, the allies of Allah – no fear will there be concerning them, nor will they grieve﴾ [Yunus: 62]. And as the angels will say to the believers at the time of death, in His saying: ﴿Indeed, those who say, "Our Lord is Allah," and then remain steadfast – the angels will descend upon them, [saying], "Do not fear and do not grieve, but receive good tidings of Paradise, which you were promised"﴾ [Fussilat: 30].

Ibn Abi Hatim said: My father narrated to us, Ibn Abi Umar al-Adani narrated to us, Sufyan narrated to us, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, who said: Salman said: "I asked the Prophet (ﷺ) about a religious people with whom I had been, and I mentioned their prayers and their worship, so there was revealed: ﴿Indeed, those who believed and those who were Jews and the Christians and the Sabians – whoever believes in Allah and the Last Day﴾ up to the end of the verse."

Al-Suddi said: "﴿Indeed, those who believed and those who were Jews and the Christians and the Sabians – whoever believes in Allah and the Last Day and does righteous deeds﴾ – the verse was revealed concerning the companions of Salman al-Farisi. While he was speaking to the Prophet (ﷺ), he mentioned his companions, and informed him of their news. He said: 'They used to fast, pray, believe in you, and bear witness that you would be sent as a prophet.' When Salman finished praising them, the Prophet of Allah (ﷺ) said to him: 'O Salman, they are among the people of the Fire.' This weighed heavily upon Salman, so Allah revealed this verse. The faith of the Jews was that whoever held fast to the Torah and the way (sunnah) of Musa, peace be upon him, [was saved], until Isa came. When Isa came, whoever held fast to the Torah and followed the way of Musa, but did not abandon it and did not follow Isa, was lost. The faith of the Christians was that whoever among them held fast to the Gospel and the laws of Isa was a believer, accepted from him, until Muhammad (ﷺ) came. Whoever among them did not follow Muhammad (ﷺ) and did not abandon what he had of the way of Isa and the Gospel was lost."

Ibn Abi Hatim also said: It was narrated from Sa'id ibn Jubayr something similar to this.

I say: This does not contradict what Ali ibn Abi Talhah narrated from Ibn Abbas regarding: ﴿Indeed, those who believed and those who were Jews and the Christians and the Sabians – whoever believes in Allah and the Last Day﴾ – the verse. Then Allah revealed after that: ﴿And whoever seeks other than Islam as a religion – it will never be accepted from him, and he, in the Hereafter, will be among the losers﴾ [Al 'Imran: 85].

What Ibn Abbas said is an announcement that Allah will not accept from anyone any path or deed except what conforms to the Shari'ah of Muhammad (ﷺ) after Allah sent him with what He sent him with. As for before that, everyone who followed the Messenger of his time was upon guidance, the right path, and salvation. Thus the Jews were the followers of Musa, peace be upon him, who would judge by the Torah in their time.

The word "Yahud" (Jews) derives from al-hawadah, which means affection (mawaddah), or al-tahawwud, which means repentance (tawbah), as in the saying of Musa, peace be upon him: ﴿Indeed, we have turned back to You﴾ [al-A'raf: 156], meaning: we have repented. So it seems they were named thus originally because of their repentance and their affection for one another.

[It is also said that they are named after Yahudha (Judah), the eldest son of Ya'qub, peace be upon him. Abu Amr ibn al-Ala' said: It is because they "yatahawwadun," that is, they move (sway) while reciting the Torah.]

When Isa (ﷺ) was sent, the Children of Israel were obligated to follow him and submit to him. His companions and the people of his religion are the Christians, and they were named thus for their mutual support (tanasur) among themselves. They are also sometimes called ansar (helpers), as Isa, peace be upon him, said: ﴿Who are my helpers for Allah?' The disciples said, 'We are the helpers of Allah'﴾ [Al 'Imran: 52]. It is also said that they were named so because they settled in a land called Nasirah, as stated by Qatadah and Ibn Juraij, and it is narrated from Ibn Abbas as well. And Allah knows best.

"Al-Nasara" is the plural of Nasran, like nashawa, the plural of nashwan, and sukara, the plural of sakran. A woman is called Nasranah. The poet said:

*A Christian woman who did not incline...*

[The verse is in Tafsir al-Tabari (2/144), and it is by Abu al-Akhzar al-Hamani. This is part of it, and in full it is: "So both of them fell down and prostrated their heads, as a Christian woman prostrates who has not bowed."]

When Allah sent Muhammad (ﷺ) as the seal of the prophets and as a messenger to the children of Adam in general, it became obligatory upon them to believe him in what he informed, to obey him in what he commanded, and to refrain from what he forbade. These are the true believers. The community of Muhammad (ﷺ) was named "believers" because of the abundance of their faith and the strength of their certainty, and because they believe in all the earlier prophets and in the unseen matters yet to come.

As for the Sabians, there has been disagreement concerning them. Sufyan al-Thawri said, from Layth ibn Abi Sulaym, from Mujahid, who said: The Sabians are a people between the Magians, the Jews, and the Christians, having no religion of their own. Ibn Abi Najih also narrated this from him. It was narrated from Ata' and Sa'id ibn Jubayr something similar to this.

Abu al-Aliyah, al-Rabi' ibn Anas, al-Suddi, Abu al-Sha'tha' Jabir ibn Zayd, al-Dahhak, and [Ishaq ibn Rahawayh] said: The Sabians are a sect of the People of the Book who recite the Zabur (Psalms).

[For this reason Abu Hanifah and Ishaq said: There is no harm in eating their slaughtered animals or marrying their women.]

Hushaym narrated from Mutarrif: We were with al-Hakam ibn Utaybah, and a man from Basra narrated to him from al-Hasan that he used to say about the Sabians that they are like the Magians. Al-Hakam said: Did I not inform you of this?

Abd al-Rahman ibn Mahdi said, from Mu'awiyah ibn Abd al-Karim: I heard al-Hasan mention the Sabians, and he said: They are a people who worship the angels.

[Ibn Jarir said: Muhammad ibn Abd al-A'la narrated to us, al-Mu'tamir ibn Sulayman narrated to us, from his father, from al-Hasan, who said: Ziyad informed [us] that the Sabians pray toward the qiblah and perform the five prayers. He said: So he wanted to remove the jizya (poll tax) from them. He said: Then it was later reported to him that they worship the angels.]

Abu Ja'far al-Razi said: It has reached me that the Sabians are a people who worship the angels, recite the Zabur, and pray toward the qiblah.

Similarly said Sa'id ibn Abi Arubah, from Qatadah.

Ibn Abi Hatim said: Yunus ibn Abd al-A'la narrated to us, Ibn Wahb informed us, Ibn Abi al-Zinad informed me, from his father, who said: The Sabians are a people from the direction of Iraq, and they are at Kuthaa. They believe in all the prophets, fast thirty days of every year, and pray toward Yemen five prayers every day.

Wahb ibn Munabbih was asked about the Sabians, and he said: One who knows Allah alone, and has no law to act by, and has not introduced disbelief.

Abd Allah ibn Wahb said: Abd al-Rahman ibn Zayd said: The Sabians are a people of one of the religions. They were in the island of Mosul, saying: "There is no god but Allah," and they had no deed, no book, and no prophet except the saying "There is no god but Allah." He said: And they did not believe in any messenger. Therefore the polytheists used to call the Prophet (ﷺ) and his companions "the Sabians," likening them to them in the saying "There is no god but Allah."

Al-Khalil said: They are a people whose religion resembles the religion of the Christians, except that their qiblah is toward the south-west, claiming that they are upon the religion of Nuh, peace be upon him. Al-Qurtubi related from Mujahid, al-Hasan, and Ibn Abi Najih that they are a people whose religion is a mixture between the Jews and the Magians, and their slaughtered animals are not eaten. Ibn Abbas said: And their women are not married. Al-Qurtubi said: What is established of their doctrine, as mentioned by some scholars, is that they are monotheists who believe in the influence of the stars, and that they are doers (of actions). For this reason Abu Sa'id al-Istakhri issued a ruling of their disbelief to al-Qadir billah when he asked him about them. Fakhr al-Din al-Razi chose that the Sabians are a people who worship the stars, in the sense that Allah made them a direction for worship and supplication, or in the sense that Allah entrusted the management of the affairs of this world to them. He said: This view is attributed to the Kashraniyyin, to whom Ibrahim al-Khalil, peace be upon him, came, refuting them and nullifying their saying.

The most apparent of the opinions, and Allah knows best, is the saying of Mujahid and his followers, and Wahb ibn Munabbih: that they are a people who are not upon the religion of the Jews, nor the Christians, nor the Magians, nor the polytheists, but are a people remaining upon their natural disposition (fitrah), with no established religion for them to follow or pursue. For this reason the polytheists used to revile whoever embraced Islam by calling him "Sabi," meaning that he had left all the religions of the people of the earth at that time.

Some scholars said: The Sabians are those whom the call of any prophet has not reached. And Allah knows best.

Allah, exalted is He, says, reminding the Children of Israel of the covenants and pledges taken from them to believe in Him alone, with no partner, and to follow His messengers. He also informs that when He took the covenant from them, He raised the mountain above their heads so that they would affirm what they had been bound to, and take it (with [[In J, T: "So they took it."]]) strength, resolve, determination and compliance, as He said: ﴿And [recall] when We raised the mountain above them as if it were a canopy, and they thought it would fall upon them: "Take what We have given you with determination and remember what is in it, that you may become righteous."﴾ [Al-A'raf: 171]. At-Tur is the mountain, as explained by the verse in Al-A'raf, and this was stated by Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, 'Ata', 'Ikrimah, al-Hasan, ad-Dahhak, ar-Rabi' ibn Anas, and others than them. This is the apparent meaning.

It is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas: At-Tur is whatever of the mountains bears vegetation; what does not bear vegetation is not a tur.

In the hadith of al-Futun, from Ibn 'Abbas: when they refused obedience, He raised the mountain over them so that they would listen [and they prostrated].

As-Suddi said: When they refused to prostrate, Allah commanded the mountain to fall upon them. They looked at it, and it had covered them, so they fell prostrate, [and they prostrated] on one side, while looking with the other side. Allah had mercy on them and lifted it from them. They said: "By Allah, there is no prostration more beloved to Allah than a prostration by which He removed the punishment from us." So they still prostrate in that manner, and that is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And We raised over you the mountain.﴾

Al-Hasan said regarding His saying: ﴿Take what We have given you with strength﴾, that it means the Torah.

Abu al-'Aliyah and ar-Rabi' ibn Anas said: ﴿with strength﴾ means with obedience. Mujahid said: "with strength" means by acting upon what is in it. Qatadah said: ﴿Take what We have given you with strength﴾ — the strength is earnestness, otherwise I will drop it upon you.

He said: So they affirmed that they would take what they were given with strength. The meaning of his saying "otherwise I will drop it upon you" is: I will cast it down upon you, meaning the mountain.

Abu al-'Aliyah and ar-Rabi' said: ﴿And remember what is in it﴾ means: read what is in the Torah and act upon it.

* *

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Then you turned away after that﴾ — Allah, exalted is He, says: then after this firm, great covenant, you turned away from it, deviated, and broke it. ﴿Had it not been for the bounty of Allah upon you and His mercy﴾ — that is, His forgiveness of you and His sending to you the prophets and messengers — ﴿you would have been among the losers﴾ by your breaking that covenant, in this world and the Hereafter.

He also informs that when He took the covenant from them, He raised the mountain above their heads so that they would affirm what they had been bound to, and take it (with [[In J, T: "So they took it."]]) strength, resolve, determination and compliance, as He said: ﴿And [recall] when We raised the mountain above them as if it were a canopy, and they thought it would fall upon them: "Take what We have given you with determination and remember what is in it, that you may become righteous."﴾ [Al-A'raf: 171].
