Ibn Kathir's commentary on Surah 2, verse 185 (part 1 of 2):

Allah praises the month of fasting (Ramadan) above all other months, in that He chose it from among them for the revelation of the Mighty Qur'an within it. Just as He singled it out for this, a hadith has been narrated that it is the month in which the divine scriptures were sent down to the Prophets.

Imam Ahmad ibn Hanbal, may Allah have mercy on him, said: Abu Sa'id, the client (mawla) of the Banu Hashim, narrated to us: 'Imran Abu al-'Awwam narrated to us, from Qatadah, from Abu al-Malih, from Wathilah (meaning Ibn al-Asqa'), that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "The scrolls of Ibrahim were sent down on the first night of Ramadan. The Torah was sent down on the sixth night of Ramadan, the Injil on the thirteenth night of Ramadan [[In manuscript "A", after this: "And the Zabur was sent down on the eighteenth night of Ramadan."]], and Allah sent down the Qur'an on the twenty-fourth night of Ramadan." [[Al-Musnad (4/107).]]

It has also been narrated through the hadith of Jabir ibn 'Abdullah, in which it is stated that the Zabur was sent down on the twelfth night of Ramadan, and the Injil on the eighteenth, and the rest as mentioned previously. Ibn Mardawayh narrated it. [[In manuscript "J": "nazalat" and in "A": "nazal".]]

As for the scrolls, the Torah, the Zabur and the Injil, each of them was sent down upon the Prophet to whom it was revealed all at once. As for the Qur'an, it was sent down all at once to the House of Honour (Bayt al-'Izzah) in the lowest heaven, and that took place in the month of Ramadan, on the Night of Decree (Laylat al-Qadr) within it, as Allah the Exalted says: ﴿Indeed, We sent it down on the Night of Decree﴾ [al-Qadr: 1]. And He says: ﴿Indeed, We sent it down on a blessed night﴾ [al-Dukhan: 3]. Then it was afterwards sent down gradually (mufarriqan), according to events, upon the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). This has been narrated through more than one chain from Ibn 'Abbas, as Isra'il narrated from al-Suddi, from Muhammad ibn Abi al-Mujalid, from Miqsam, from Ibn 'Abbas, that 'Atiyyah ibn al-Aswad asked him, saying: "Doubt has entered my heart concerning Allah's words: ﴿The month of Ramadan in which the Qur'an was sent down﴾, and His words: ﴿Indeed, We sent it down on a blessed night﴾, and His words: ﴿Indeed, We sent it down on the Night of Decree﴾, while it was sent down in Shawwal, in Dhu al-Qa'dah, in Dhu al-Hijjah, in Muharram, in Safar, and in Rabi' [[In manuscript "J": "wa hadha" (and this).]]." Ibn 'Abbas said: "It was sent down in Ramadan, on the Night of Decree and on a blessed night, all at once. Then it was sent down in accordance with the setting-places of the stars (mawaqi' al-nujum), gradually (tartilan) over the months and days." Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn Mardawayh narrated it, and this is his wording.

In the narration of Sa'id ibn Jubayr from Ibn 'Abbas, he said: "The Qur'an was sent down in the middle of the month of Ramadan to the lowest heaven and was placed in the House of Honour, then it was sent down upon the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) over twenty years, in response to the words of the people."

In the narration of 'Ikrimah from Ibn 'Abbas, he said: "The Qur'an was sent down in the month of Ramadan, on the Night of Decree, to this lowest heaven, all at once. Allah renews for His Prophet whatever He wills. The polytheists did not bring any argument with which they disputed except that Allah brought them its answer." That is His saying: ﴿And those who disbelieve say, "Why was the Qur'an not sent down to him all at once?" Thus [it was sent], that We may strengthen your heart thereby, and We have spaced it out in gradual recitation. And they do not bring you any argument except that We bring you the truth and the best explanation﴾ [al-Furqan: 32-33].

[Fakhr al-Din (al-Razi) said: "It is possible that in every Night of Decree, what the people need of it was sent down from the Preserved Tablet (al-Lawh al-Mahfuz) to its like in the lowest heaven." He paused, asking whether this is preferable or the former view. This, which he presented as a possibility, was transmitted by al-Qurtubi from Muqatil ibn Hayyan. He also reported a consensus that the Qur'an was sent down all at once from the Preserved Tablet to the House of Honour in the lowest heaven. Al-Razi related from Sufyan ibn 'Uyaynah and others that the meaning of His words ﴿in which the Qur'an was sent down﴾ is: "in its virtue" or "the obligation of fasting it." This is very strange.] [[Added from manuscripts "J" and "A".]]

* *

As for His words: ﴿a guidance for the people and clear proofs of guidance and the Criterion﴾, this is praise of the Qur'an which Allah sent down as guidance for the hearts of the servants, for those who believe in it, affirm it and follow it. ﴿And clear proofs﴾ means: evidences and clear, manifest and evident arguments for whoever understands and reflects upon them, indicating the truth of what it brought of guidance, which opposes misguidance, and right direction which contradicts error, and distinguishing between truth and falsehood, and between the lawful and the unlawful.

It has been narrated from some of the early generations (salaf) that they disliked saying "Ramadan" alone without saying "the month of Ramadan". Ibn Abi Hatim said: My father narrated to us, Muhammad ibn Bakkar ibn al-Rayyan narrated to us, Abu Ma'shar narrated to us, from Muhammad ibn Ka'b al-Qurazi and Sa'id (who is al-Maqburi), from Abu Hurayrah, who said: "Do not say 'Ramadan', for Ramadan is one of the names of Allah the Exalted, but say 'the month of Ramadan'."

Ibn Abi Hatim said: It has been narrated from Mujahid and Muhammad ibn Ka'b something similar to this, and Ibn 'Abbas and Zayd ibn Thabit permitted it.

I say: Abu Ma'shar is Najih ibn 'Abd al-Rahman al-Madani, an imam [in] the campaigns (maghazi) and biographies (siyar), but there is weakness in him. His son Muhammad narrated it from him, making it marfu' (traced to the Prophet) from Abu Hurayrah. The hadith scholar Ibn 'Adi denied this against him, and he deserves to be denied, for he is abandoned (matruk). He erred in raising this hadith. Al-Bukhari, may Allah have mercy on him, defended this view in his book, saying: "Chapter: whether it may be said 'Ramadan'", and he cited hadiths on this, among them: "Whoever fasts Ramadan out of faith and seeking reward, his previous sins will be forgiven," and similar.

* *

As for His words: ﴿So whoever of you witnesses the month, let him fast it﴾, this is a definite obligation upon whoever witnesses the beginning of the month, that is, was resident in the town when the month of Ramadan began, and is healthy in his body, to fast it without fail. This verse abrogated (nasakha) the earlier permission for one who was healthy and resident to break the fast and pay the ransom by feeding a poor person for each day, as was explained previously. And when it made fasting obligatory, it repeated the concession for the sick and the traveller to break the fast, on condition of making it up, saying: ﴿And whoever is sick or on a journey, [then a number of other days]﴾. Its meaning: whoever has an illness in his body that makes fasting difficult for him, or harms him, or who is on a journey, that is, in a state of travel, may break the fast. If he breaks it, then he must make up the number of days he broke during the journey. For this reason He said: ﴿Allah intends for you ease and does not intend for you hardship﴾, meaning: He only granted you concession to break the fast during illness and travel, while making it binding upon the resident healthy person, as an ease for you and a mercy towards you.

Here are some issues related to this verse:

The first: some of the early generations held that whoever was resident at the beginning of the month and then travelled during it, may not break the fast on account of travel in this situation, because of His words: ﴿So whoever of you witnesses the month, let him fast it﴾, and the concession to break the fast applies only to a traveller who began the month while already travelling. This view is strange, transmitted by Abu Muhammad ibn Hazm in his book al-Muhalla from a group of Companions and Successors. But what he attributed to them is open to question, and Allah knows best. For it is established in the Sunnah from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) that he set out in Ramadan for the Conquest campaign, and he continued until he reached al-Kadid, then he broke his fast and ordered the people to break their fast. Both compilers of the Sahih (al-Bukhari and Muslim) narrated it. [[Sahih al-Bukhari no. (1948, 4279) and Sahih Muslim no. (1113).]]

The second: others among the Companions and Successors held that it is obligatory to break the fast while travelling, based on His words: ﴿then [a number of] other days﴾. The sound view is the view of the majority (jumhur) that the matter in this is one of choice, not obligation, because they used to go out with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) in Ramadan. [Anas] said: "Some of us fasted and some of us broke the fast. The one who fasted did not blame the one who broke the fast, nor did the one who broke the fast blame the one who fasted." [[Narrated by Muslim in his Sahih no. (1118) from the hadith of Anas, may Allah be pleased with him.]] So if breaking the fast were the obligation, they would have been rebuked for fasting. Rather, what is established from the actions of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) is that in such a situation he was fasting, as is established in the two Sahihs from Abu al-Darda', who said: "We went out with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) in the month of Ramadan in intense heat, so much that one of us would place his hand on his head because of the intensity of the heat. And none among us was fasting except the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and 'Abdullah ibn Rawahah." [[Sahih al-Bukhari no. (1945) and Sahih Muslim no. (1122).]]

The third: a group, including al-Shafi'i, said: fasting while travelling is better than breaking the fast, because of the Prophet's (ﷺ) action as mentioned earlier. Another group said: rather, breaking the fast is better, taking the concession, and because it is established from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) that he was asked about fasting while travelling, and he said: "Whoever breaks the fast, it is good, and whoever fasts, there is no blame upon him." [[This is the wording of the hadith of Hamzah ibn 'Amr al-Aslami in Sahih Muslim no. (1121).]] And he said in another hadith: "Take up the concession of Allah which He has granted you." [[This is the wording of the hadith of Jabir, which will come.]] Another group said: both are equal, based on the hadith of 'A'ishah that Hamzah ibn 'Amr al-Aslami said: "O Messenger of Allah, I fast often; shall I fast while travelling?" He said: "If you wish, fast, and if you wish, break the fast." It is in both Sahihs. [[Sahih al-Bukhari no. (1943) and Sahih Muslim no. (1121).]] It has also been said: if fasting is hardship, then breaking the fast is better, based on the hadith of Jabir: that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) saw a man who was shaded over, and he said: "What is this?" They said: "He is fasting." He said: "It is not righteousness to fast while travelling." Both [al-Bukhari and Muslim] narrated it. [[Sahih al-Bukhari no. (1946) and Sahih Muslim no. (1121).]] As for one who turns away from the Sunnah, and regards breaking the fast as disliked to him, then in this case it becomes obligatory for him to break the fast and forbidden for him to fast. This is based on what came in the Musnad of Imam Ahmad and others, from Ibn 'Umar and Jabir and others: "Whoever does not accept the concession of Allah, upon him is a sin like the mountains of 'Arafah." [[Al-Musnad (2/71).]]

The fourth: making up the missed days, must it be consecutive, or is it permissible to separate them? On this there are two opinions. One: consecutiveness is obligatory, because making up the fast resembles performing it on time. The second: consecutiveness is not obligatory; rather, if he wishes he may separate them, and if he wishes he may make them consecutive. This is the view of the majority of the early and later scholars (salaf and khalaf), and the evidences support it. This is because consecutiveness was obligatory within the month only for the necessity of performing it within the month. But after Ramadan has ended, what is intended is fasting a number of days equal to what was broken. For this reason Allah the Exalted says: ﴿then [a number of] other days﴾, and then He says: ﴿Allah intends for you ease and does not intend for you hardship﴾. Imam Ahmad said: Abu Salamah al-Khuza'i narrated to us, Ibn Hilal narrated to us, from Humayd ibn Hilal al-'Adawi, from Abu Qatadah, from the Bedouin (a'rabi) who heard the Prophet (ﷺ) saying: "Indeed the best of your religion is its easiest, indeed the best of your religion is its easiest." [[Al-Musnad (3/479).]]

Ahmad also said: Yazid ibn Harun narrated to us, Asim ibn Hilal informed us, Ghadirah ibn Urwah al-Fuqaymi narrated to us, my father Urwah narrated to me, and he said: "We were waiting for the Prophet ﷺ, and a man came out with his head dripping from wudu' (ablution) or ghusl (ritual bath). He prayed, and when he finished the prayer, the people began asking him: 'Is there any hardship upon us in such-and-such?' The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: 'Verily, the religion of Allah is in ease,' three times, saying it each time."[[Musnad (5/69).]]

Abu Bakr ibn Mardawayh also narrated it in his tafsir of this verse, from the hadith of Muslim ibn Ibrahim, from Asim ibn Hilal, with the same wording.

Imam Ahmad also said: Muhammad ibn Ja'far narrated to us, Shu'bah narrated to us, saying: Abu al-Tayyah narrated to us, saying: I heard Anas ibn Malik say: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Make things easy and do not make them difficult; give glad tidings and do not repel people." Both (al-Bukhari and Muslim) recorded it in their Sahihs.[[Sahih al-Bukhari, no. (69), and Sahih Muslim, no. (1734).]] In the two Sahihs also: that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said to Mu'adh and Abu Musa when he sent them to Yemen: "Give glad tidings and do not repel; make things easy and do not make them difficult; cooperate and do not differ." And in the Sunan and Musnad collections, the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "I was sent with the tolerant, easy Hanifiyyah."[[Sahih al-Bukhari, nos. (4341, 4342), and Sahih Muslim, no. (1733).]]

The Hafiz Abu Bakr ibn Mardawayh said in his tafsir: 'Abdullah ibn Ishaq ibn Ibrahim narrated to us, Yahya ibn Abi Talib narrated to us, 'Abd al-Wahhab ibn 'Ata' narrated to us, Abu Mas'ud al-Juraybiri narrated to us, from 'Abdullah ibn Shaqiq, from Mihjan ibn al-Adra': that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ saw a man praying, and he looked at him with his gaze for a while, then said: "Do you think he prays sincerely?" I said: "O Messenger of Allah, he is one of the people of Madinah who prays the most." The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Do not let him hear you, lest you destroy him." And he said: "Verily, Allah only intended ease for this Ummah, and did not intend hardship for them."[[Ahmad in al-Musnad (5/32) narrated it through Hammad, from al-Juraybiri, from 'Abdullah ibn Shaqiq, from Mihjan, in similar terms.]]

The meaning of His saying: ﴿Allah intends ease for you and does not intend hardship for you, and [wants] you to complete the period﴾ is: He only granted you concession to break the fast due to illness, travel and similar excuses, because He intends ease for you; and He only commanded you to make up the days so that you may complete the number of your month.

* *

His saying: ﴿and that you may glorify Allah for having guided you﴾ means: that you may remember Allah at the conclusion of your worship, as He said: ﴿So when you have completed your rites, remember Allah as you remember your fathers or with greater remembrance﴾ [al-Baqarah: 200], and He said: ﴿So when you have finished the prayer, remember Allah standing, sitting and on your sides﴾ [al-Nisa': 103], and ﴿So when the prayer is concluded, disperse in the land and seek of Allah's bounty, and remember Allah much that you may succeed﴾ [al-Jumu'ah: 10], and He said: ﴿And glorify the praise of your Lord before the rising of the sun and before its setting. And of the night, glorify Him, and after the prostrations﴾ [Qaf: 39-40]. For this reason the Sunnah came to recommend tasbih (glorification), tahmid (praising) and takbir (magnifying Allah) after the obligatory prayers.

Ibn 'Abbas said: "We did not know the end of the Messenger of Allah's ﷺ prayer except by the takbir." For this reason, many scholars derived the legislation of takbir on the Eid al-Fitr from this verse: ﴿and that you complete the period and that you glorify Allah for having guided you﴾. Dawud ibn 'Ali al-Isfahani al-Zahiri went so far as to hold it obligatory on Eid al-Fitr, based on the apparent command in His saying ﴿and that you glorify Allah for having guided you﴾. Opposed to this is the position of Abu Hanifah, may Allah have mercy on him, that takbir is not prescribed on Eid al-Fitr. The rest hold it to be recommended, with differences among them on some details of the rulings.

* *

His saying: ﴿and perhaps you will be grateful﴾ means: if you carry out what Allah has commanded you of obedience to Him, by performing His obligations, avoiding His prohibitions and guarding His limits, then perhaps you will be among the thankful for that.

Ibn Abi Hatim said: My father narrated to us, Yahya ibn al-Mughirah narrated to us, Jarir informed us, from Abdah ibn Abi Barzah al-Sijistani [in manuscripts C, A and W: "al-Sakhtiyani"], from al-Sulb [in C: "al-Salt"] ibn Hakim ibn Mu'awiyah ibn Haydah al-Qushayri, from his father, from his grandfather, that a Bedouin said: "O Messenger of Allah, is our Lord near, so that we whisper to Him, or far, so that we call out to Him?" The Prophet (ﷺ) remained silent, so Allah revealed: ﴿And when My servants ask you concerning Me, indeed I am near. I respond to the invocation of the supplicant when he calls upon Me﴾ [1].

Ibn Mardawayh and Abu al-Shaykh al-Isfahani also narrated it from the hadith of Muhammad ibn Abi Humayd, from Jarir, with the same wording. Abd al-Razzaq said: Ja'far ibn Sulayman informed us, from Awf, from al-Hasan, who said: The companions of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) [the Prophet (ﷺ)] [[addition from C, A and W]] asked: "Where is our Lord?" So Allah, Mighty and Majestic, revealed: ﴿And when My servants ask you concerning Me, indeed I am near. I respond to the invocation of the supplicant when he calls upon Me﴾, to the end of the verse [2].

Ibn Jurayj said, from Ata': it reached him that when the verse ﴿And your Lord says: Call upon Me, I will respond to you﴾ [Ghafir: 60] was revealed, the people said: "If only we knew which hour to supplicate in!" So this verse was revealed: ﴿And when My servants ask you concerning Me, indeed I am near. I respond to the invocation of the supplicant when he calls upon Me﴾.

Imam Ahmad said: Abd al-Wahhab ibn Abd al-Majid al-Thaqafi narrated to us, Khalid al-Hadhdha' narrated to us, from Abu Uthman al-Nahdi, from Abu Musa al-Ash'ari, who said: We were with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) on a military expedition, and whenever we ascended a height, or rose upon a elevation, or descended into a valley, we raised our voices with takbir. He said: So he drew near to us and said: "O people, be gentle with yourselves, for you are not calling upon one who is deaf or absent; rather you are calling upon One who is All-Hearing, All-Seeing. Indeed, the One you call upon is closer to any one of you than the neck of his mount. O Abdullah ibn Qays, shall I not teach you a word from the treasures of Paradise? There is no power and no strength except with Allah."

Al-Bukhari and Muslim narrated it in their Sahihs, and the rest of the compilers narrated it from the hadith of Abu Uthman al-Nahdi, whose name is Abd al-Rahman ibn Mull [in C: "ibn Malbak"], from him, with similar wording [3].

Imam Ahmad said: Sulayman ibn Dawud narrated to us, Shu'bah narrated to us, Qatadah narrated to us, from Anas (may Allah be pleased with him), that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Allah, the Exalted, says: I am as My servant thinks of Me, and I am with him when he calls upon Me" [4].

Imam Ahmad said: Ali ibn Ishaq narrated to us, Abdullah informed us, Abd al-Rahman ibn Yazid ibn Jabir informed us, Isma'il ibn Ubaydullah narrated to us, from Karimah bint al-Khashkhash al-Muzaniyyah, who said: Abu Hurayrah narrated to us that he heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) say: "Allah says: I am with My servant so long as he remembers Me and his lips move with Me" [5].

I say: This is like His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, Allah is with those who fear Him and those who are doers of good﴾ [An-Nahl: 128], and like His saying to Musa and Harun, peace be upon them: ﴿Indeed, I am with you both; I hear and I see﴾ [Ta-Ha: 46]. The meaning of this is that He, Exalted is He, does not disappoint the supplication of a supplicant, and nothing distracts Him from it; rather, He is the Hearer of supplication. In it there is encouragement to supplicate, and that nothing is lost in His presence, Exalted is He. As Imam Ahmad said: Yazid narrated to us, a man narrated to us that he heard Abu Uthman (he is al-Nahdi) narrate from Salman (i.e. al-Farisi), may Allah be pleased with him, from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "Indeed Allah, Exalted is He, is shy to return empty-handed the hands of a servant who raises them to Him asking for good in them."

Yazid said: Name this man for me. They said: Ja'far ibn Maymun [6].

Abu Dawud, al-Tirmidhi and Ibn Majah also narrated it from the hadith of Ja'far ibn Maymun, the owner of the cloths [7]. Al-Tirmidhi said: Hasan gharib. Some of them narrated it without raising it to the Prophet (ﷺ).

Shaykh al-Hafiz Abu al-Hajjaj al-Mizzi, may Allah have mercy on him, said in his Atraf: "Abu Hammam Muhammad ibn al-Zibriqan followed him, from Sulayman al-Taymi, from Abu Uthman al-Nahdi, with it."

Imam Ahmad also said: Abu Amir narrated to us, Ali ibn Dawud Abu al-Mutawakkil al-Naji narrated to us, from Abu Sa'id, that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "No Muslim supplicates Allah, Mighty and Majestic, with a supplication that contains no sin and no severing of kinship, but Allah gives him one of three things: either He hastens his supplication for him, or He stores it for him in the Hereafter, or He averts from him an equivalent evil." They said: "Then we will increase [our supplications]." He said: "Allah is more abundant [in response]."

Abdullah ibn al-Imam Ahmad said: Ishaq ibn Mansur al-Kawsaj narrated to us, Muhammad ibn Yusuf informed us, Ibn Thawban narrated to us, from his father, from Makhul, from Jubayr ibn Nufayr, that Ubadah ibn al-Samit told them that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "There is no Muslim on the face of the earth who supplicates Allah, Mighty and Majestic, with a supplication except that Allah gives him what he asked, or averts from him an equivalent evil, so long as he does not supplicate for sin or severing of kinship" [8].

al-Tirmidhi narrated it from Abd Allah ibn Abd al-Rahman al-Darimi, from Muhammad ibn Yusuf al-Firyabi, from Ibn Thawban, who is Abd al-Rahman ibn Thabit ibn Thawban, with it [9]. He said: Hasan sahih gharib from this route.

Imam Malik said, from Ibn Shihab, from Abu Ubayd, client of Ibn Azhar, from Abu Hurayrah, that the Messenger of Allah (ṣallā Allāhu ʿalayhi wa-sallam) said: "One of you will be answered so long as he does not hasten, saying: I supplicated, but I was not answered."

Al-Bukhari and Muslim both narrated it in their Sahihs from the hadith of Malik, with it [10]. This is the wording of al-Bukhari, may Allah have mercy on him and reward him with Paradise.

Muslim also said [in his Sahih]: Abu al-Tahir narrated to us, Ibn Wahb narrated to us, Mu'awiyah ibn Salih informed me, from Rabi'ah ibn Yazid, from Abu Idris al-Khawlani, from Abu Hurayrah, from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "The supplication of the servant continues to be answered so long as he does not supplicate for sin or severing of kinship, so long as he does not hasten." It was said: "O Messenger of Allah, what is hastening?" He said: "He says: I have supplicated, and I have supplicated, but I have not seen it answered for me; so he becomes weary at that point and abandons supplication" [11].

Imam Ahmad said: Abd al-Samad narrated to us, Ibn Hilal narrated to us, from Qatadah, from Anas, that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "The servant will remain in good so long as he does not hasten." They said: "And how does he hasten?" He said: "He says: I have supplicated my Lord, but He has not answered me" [12].

Imam Abu Ja'far al-Tabari said in his Tafsir: Yunus ibn Abd al-Ala narrated to me, Ibn Wahb narrated to us, Abu Sakhr narrated to me that Yazid ibn Abd Allah ibn Qusayt narrated to him, from Urwah ibn al-Zubayr, from Aisha, may Allah be pleased with her, that she said: "No believing servant supplicates Allah with a supplication that goes unanswered, until it is either hastened for him in this world or stored for him in the Hereafter, so long as he does not hasten or despair." Urwah said: I said: "O mother, how is his hastening and despair?" She said: "He says: I asked and I was not given; I supplicated and I was not answered."

Ibn Qusayt said: I also heard Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab say the same as the saying of Aisha exactly.

Imam Ahmad said: Hasan narrated to us, Ibn Lahi'ah narrated to us, Bakr ibn Amr narrated to us, from Abu Abd al-Rahman al-Hubuli, from Abd Allah ibn Amr, that the Messenger of Allah (ṣallā Allāhu ʿalayhi wa-sallam) said: "Hearts are vessels, and some of them are more capacious than others. So when you ask Allah, O people, ask Him while you are certain of being answered, for He does not respond to a servant who supplicates Him from a heedless heart."

Ibn Mardawayh said: Muhammad ibn Ishaq ibn Ayyub narrated to us, Ishaq ibn Ibrahim ibn Ubayy ibn Nafi' ibn Ma'd Yakrib narrated to us in Baghdad, Ubayy ibn Nafi' narrated to me, my father Nafi' ibn Ma'd Yakrib narrated to me, who said: "I and Aisha asked the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) about the verse: ﴿I respond to the invocation of the supplicant when he calls upon Me﴾." He said: "O Lord, the question is Aisha's." Then Jibril descended and said: "Allah sends you His greetings. This is My righteous servant with a sincere intention, and his heart is pure; he says: O Lord, and I say: Here I am. So I fulfil his need."

This is a gharib hadith from this route [13].

Al-Bazzar narrated from al-Kalbi, from Abu Salih, from Ibn Abbas: Jabir ibn Abd Allah narrated to me that the Prophet (ﷺ) recited: ﴿And when My servants ask you concerning Me, indeed I am near. I respond to the invocation of the supplicant when he calls upon Me﴾, to the end of the verse. Then the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "O Allah, You commanded supplication and guaranteed response. Here I am, O Allah, here I am. Here I am, no partner is Yours. Here I am; indeed all praise and blessing are Yours, and sovereignty, no partner is Yours. I bear witness that You are One, the Eternal Refuge, who neither begets nor is begotten, and to whom none is equal. I bear witness that Your promise is true, Your meeting is true, Paradise is true, the Fire is true, the Hour is coming with no doubt, and You will resurrect those in the graves."

Al-Hafiz Abu Bakr al-Bazzar said: al-Hasan ibn Yahya al-Arzi [in C: "al-Azdi"] and Muhammad ibn Yahya al-Quta'i [in C: "al-Muqta'i"] narrated to us, saying: al-Hajjaj ibn Minhal narrated to us, Salih al-Murri narrated to us, from al-Hasan, from Anas, from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "Allah, Exalted is He, says: O son of Adam, one is for you, one is for Me, and one is between Me and you. As for the one for Me, you worship Me and associate nothing with Me. As for the one for you, whatever deed you do, I will repay you for it. As for the one between Me and you, from you is the supplication and from Me is the answer."

Concerning the mention of His Exalted words in this verse urging supplication, placed between the rulings of fasting, is a guidance to striving in supplication at the completion of the month, and indeed at every iftar, as Imam Abu Dawud al-Tayalisi narrated in his Musnad:

Abu Muhammad al-Maliki narrated to us, from Amr, that is Ibn Shu'ayb ibn Muhammad ibn Abd Allah ibn Amr, from his father, from his grandfather Abd Allah ibn Amr, who said: I heard the Messenger of Allah (ṣallā Allāhu ʿalayhi wa-sallam) say: "The fasting person has an answered supplication at the time of his iftar." So Abd Allah ibn Amr, when he broke his fast, would call his family, his children, and supplicate [14].
