Ibn Mardawayh also said: Muhammad ibn al-Hasan ibn Ziyad al-Muqri informed us: Yahya ibn Durustuwayh al-Marwazi [in one copy: "ibn Sasuwayh al-Marwazi"] informed us: Ziyad ibn Ibrahim informed us: Abu Hamzah al-Sukkari informed us, from al-Muthanna, from Qatadah, from al-Hasan, from Abu Musa al-Ash'ari, from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "Allah revealed to Musa ibn Imran (peace be upon him): 'Recite Ayat al-Kursi after every obligatory prayer, for whoever recites it after every obligatory prayer, I will place in him the heart of the grateful, the tongue of those who remember Me, the reward of those who turn in repentance, the deeds of the truthful. None will persist in this except a prophet, a truthful one, or a servant whose heart I have tested for faith, or whom I intend to kill in the way of Allah.'" [In its isnad is Muhammad ibn al-Hasan al-Naqqash, of whom al-Barqani said: "All his hadith is munkar (rejected)." Al-Khatib said: "His hadith contains rejected reports." A similar report was narrated from Jabir (may Allah be pleased with him), but it is weak.] This is a very munkar hadith.

Another hadith that it protects whoever recites it at the beginning of the day and at the beginning of the night: Abu Isa al-Tirmidhi said: Yahya ibn al-Mughirah Abu Salamah al-Makhzumi al-Madini narrated to us: Ibn Abi Fudayk informed us, from Abd al-Rahman al-Maliki, from Zurarah ibn Mus'ab, from Abu Salamah, from Abu Hurayrah, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Whoever recites Ha, Mim (Surat Ghafir) up to: 'To Him is the destination' (40:3), and Ayat al-Kursi when he enters the morning, will be protected by them until evening, and whoever recites them when he enters the evening will be protected by them until morning." Then he said: "This is a gharib hadith. Some scholars have spoken about Abd al-Rahman ibn Abi Bakr ibn Abi Mulaykah al-Maliki because of his memory." [Sunan al-Tirmidhi no. 2879.]

Many other hadiths have been reported concerning its merit, which we have left out for brevity because they are not authentic and their isnads are weak, such as a hadith that reciting it during cupping is equal to two cuppings, and a hadith of Abu Hurayrah about writing it on the left hand with saffron seven times and then licking it for memorization and to prevent forgetting. Ibn Mardawayh narrated these two and others. This verse contains ten independent clauses.

Commentary of Ibn Kathir (Tafsir al-Quran al-'Azim) on surah 2, verse 255 (part 3 of 4):

His saying, ﴿Allah, there is no god but He﴾, is a statement that He alone is the one deserving of worship (ilahiyyah) by all creation. ﴿The Living, the Self-Subsisting﴾: that is, the Living in Himself, who never dies, and the Sustainer (al-Qayyim) of everything else. Umar used to recite it as "al-Qayyam." All existing things are in need of Him, while He is free of need of them, and they have no subsistence without His command, as in His saying: ﴿And among His signs is that the heaven and the earth stand by His command﴾ [al-Rum: 25]. His saying, ﴿Neither drowsiness nor sleep overtakes Him﴾, means that no deficiency, heedlessness, or inattentiveness toward His creation affects Him. Rather, He is watchful over every soul for what it has earned, and He is Witness over everything; nothing is hidden from Him, and no hidden thing escapes Him. [[In manuscript A: "nothing escapes Him."]] Part of the completeness of His self-subsistence is that neither drowsiness nor sleep overtakes Him. So His saying, ﴿Neither overtakes Him﴾, means that drowsiness, which is slumber and light sleep, does not overcome Him. For this reason He said, ﴿nor sleep﴾, because sleep is stronger than drowsiness.

In the Sahih, it is related from Abu Musa, who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ stood among us and spoke four sentences. He said: "Allah does not sleep, and it is not fitting for Him to sleep. He lowers the scale and raises it. The deeds of the day are lifted up to Him before the deeds of the night, and the deeds of the night before the deeds of the day. His veil is light, or fire. If He were to uncover it, the glories of His Face would burn away whatever of His creation His sight reaches." [Sahih Muslim, no. 179.]

Abd al-Razzaq said: Ma'mar informed us, al-Hakam ibn Aban informed me, from Ikrimah, the freed slave of Ibn Abbas, concerning His saying, ﴿Neither drowsiness nor sleep overtakes Him﴾, that Musa (peace be upon him) asked the angels, "Does Allah, Mighty and Majestic, sleep?" Allah revealed to the angels and commanded them to keep him awake for three [nights]. [[In manuscript A: "a little."]] They were not to let him sleep. They did so. Then they gave him two flasks, and he held them. Then they left him, warning him not to break them. He said: So he began to doze while the two flasks were in his hands, one in each hand. He kept dozing and waking, dozing and waking, until he dozed off once, and struck one against the other and broke them. Ma'mar said: This is only a parable that Allah, Mighty and Majestic, struck, meaning: likewise, the heavens and the earth are in His two hands.

Ibn Jarir related it in this same form from al-Hasan ibn Yahya, from Abd al-Razzaq, and mentioned it. It is from the reports of the Children of Israel (Isra'iliyyat: narratives taken from Jewish and Christian sources). It is known that Musa (peace be upon him) would not be unaware of such a matter concerning Allah, Mighty and Majestic, and that He is far removed from such a thing.

Even more strange than all of this is the hadith that Ibn Jarir related: Ishaq ibn Abi Isra'il told us, Hisham ibn Yusuf told us, from Umayyah ibn Shibl, from al-Hakam ibn Aban, from Ikrimah, from Abu Hurayrah, who said: I heard the Messenger of Allah ﷺ relate from Musa (peace be upon him) on the pulpit, saying: "It occurred to the mind of Musa: Does Allah sleep? So Allah sent an angel to him, who kept him awake for three [nights]. Then He gave him two flasks, one in each hand, and commanded him to guard them." He said: "So he began to sleep, and his hands almost met. He would wake up and hold one against the other, until he slept a sleep, and his hands clapped together, and the two flasks broke." He said: "Allah, Mighty and Majestic, struck a parable for him: If Allah were to sleep, the heavens and the earth would not remain upheld."

[[Tafsir al-Tabari (5/394). Al-Hafiz Ibn Hajar said in his biography of Umayyah ibn Shibl: "He has a munkar (rejected) hadith, which he related from al-Hakam ibn Aban, from Ikrimah, from Abu Hurayrah, marfu' (traced to the Prophet ﷺ), saying: 'It occurred to the mind of Musa (peace be upon him): Does Allah sleep?' The hadith, which Hisham ibn Yusuf related, was opposed by Ma'mar, who related from al-Hakam, from Ikrimah, and made it mawquf (traced only to a companion, here Ikrimah or Ibn Abbas). This [latter version] is closer to correct. It is not valid that this occurred to the mind of Musa (peace be upon him); rather, what is reported is that the Children of Israel asked Musa about this."]]

This is a very strange hadith. The more apparent view is that it is an Isra'iliyyat report, not a marfu' hadith. And Allah knows best.

Ibn Abi Hatim said: Ahmad ibn al-Qasim ibn Atiyyah told us, Ahmad ibn Abd al-Rahman al-Dashtaki told us, my father told me, from his father, Ashath ibn Ishaq told us, from Ja'far ibn Abi al-Mughirah, from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, from Ibn Abbas: The Children of Israel said, "O Musa, does your Lord sleep?" He said, "Fear Allah." Then his Lord, Mighty and Majestic, called to him: "O Musa, they asked you: Does your Lord sleep? Take two glass vessels in your hands and stand up at night." Musa did so. When a third of the night had passed, he dozed and fell onto his knees. Then he jerked up and held them. When it was the last part of the night, he dozed, and the two glass vessels fell and broke. He said: "O Musa, if I were to sleep, the heavens and the earth would perish and be destroyed just as the two glass vessels in your hands were destroyed." And Allah revealed to His Prophet ﷺ the Verse of the Throne (Ayat al-Kursi).

* *

His saying, ﴿To Him belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth﴾, is a statement that all of them are His servants, under His dominion, and beneath His subjugation and authority, as in His saying: ﴿There is none in the heavens and the earth but that he comes to the Most Merciful as a servant. He has enumerated them and counted them precisely. And each of them will come to Him on the Day of Resurrection alone﴾ [Maryam: 93-95].

* *

His saying, ﴿Who is it that can intercede with Him except by His permission?﴾ is like His saying: ﴿And how many an angel is there in the heavens whose intercession will not avail at all except after Allah gives permission to whom He wills and approves﴾ [al-Najm: 26], and like His saying: ﴿And they do not intercede except for one whom He approves﴾ [al-Anbiya': 28]. This is part of His greatness, majesty, and grandeur, Mighty and Majestic: no one dares to intercede with Him except by His permission for him to intercede [[In manuscripts A and B: "except that He permits him."]], as in the hadith of intercession: "I come beneath the Throne, and I fall down in prostration [[In manuscripts A and B: "I fall down in prostration to Allah."]]. He leaves me as long as Allah wills to leave me. Then it is said: 'Raise your head, speak and you will be heard, intercede and your intercession will be accepted.'" He said: "Then He sets a limit for me, and I bring them into Paradise." [[The hadith of intercession is recorded in the Two Sahihs from the hadith of Anas (may Allah be pleased with him). Its full text and its chains will be mentioned when commenting on verse 79 of surah al-Isra'.]]

* *

His saying, ﴿He knows what is before them and what is behind them﴾, is evidence of the comprehensiveness of His knowledge of all existing things: the past, the present, and the future. Like His saying, reporting about the angels: ﴿And we do not descend except by the command of your Lord. To Him belongs what is before us and what is behind us and what is between that, and your Lord is never forgetful﴾ [Maryam: 64].

* *

His saying, ﴿And they encompass nothing of His knowledge except what He wills﴾, means: no one has access to any part of Allah's knowledge except what Allah, Mighty and Majestic, informs him of and causes him to know. It is also possible that the meaning is: they do not know any part of the knowledge of His essence and attributes except what Allah has informed them of, as in His saying: ﴿And they cannot encompass Him in knowledge﴾ [Ta-Ha: 110].

* *

His saying, ﴿His Throne (Kursi) extends over the heavens and the earth﴾. Ibn Abi Hatim said: Abu Sa'id al-Ashajj told us, Ibn Idris told us, from Mutarrif ibn Tarif, from Ja'far ibn Abi al-Mughirah, from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, from Ibn Abbas, concerning His saying, ﴿His Throne extends﴾, that he said: "His knowledge." Ibn Jarir also related it in the same way from the hadith of Abdullah ibn Idris and Hushaym, both from Mutarrif ibn Tarif.

Ibn Abi Hatim said: It was also related from Sa'id ibn Jubayr something similar. Then Ibn Jarir said: Others said: the Kursi is the place of the two feet. Then he related this from Abu Musa, al-Suddi, al-Dahhak, and Muslim al-Batin.

Shuja' ibn Makhlad said in his Tafsir: Abu Asim informed us, from Sufyan, from Ammar al-Duhni, from Muslim al-Batin, from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, from Ibn Abbas, who said: The Prophet ﷺ was asked about the saying of Allah: ﴿His Throne extends over the heavens and the earth﴾, and he said: "His Kursi is the place of His two feet, and the Throne, no one can measure its measure except Allah, Mighty and Majestic."

Thus al-Hafiz Abu Bakr ibn Mardawayh cited this hadith from the route of Shuja' ibn Makhlad al-Fallas, and mentioned it. It is an error. Waki' related it in his Tafsir: Sufyan told us, from Ammar al-Dhahabi [[In manuscript A: "from Ali al-Dhahabi."]], from Muslim al-Batin, from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, from Ibn Abbas, who said: The Kursi is the place of the two feet, and no one can measure the measure of the Throne. Al-Hakim also related it in his Mustadrak from Abu al-Abbas Muhammad ibn Ahmad al-Mahbubi, from Muhammad ibn Mu'adh, from Abu Asim, from Sufyan (that is, al-Thawri), with its chain, from Ibn Abbas as mawquf, similar to it. He said: It is sahih according to the conditions of the two Shaykhs (al-Bukhari and Muslim), though they did not record it. [[Al-Mustadrak (2/282). Ibn Abi Shaybah related it in Sifat al-Arsh, no. 61, from Abu Asim, from Sufyan, as mawquf.]] Ibn Mardawayh also related it through al-Hakim ibn Zuhayr al-Fazari al-Kufi, who is matruk (abandoned), from al-Suddi, from his father, from Abu Hurayrah, as marfu', and it is also not sound.

Al-Suddi said, from Abu Malik: The Kursi is beneath the Throne. Al-Suddi also said: The heavens and the earth are within the Kursi, and the Kursi is in front of the Throne. Al-Dahhak said, from Ibn Abbas: "If the seven heavens and the seven earths were spread out and then joined to one another, they would be in the expanse of the Kursi no more than a ring thrown into a desert."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim related this.

Ibn Jarir said: Yunus told me, Ibn Wahb informed me, who said: Ibn Zayd said: My father told me, who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "The seven heavens in relation to the Kursi are no more than seven dirhams thrown onto a shield." He said: Abu Dharr also said: I heard the Messenger of Allah ﷺ say: "The Kursi in relation to the Throne is no more than an iron ring thrown down in the middle of a desert of the earth." [[Tafsir al-Tabari (5/399). It is munqati' (with a broken chain). It has come connected (muwassal), as Ibn Abi Shaybah related it in Sifat al-Arsh, no. 58, from the route of al-Mukhtar ibn Ghassan, from Isma'il ibn Muslim, from Abu Idris al-Khawlani, from Abu Dharr al-Ghifari (may Allah be pleased with him), as marfu', in similar wording. It will also come connected through another route, which is the one that follows, from the narration of Ibn Mardawayh.]]

Abu Bakr ibn Mardawayh said: Sulayman ibn Ahmad informed us, Abdullah ibn Wuhayb al-Ghazzi informed us, Muhammad ibn Abi al-Sarri al-Asqalani informed us, Muhammad ibn Abdullah al-Tamimi informed us, from al-Qasim ibn Muhammad al-Thaqafi, from Abu Idris al-Khawlani, from Abu Dharr al-Ghifari, that he asked the Prophet ﷺ about the Kursi. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "By the One in whose hand is my soul, the seven heavens and the seven earths, in relation to the Kursi, are no more than a ring dropped in a desert land. And the excellence of the Throne over the Kursi is like the excellence of the desert over that ring." [[In its chain is Muhammad ibn Abi al-Sarri al-Asqalani. Abu Hatim declared him weak, while Ibn Ma'in deemed him trustworthy, and Ibn Adi said: "He makes many errors."]]

Al-Hafiz Abu Ya'la al-Mawsili said in his Musnad: Zuhayr told us, Ibn Abi Bukayr told us, Israil told us, from Abu Ishaq, from Abdullah ibn Khalifah, from Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: A woman came to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and said: "Pray to Allah that He admit me into Paradise." He said: So he glorified the Lord, blessed and exalted, and said: "His Kursi extends over the heavens and the earth, and it creaks [with a sound] like the creaking of a new saddle from its weight." [[Al-Diya' related it through his route in al-Mukhtarah, no. 151.]]

The Hafiz al-Bazzar related it in his well-known Musnad, and ʿAbd ibn Humayd and Ibn Jarir in their two tafsirs, and al-Tabarani and Ibn Abi ʿAsim in their two books of Sunnah, and the Hafiz Diya' [al-Maqdisi] in his book *al-Mukhtar*, from the hadith of Abu Ishaq al-Sabiʿi, from ʿAbd Allah ibn Khalifa. [Variant in manuscript A: "ʿan Abi al-Qasim".] He is not the well-known transmitter, and there is doubt about his hearing from ʿUmar. [Sources: Musnad al-Bazzar no. 39 (Kashf al-Astar); Tafsir al-Tabari (5/400); al-Sunnah of Ibn Abi ʿAsim no. 574; al-Mukhtarah of al-Diya' al-Maqdisi nos. 151–154.] Then some of them relate it from him from ʿUmar as a mawquf (a report ending at a companion), and some relate it from him as a mursal (a report with a missing companion), and some add a strange addition to its text, and some omit it. [The mursal report: Tafsir al-Tabari (5/400).]

Even stranger than this is the hadith of Jubayr ibn Mutʿim concerning the description of the Throne, as related by Abu Dawud in his book of Sunnah from his Sunan. [Sunan Abi Dawud no. 4726.] And Allah knows best.

Ibn Mardawayh and others related hadiths from Buraydah, Jabir and others about the placing of the Kursi (Footstool) on the Day of Resurrection for the judgment to be decided, and the apparent meaning is that this is other than what is mentioned in this verse.

Some of those who speak on the science of astronomy (ʿilm al-hayʾah) among the Muslims have claimed that the Kursi, according to them, is the eighth sphere, which is the sphere of the fixed stars, above which is the ninth sphere, which is the sphere of the aether, and it is called al-Atlas. Others have refuted them on this.

Ibn Jarir related through the route of Juwaybir from al-Hasan al-Basri that he used to say: the Kursi is the Throne. But the correct view is that the Kursi is other than the Throne, and the Throne is greater than it, as the reports and narrations indicate. Ibn Jarir relied on the hadith of ʿAbd Allah ibn Khalifa from ʿUmar in this matter, but in my view there is doubt about its authenticity. And Allah knows best.

* *

His saying: ﴿And their preserving does not weary Him﴾ means: it does not burden Him nor does the preservation of the heavens and the earth, and whoever is in them and between them, tire Him. Rather, that is easy for Him and simple before Him. He is the One who stands over every soul for what it has earned, the Watcher over all things, so nothing escapes Him and nothing is hidden from Him. All things are insignificant before Him, humble, abased, small in comparison to Him, needy and poor. He is the Self-Sufficient, the Praiseworthy, the Doer of what He wills, who is not questioned about what He does, while they will be questioned. He is the Subduer of everything, the Reckoner over everything, the Watcher. The Most High, the Mighty; there is no god but Him and no lord besides Him. So His saying ﴿And He is the Most High, the Mighty﴾ is like His saying ﴿the Most High, the Great﴾, and like His saying [addition from manuscripts A and Q:] ﴿the Great, the Exalted﴾ [al-Ra'd: 9].

These verses and what is similar to them in the sound hadiths: the best approach concerning them is the way of the righteous predecessors (al-salaf al-salih), which is to let them pass as they came, without asking how (takyif) and without likening (tashbih).

Ibn Kathir said, commenting on Allah's words: ﴿There is no compulsion in religion﴾. That is, do not compel anyone to enter the religion of Islam, for its proofs and evidences are clear, manifest and plain, and no one needs to be forced to enter it. Rather, whoever Allah guides to Islam, opens his breast to it and illuminates his insight, enters it with clear understanding. But whoever Allah blinds the heart of, and sets a seal upon his hearing and his sight, entering the religion while compelled and coerced will not benefit him. They have mentioned that the cause of the revelation of this verse concerned a group of the Ansar, although its ruling is general.

Ibn Jarir said: Ibn Bashshar narrated to us, Ibn Abi 'Adiy narrated to us, from Shu'bah, from Abu Bishr, from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: A woman would be barren, and she would make a vow upon herself that if a child of hers survived, she would make him a Jew. When the Banu al-Nadir were expelled, among them were sons of the Ansar, and they said: "We will not leave our sons." So Allah, Mighty and Majestic, revealed: ﴿There is no compulsion in religion. Right guidance has become distinct from error﴾.

Abu Dawud and al-Nasa'i both related it from Bundar with the same chain. It is also reported through other routes from Shu'bah with similar wording. Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn Hibban in his Sahih also related it from the hadith of Shu'bah with this chain. Likewise, Mujahid, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, al-Sha'bi, al-Hasan al-Basri and others mentioned that it was revealed concerning this matter.

Muhammad ibn Ishaq said, from Muhammad ibn Abi Muhammad al-Jurashi, from [a client (mawla)] of Zayd ibn Thabit, from 'Ikrimah or from Sa'id [ibn Jubayr], from Ibn 'Abbas, regarding His words ﴿There is no compulsion in religion﴾, he said: It was revealed concerning a man from the Ansar of Banu Salim ibn 'Awf called al-Husayni, who had two Christian sons, while he himself was a Muslim. He said to the Prophet ﷺ: "Shall I not compel them, since they have refused anything but Christianity?" So Allah revealed this concerning him.

Ibn Jarir related it. Al-Suddi related something similar and added: The two had become Christians at the hands of merchants who came from Syria carrying oil. When the two resolved to go with them, their father wished to compel them, and he asked the Messenger of Allah ﷺ to send someone after them, and then this verse was revealed.

Ibn Abi Hatim said: My father narrated to us, 'Amr ibn 'Awf narrated to us, Sharik informed us, from Abu Hilal, from Usaq, who said: I was a Christian slave of 'Umar ibn al-Khattab in their religion. He would offer me Islam and I would refuse, and he would say: ﴿There is no compulsion in religion﴾, and he would say: "O Usaq, if you were to embrace Islam, we would seek your help in some affairs of the Muslims."

A large group of scholars held that this verse applies to the People of the Book and those who entered their religion before abrogation and alteration, when they pay the jizyah (poll tax). Others said: Rather, it has been abrogated by the verse of fighting (ayat al-qital), and all nations must be called to enter the upright religion of Islam. If any of them refuses to enter it and does not submit to it, or does not pay the jizyah, he is to be fought until he is killed. This is the meaning of compulsion. Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿You will be called to a people of great military might; you will fight them, or they will submit﴾ [al-Fath: 16]. And Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿O Prophet, strive against the disbelievers and the hypocrites, and be harsh with them﴾ [al-Tahrim: 9]. And Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿O you who have believed, fight those of the disbelievers who are adjacent to you, and let them find harshness in you; and know that Allah is with the righteous﴾ [al-Tawbah: 123]. And in the Sahih: "Your Lord marvels at a people who are led into Paradise in chains." (Sahih al-Bukhari, from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with him). He means the captives who are brought to the lands of Islam in shackles, fetters, bonds and chains; then after that they embrace Islam, their deeds and inner states become righteous, and they become among the people of Paradise.

As for the hadith that Imam Ahmad related: Yahya narrated to us, from Humayd, from Anas, that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said to a man: "Embrace Islam." He said: "I find myself averse." He said: "Even if you are averse." (Musnad, 3/181). Its chain is sahih (sound) in three links, but it does not belong to this category, for the Prophet ﷺ did not compel him to Islam; rather he invited him to it, and the man informed him that his soul was not receptive to it, but was averse. So he said to him: "Embrace Islam even though you are averse, for Allah will grant you good intention and sincerity."

* *

As for His words: ﴿Whoever disbelieves in the Taghut and believes in Allah has grasped the most trustworthy handhold, which will not break. And Allah is Hearing and Knowing﴾. That is, whoever renounces the rivals (andad), the idols, and whatever Satan calls to of worshipping everything that is worshipped besides Allah, and affirms the oneness of Allah, worships Him alone and testifies that there is no god but Him, ﴿has grasped the most trustworthy handhold﴾, that is, he has firmly established himself in his affair and remained steadfast upon the best path and the straight way.

Abu al-Qasim al-Baghawi said: Abu Rawh al-Baladi narrated to us, Abu al-Ahwas Sallam ibn Sulaym narrated to us, from Abu Ishaq, from Hassan (who is Ibn Fa'id al-Abasi), who said: 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, said: "Al-Jibt is magic, and al-Taghut is Satan. Courage and cowardice are dispositions that exist in men: the brave man fights for one he does not know, and the coward flees from his own mother. A man's nobility is his religion, his lineage is his character, even if he is Persian or Nabataean." Likewise Ibn Jarir (5/417) and Ibn Abi Hatim related it from the hadith of al-Thawri, from Abu Ishaq, from Hassan ibn Fa'id al-Abasi, from 'Umar, and mentioned it.

The meaning of his saying regarding al-Taghut is that it is Satan, who is extremely powerful, for it encompasses every evil that the people of the Jahiliyyah (pre-Islamic ignorance) practised, from worshipping idols, to judging by them, to seeking help from them.

* *

As for His words: ﴿Has grasped the most trustworthy handhold, which will not break﴾, that is: he has grasped from the religion the strongest means. It is likened to the most trustworthy handhold that does not break, for it is in itself firm, sound and strong, and its binding is powerful and tight. Therefore He said: ﴿Has grasped the most trustworthy handhold, which will not break. And Allah is Hearing and Knowing﴾.

Mujahid said: ﴿Has grasped the most trustworthy handhold﴾ means: faith (al-iman). Al-Suddi said: it is Islam. Sa'id ibn Jubayr and al-Dahhak said: it means "There is no god but Allah." And from Anas ibn Malik: ﴿the most trustworthy handhold﴾ is the Qur'an. And from Salim ibn Abi al-Ja'd, he said: it is love for the sake of Allah and hatred for the sake of Allah.

All these statements are sound, and there is no contradiction among them.

Mu'adh ibn Jabal said, regarding His words ﴿which will not break﴾: that is, there is no severance from it short of entering Paradise.

Mujahid and Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: ﴿has grasped the most trustworthy handhold, which will not break﴾, then he recited: ﴿Indeed, Allah does not change the condition of a people until they change what is in themselves﴾ [al-Ra'd: 11].

Imam Ahmad said: Ishaq ibn Yusuf narrated to us, Ibn 'Awn narrated to us, from Muhammad, from Qays ibn 'Abbad, who said: I was in the mosque when a man came, with a trace of humility upon his face, entered, and prayed two rak'ahs, shortening them. The people said: "This is a man of Paradise." When he left, I followed him until he entered his house, and I entered with him and spoke with him. When he became at ease, I said to him: "When you entered the mosque earlier, the people said such and such." He said: "Glory be to Allah! It is not right for anyone to say what he does not know. I will tell you why: I saw a dream during the time of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, and I related it to him. I saw as if I were in a green garden" (Ibn 'Awn said: he mentioned its greenness and expanse), "in its middle was a column of iron, its base in the earth and its top in the sky, and at its top was a handhold (urwah). I was told: 'Climb it.' I said: 'I cannot.' Then a servant (Minsaf; Ibn 'Awn said: it is al-Wasif) came to me and lifted my garments from behind and said: 'Climb.' So I climbed until I took hold of the handhold. He said: 'Hold fast to the handhold.' Then I woke up and it was still in my hand. I came to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and related it to him. He said: 'As for the garden, it is the garden of Islam; as for the column, it is the pillar of Islam; and as for the handhold, it is the most trustworthy handhold. You are upon Islam until you die.'" (Musnad, 5/452).

He said: And he was 'Abdullah ibn Salam. Both (al-Bukhari and Muslim) related it in their Sahihs from the hadith of 'Abdullah ibn 'Awn. Al-Bukhari also related it through another route, from Muhammad ibn Sirin, with the same content.

Another route and different wording: Imam Ahmad said: Hasan ibn Musa and 'Affan narrated to us, both said: Hammad ibn Salamah narrated to us, from 'Asim ibn Bahdalah, from al-Musayyab ibn Rafi', from Kharashah ibn al-Hurr, who said: I came to Madinah and sat with some elders in the mosque of the Prophet ﷺ. An old man came leaning on his staff, and the people said: "Whoever would like to look at a man of Paradise, let him look at this one." He stood behind a pillar and prayed two rak'ahs. I got up to him and said to him: "Some of the people have said such and such." He said: "Paradise belongs to Allah; He admits whom He wills. I saw a dream during the time of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ: I saw as if a man came to me and said: 'Come.' So I went with him, and he led me along a great path. A road appeared to my left, and I wanted to take it. He said: 'You are not of its people.' Then a road appeared to my right, and I took it until it ended at a slippery mountain. He took hold of my hand and lifted me, and suddenly I was on its summit. I did not stay steady and I could not hold on, when there was an iron pillar at its top with a golden ring. He took my hand and lifted me until I took hold of the handhold, and he said: 'Hold fast.' I said: 'Yes.' Then he struck the pillar with his foot and I held fast to the handhold." I related it to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, and he said: "You have seen good. As for the great path, it is the gathering place (al-mahshar). As for the road that appeared to your left, it is the road of the people of the Fire, and you are not of its people. As for the road that appeared to your right, it is the road of the people of Paradise. As for the slippery mountain, it is the abode of the martyrs. As for the handhold you held, it is the handhold of Islam; so hold fast to it until you die." He said: "I only hope to be among the people of Paradise." He said: And behold, he was 'Abdullah ibn Salam (Musnad, 5/452, 453).

Thus al-Nasa'i related it from Ahmad ibn Sulayman, from 'Affan, and Ibn Majah from Abu Bakr ibn Abi Shaybah, from al-Hasan ibn Musa al-Ashyab, both from Hammad ibn Salamah with similar content. Muslim related it in his Sahih from the hadith of al-A'mash, from Sulayman ibn Mihran, from Kharashah ibn al-Hurr al-Fazari.

He, exalted is He, informs us that He guides whoever pursues His good pleasure to the paths of peace, and brings His believing servants out of the darknesses of disbelief, doubt and uncertainty into the light of the truth, which is clear, manifest, evident, plain and radiant. And that the disbelievers, their only protector is the devils, who make attractive to them the ignorance and misguidance they are in, and who drive them and lead them away from the way of truth toward disbelief and falsehood. ﴿Those are the companions of the Fire; they will abide therein forever.﴾

For this reason He, exalted is He, used the singular word "light" and the plural "darknesses," because the truth is one, while disbelief has many kinds, and all of them are false, as He said: ﴿And [say], "This is My path, straight, so follow it, and do not follow other ways, lest they separate you from His way. This He has enjoined upon you that you may become righteous."﴾ [al-An'am: 153]. He also said: ﴿and made the darknesses and the light﴾ [al-An'am: 1], and He said: ﴿[and their shadows incline] from the right and the left﴾ [al-Nahl: 48]. There are other verses of this kind, whose wording indicates the singularity of the truth and the spreading, multiplicity and diversity of falsehood.

Ibn Abi Hatim said: My father narrated to us, from 'Ali ibn Maysarah, from 'Abd al-'Aziz ibn Abi 'Uthman, from Musa ibn 'Ubayda, from Ayyub ibn Khalid, who said: "The people of desires [[In A: "the markets".]] will be raised up – or he said: the people of trials – so whoever's desire was faith, his trial will be white and luminous, and whoever's desire was disbelief, his trial will be black and dark." Then he recited this verse: ﴿Allah is the Ally of those who believe; He brings them out of the darknesses into the light. And those who disbelieve, their allies are the taghut; they bring them out of the light into the darknesses. Those are the companions of the Fire; they will abide therein forever.﴾

This is the one who argued with Abraham about his Lord, when Allah had given him the kingdom. He was the king of Babylon, Nimrod son of Canaan son of Kush son of Ham son of Noah. It is also said: Nimrod son of Falikh son of Abir son of Shalikh son of Arpakhshad son of Shem son of Noah. The first genealogy is the view of Mujahid and others.

Mujahid said: Four people ruled the whole world, its east and its west: two believers and two disbelievers. The two believers were Solomon son of David and Dhu al-Qarnayn. The two disbelievers were Nimrod [son of Canaan] [[Addition from ج.]] and Nebuchadnezzar. And Allah knows best.

The meaning of His words ﴿Have you not considered﴾, i.e., with your heart, O Muhammad, ﴿the one who argued with Abraham about his Lord﴾, i.e., [concerning] [[Addition from أ and و.]] the existence of his Lord. This is because he denied that there is any god other than himself, just as Pharaoh said afterwards to his chiefs: ﴿I know of no god for you other than myself﴾ [al-Qasas 28:38]. What led him to this tyranny, this gross disbelief and this fierce obstinacy was only his arrogance and the length of his reign. It is said that he remained in his kingdom for four hundred years. Therefore He said: ﴿because Allah had given him the kingdom﴾. It seems that he asked Abraham for proof of the existence of the Lord to whom he was calling, so Abraham said: ﴿My Lord is the One who gives life and causes death﴾. That is, the proof of His existence is the coming into being of these observable things after their non-existence, and their non-existence after their existence. This is a proof of the existence of the Agent who chooses, by necessity, because these things did not come into being by themselves; they must have an originator who brought them into being, and He is the Lord to whom I call, to worship Him alone, with no partner. At that point the one who argued, namely Nimrod, said: ﴿I give life and cause death﴾.

Qatadah, Muhammad ibn Ishaq, al-Suddi and others said: This means that I am brought two men who deserve execution; I order one of them to be killed, and he is killed, and I pardon the other, and he is not killed. That is the meaning of giving life and causing death.

The apparent meaning, and Allah knows best, is that he did not intend this, because it is not an answer to what Abraham said, nor does it have the same meaning, since it does not prevent the existence of the Creator. Rather, he intended to claim this status for himself out of obstinacy and stubbornness, and to give the impression that he was the one who does this, and that he is the one who gives life and causes death, just as Pharaoh followed him in saying: ﴿I know of no god for you other than myself﴾. Therefore, when he made this stubborn claim, Abraham said to him: ﴿Indeed, Allah brings the sun from the east, so bring it from the west﴾. That is: if you are as you claim, that you give life and cause death, then the One who gives life and causes death is the One who directs existence, in creating its essences and subjecting its stars and their movements. This sun rises every day from the east; so if you are a god as you claim, who gives life and causes death, then bring it from the west. When he knew his inability and his helplessness, and that he could not continue the obstinacy in this position, he was ﴿confounded﴾, i.e., silenced, so he could not speak, and the proof was established against him. Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿And Allah does not guide the wrongdoing people﴾, i.e., He does not inspire them with proof or evidence; rather, their argument is void in the sight of their Lord, and upon them is wrath, and for them is severe punishment.

This interpretation of the verse is better than what many of the logicians (al-mantiqiyyin) have mentioned, that Abraham's shift from the first argument to the second was a move from one proof to a clearer one. Some of them even used a faulty expression. That is not what they said; rather, the first argument serves as a preface to the second, and it demonstrates the falsehood of what Nimrod claimed in both the first and the second. And to Allah belong all praise and grace.

Al-Suddi mentioned that this debate took place between Abraham and Nimrod after Abraham came out of the fire, and the king had not met him until that day, so this debate occurred between them.

ʿAbd al-Razzaq narrated from Maʿmar, from Zayd ibn Aslam: Nimrod had [in his hand] [[In أ: "كان بيده" (had in his hand).]] food, and people would come to him to buy grain. Abraham came among those who came for grain, and this debate took place between them. Nimrod did not give Abraham food as he gave the people; rather, Abraham left with no food at all. When he drew near to his family, he deliberately took a heap of earth and filled his two saddlebags with it, saying: "I will occupy my family with this when I come to them." When he arrived, he unloaded his baggage, came in, reclined and fell asleep. His wife Sarah stood up to the two saddlebags and found them full of good food, so she prepared a meal from it. When Abraham woke up, he found what they had prepared, and he said: "Where did this come from?" She said: "From what you brought." He recognised that it was a provision that Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, had given them.

Zayd ibn Aslam also said: Allah sent to that tyrant king an angel instructing him to believe in Allah. He refused. Then he called him a second time, and he refused; then a third time, and he refused, and said: "Gather your hosts, and I will gather mine." So Nimrod gathered his army and his soldiers at sunrise. Allah sent against them a swarm of gnats, so thick that they could not see the sun. Allah set them upon them, and they ate their flesh and blood and left their bones exposed. One of them entered the nostril of the king and remained in his nostrils for four hundred years. Allah punished him with it, and throughout this whole period he would beat his head with hammers, until Allah destroyed him through it.

Commentary of Ibn Kathir (Tafsir al-Quran al-'Azim) on surah 2, verse 259:

The words of Allah the Exalted have already been mentioned: ﴿Have you not considered the one who argued with Abraham about his Lord, when Allah had given him kingship?﴾ This carries the sense of the words: "Have you seen the likeness of the one who argued with Abraham about his Lord?" For this reason He joined to it the words: ﴿Or like the one who passed by a town that had fallen into ruin upon its roofs?﴾ The scholars differed over who this passer-by was. Ibn Abi Hatim related from Issam ibn Rawwad, from Adam ibn Abi Iyas, from Israil, from Abu Ishaq, from Najiyah ibn Ka'b, from Ali ibn Abi Talib, that he said: "He was Uzair."

Ibn Jarir also related it from Najiyah himself. Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported this from Ibn Abbas, al-Hasan, Qatadah, al-Suddi and Sulayman ibn Buraydah, and this view is the well-known one.

Wahb ibn Munabbih and Abdullah ibn Ubayd ibn Umayr said: he was Armiya ibn Halqiya. Muhammad ibn Ishaq said, from one whom he does not suspect, from Wahb ibn Munabbih, that he said: "And this is the name of al-Khidr, peace be upon him."

Ibn Abi Hatim said: My father told us, saying: I heard Sulayman ibn Muhammad al-Yasari al-Jari (of the people of al-Jar, the cousin of Mutarrif) say: I heard a man from the people of Syria say: "The one whom Allah caused to die for a hundred years and then raised up was named Hizqil ibn Bura."

Mujahid ibn Jabr said: he was a man from the Children of Israel.

[Many have mentioned that he died when he was forty years old, and Allah raised him up while he was still that age. He had a son who reached the age of one hundred and twenty, and his son's son reached ninety, while the grandfather was young, and his son and his son's son were two elderly men who had reached decrepitude. Some of the poets recited to me:

The head of a youth turned black before his son's,
and before his son, his son's son was older.
He sees himself as an old man who walks with a staff,
while his beard is black and his head is hoary.
His son has no strength, nor any vigour;
he stands as a small child stands, and stumbles.
His son's age is forty, its passing lengthy,
and his son's son among the people is ninety, grey-haired.]

As for the town, the well-known view is that it was Jerusalem (Bayt al-Maqdis), which he passed after Bukhtnassar (Nebuchadnezzar) had laid it waste and slain its people. ﴿And it was empty﴾, meaning there was no one in it, from the expression: the house became empty (khawat al-dar, takhwi khawa'an wa khuwiyan).

* *

His words ﴿upon its roofs﴾ mean that its roofs and walls had fallen onto its courtyards. He stood reflecting on what its state had come to after its great prosperity, and said: ﴿How will Allah bring this to life after its death?﴾ This was because of what he saw of its ruin, the severity of its desolation, and its remoteness from returning to what it had been. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿So Allah caused him to die for a hundred years, then raised him up.﴾ They said: the town was rebuilt after seventy years had passed since his death, its inhabitants were restored, and the Children of Israel returned to it. When Allah, Mighty and Majestic, raised him after his death, the first thing Allah brought back to life in him were his eyes, so that he could look with them at the handiwork of Allah in him, how He was giving life to his body. When he stood up whole, Allah said to him, that is through an angel: ﴿How long have you remained?﴾ He said: ﴿I have remained a day or part of a day.﴾ They said: that was because he had died at the start of the day, and Allah raised him at the end of the day. When he saw the sun still present, he thought it was the sun of that same day, so he said: ﴿or part of a day.﴾ He said: ﴿Nay, you have remained a hundred years. Look at your food and your drink, they have not changed with time.﴾ This was because, as was mentioned, he had with him grapes, figs and grape juice; he found them as he had left them, nothing in them had changed: the juice had not turned, the figs had not soured or rotted, and the grapes had not decayed. ﴿And look at your donkey﴾, meaning: how Allah, Mighty and Majestic, gives it life while you are watching. ﴿And that We may make you a sign for the people﴾, meaning: a proof of the Return. ﴿And look at the bones, how We raise them﴾, meaning: We lift them up so that some are assembled upon others.

Al-Hakim related in his Mustadrak, from the hadith of Nafi' ibn Abi Nu'aym, from Isma'il ibn Abi Hakim, from Kharijah ibn Zayd ibn Thabit, from his father, that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ recited: ﴿how We raise them﴾ with the letter zay, then said: "Its chain is sound, though they did not record it." [[Al-Mustadrak (2/234); al-Dhahabi criticised it saying: "In it is Isma'il ibn Qays, a descendant of Ibn Thabit, and they have declared him weak."]]

It was also read as (nunshiruha), meaning: We give it life, as Mujahid said. ﴿Then We clothe them with flesh.﴾

Al-Suddi and others said: the bones of his donkey were scattered around him, to the right and to the left, and he looked at them while they were glistening white. Allah sent a wind which gathered them from every place in that area, then each bone was fitted into its place until it became a standing donkey made of bones with no flesh on it. Then Allah clothed it with flesh, sinews, veins and skin, and Allah sent an angel who blew into the donkey's nostrils, and it brayed entirely by the permission of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, and all of this was before the eyes of Uzair. At that point, when all this had become clear to him, ﴿he said: I know that Allah is over all things capable.﴾ That is: I know this, and I have seen it with my own eyes, so I am the most knowledgeable person of my time about it. Others read: "qāla i'lam" (he said: know!), as a command to him to acquire knowledge.

They mentioned, in answer to the question of Ibrahim (peace be upon him), several reasons. Among them: when he said to Nimrod, ﴿My Lord is He who gives life and causes death﴾, he wished to ascend from *'ilm al-yaqin* (knowledge of certainty, the certainty that comes through reasoning) in this matter to *'ayn al-yaqin* (the certainty of seeing with one's own eyes), and to witness it directly. So he said: ﴿My Lord, show me how You give life to the dead.' He said, 'Do you not believe?' He said, 'Yes, but that my heart may be at rest.﴾

As for the hadith that al-Bukhari narrated at this verse: Ahmad ibn Salih narrated to us, Ibn Wahb narrated to us, Yunus informed me, from Ibn Shihab, from Abu Salamah and Sa'id, from Abu Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "We have more right to doubt than Ibrahim, when he said: 'My Lord, show me how You give life to the dead.' He said: 'Do you not believe?' He said: 'Yes, but that my heart may be at rest.'" Muslim also narrated it, from Harmalah ibn Yahya, from Ibn Wahb, with the same wording.[[Sahih al-Bukhari, no. (4537), and Sahih Muslim, no. (151).]] Here, the meaning of doubt is not what someone without knowledge might understand, and this is without any disagreement. Answers have been given to this hadith in several ways. The first of them is the statement of Isma'il al-Muzani: the Prophet (ﷺ) did not doubt, nor did Ibrahim (peace be upon him), that Allah, glorified is He, is able to give life to the dead; rather, the matter occurred to an ignorant person who answered them in what they asked. Al-Khattabi said regarding his words, "We have more right to doubt than Ibrahim": it is not an admission of doubt on his own part or on Ibrahim's part; rather, it negates doubt from both of them. He says: if I do not doubt Allah's power to give life to the dead, then Ibrahim is more deserving of not doubting. He said this out of humility and self-abasement. Likewise his words: "Had I remained in prison as long as Yusuf remained, I would have answered the caller." In it is the indication that the request of Ibrahim did not arise from doubt, but from the desire for increased knowledge through direct observation, because it gives a knowledge and tranquility that reasoning does not give. It was also said: the Prophet (ﷺ) said this out of humility and to give precedence to Ibrahim's words: "Do you not believe?" He said: "Yes, I have believed."

I think this is an alteration by the copyist, because there was a blank left in the original at that place. Shaykh Ahmad Shakir said at this point in his book *al-'Umdah*, which is an abridgement of the tafsir of Ibn Kathir (2/170):

"There is a blank here in the Azhar manuscript and in the printed edition. Perhaps the Hafiz Ibn Kathir left it so that he could write the statements on this matter, but then he did not do so, through forgetfulness or oversight. Hafiz Ibn Hajar expounded at length on the statements of the scholars in this matter in *Fath al-Bari* (6/294, 295). The best of these, in my opinion, is the statement of Ibn 'Atiyyah: 'The hadith is based on the negation of doubt, and the doubt meant in it is passing thoughts that do not settle. As for doubt in the technical sense, which is suspension between two matters without preference for one over the other, it is definitely negated for the Friend (Khalil, Ibrahim), because it is unlikely to occur from one whose faith has taken firm root in his heart, so how about one who has reached the rank of prophethood? Also, since the question came with 'how' (kayfa), it indicates the state of a thing that exists and is established for both the questioner and the one questioned, as you say, 'How did so-and-so know?' So 'how' in the verse is a question about the manner of giving life, not about the giving of life itself, which is established and affirmed.' Another said: its meaning is: if we do not doubt, then Ibrahim is more deserving of not doubting; that is, if doubt were to reach the prophets, I would be more deserving of it than he is. You know that I did not doubt, so know that he did not doubt either, and he only said that out of humility."

* *

As for His words, ﴿Take four birds and train them to come to you﴾, the exegetes differed about what these four were, although there is no benefit in specifying them, since if there were some benefit in it, the Qur'an would have stated it explicitly. It is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that he said: they were the *ghurnuq* (a kind of water bird), the peacock, the rooster, and the dove. And also from him: he took a *wazz* (a water bird), a *ra'l* (a young ostrich), a rooster, and a peacock. Mujahid and 'Ikrimah said: they were a dove, a rooster, a peacock, and a crow.

* *

As for His words, ﴿train them to come to you﴾, that means: cut them up. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas, 'Ikrimah, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, Abu Malik, Abu al-Aswad al-Du'ali, Wahb ibn Munabbih, al-Hasan, al-Suddi, and others.

Al-'Awfi said, from Ibn 'Abbas: ﴿train them﴾ means: bind them. When he had bound them, he slaughtered them, then placed a portion of them on each mountain. They mentioned that he took four birds and slaughtered them, then cut them up, plucked their feathers, tore them apart, and mixed some of them with others, then divided them into parts and placed on each mountain a portion of them. It was said: four mountains. And it was said: seven. Ibn 'Abbas said: he took their heads in his hand, then Allah, mighty and majestic, commanded him to call them. He called them as Allah had commanded him. So he began to watch the feathers flying to the feathers, the blood to the blood, the flesh to the flesh, and the parts of each bird joining one another, until each bird stood up on its own, and they came to him walking swiftly, so that the vision he had asked for would be more complete. Each bird came to take its head, which was in Ibrahim's hand, and if he offered it a head other than its own, it refused. When he offered it its own head, it was joined with the rest of its body by the power and might of Allah. For this reason He said: ﴿And know that Allah is Mighty, Wise﴾, meaning: Mighty, nothing overcomes Him, nothing prevents Him, and whatever He wills occurs without any hindrance, for He is the Great, the Subduer of everything. Wise in His statements, His actions, His law, and His decree.

'Abd al-Razzaq said: Ma'mar informed us, from Ayyub, regarding His words, ﴿but that my heart may be at rest﴾, that he said: Ibn 'Abbas said: there is no verse in the Qur'an more hopeful to me than this one.

Ibn Jarir said: Muhammad ibn al-Muthanna narrated to me, Muhammad ibn Ja'far narrated to us, Shu'bah narrated to us, I heard Zayd ibn 'Ali narrate, from a man, from Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib, who said: 'Abd Allah ibn 'Abbas and 'Abd Allah ibn 'Amr ibn al-'As agreed to meet. He said: and we were young. One of them said to the other: "Which verse in the Book of Allah is most hopeful for this Ummah?" 'Abd Allah ibn 'Amr said: the words of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿O My servants who have transgressed against themselves, do not despair of the mercy of Allah; indeed, Allah forgives all sins﴾ [al-Zumar: 53], and so on. Ibn 'Abbas said: As for you saying this, and that it is the most hopeful for this Ummah, then the words of Ibrahim are more hopeful than it: ﴿My Lord, show me how You give life to the dead.' He said, 'Do you not believe?' He said, 'Yes, but that my heart may be at rest.﴾[[Tafsir al-Tabari (5/489).]]

Ibn Abi Hatim said: my father narrated to us, 'Abd Allah ibn Salih, the scribe of al-Layth, narrated to us, Ibn Abi Salamah narrated to me, from Muhammad ibn al-Munkadir, that he said: 'Abd Allah ibn 'Abbas met 'Abd Allah ibn 'Amr ibn al-'As, and Ibn 'Abbas said to Ibn 'Amr ibn al-'As: "Which verse in the Qur'an is most hopeful to you?" 'Abd Allah ibn 'Amr said: the words of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic: ﴿O My servants who have transgressed against themselves, do not despair of the mercy of Allah﴾, and so on. Ibn 'Abbas said: "But I say: the words of Allah: ﴿And when Ibrahim said, 'My Lord, show me how You give life to the dead.' He said, 'Do you not believe?' He said, 'Yes.'﴾" So He was pleased with Ibrahim's saying: "Yes." He said: this is for what arises in souls and what Satan whispers.

Likewise al-Hakim narrated it in *al-Mustadrak*, from Abu 'Abd Allah Muhammad ibn Ya'qub ibn al-Akhram, from Ibrahim ibn 'Abd Allah al-Sa'di, from Bishr ibn 'Umar al-Zahrani, from 'Abd al-'Aziz ibn Abi Salamah, with its chain, the same. Then he said: its chain is sound, but they (al-Bukhari and Muslim) did not narrate it.[[Al-Mustadrak (1/60), and al-Dhahabi criticized it, saying that there is a break in its chain.]]

This is a parable which Allah, exalted is He, struck to illustrate the multiplication of reward for one who spends in His way and seeks His good pleasure, and that a good deed is multiplied tenfold up to seven hundred times. He says: ﴿The example of those who spend their wealth in the way of Allah﴾. Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: "In the obedience of Allah." Makhul said: "It means spending in jihad, such as on the tethering of horses, preparing weapons, and other things." Shabib ibn Bishr narrated from Ikrimah, from Ibn 'Abbas: "Jihad and Hajj; a dirham is multiplied in both up to seven hundred times." Therefore Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿Like a grain that grows seven spikes, in each spike a hundred grains﴾.

This parable is more forceful upon the souls than mentioning the number seven hundred, for it indicates that Allah, mighty and majestic, causes good deeds to grow for their doers, just as the farmer's crop grows for one who sows it in good soil. The Sunnah (the prophetic tradition) has also come with the multiplication of a good deed up to seven hundred times. Imam Ahmad said:

Ziyad ibn al-Rabi' Abu Khidash narrated to us: Wasil, the client of Ibn 'Uyaynah, narrated to us, from Bashshar ibn Abi Sayf al-Jurmi, from 'Iyad ibn Ghatif, who said: "We entered upon Abu 'Ubaydah [ibn al-Jarrah] [[Addition from al-Musnad (1/195).]] to visit him during an illness that had afflicted him, while his wife Tuhayfah was sitting at his head. We said: 'How did Abu 'Ubaydah spend the night?' She said: 'By Allah, he spent the night in reward.' Abu 'Ubaydah said: 'I did not spend the night in reward.' He was turned with his face toward the wall, so he turned his face to the people and said: 'Will you not ask me about what I said?' They said: 'What you said did not impress us so that we should ask you about it.' He said: 'I heard the Messenger of Allah ﷺ say: "Whoever spends a generous expenditure in the way of Allah, it is (multiplied) by seven hundred. Whoever spends on himself and his family, or visits a sick person, or removes something harmful, then the good deed is (multiplied) tenfold. Fasting is a shield as long as one does not tear it. Whoever Allah, mighty and majestic, tests with an affliction in his body, it is for him an expiation of sins."'"

Al-Nasa'i narrated part of it in the chapter on fasting, from the narration of Wasil, and from another route as a mawquf (a report ending at a Companion) [[Al-Musnad (1/195) and Sunan al-Nasa'i (4/167, 168).]].

Another hadith: Imam Ahmad said: Muhammad ibn Ja'far narrated to us: Shu'bah narrated to us, from Sulayman, I heard Abu 'Amr al-Shaybani, from Ibn Mas'ud, that a man gave in charity a she-camel with a halter in the way of Allah, so the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "On the Day of Resurrection you will come with seven hundred halter-bearing she-camels."

Muslim and al-Nasa'i also narrated it, from the hadith of Sulayman ibn Mihran, from al-A'mash, with the same wording [[Sahih Muslim no. (1892) and Sunan al-Nasa'i (6/49).]]. The wording of Muslim is: A man came with a halter-bearing she-camel and said: "O Messenger of Allah, this is in the way of Allah." He said: "For you, on the Day of Resurrection, in exchange for it, are seven hundred she-camels."

Another hadith: Ahmad said: Amr ibn Majma' Abu al-Mundhir al-Kindi narrated to us: Ibrahim al-Hijri informed us, from Abu al-Ahwas, from 'Abdullah ibn Mas'ud, who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Indeed Allah, mighty and majestic, has made the good deed of the son of Adam multiplied tenfold, up to seven hundred times, except fasting. Fasting is for Me and I reward for it. The fasting person has two joys: a joy at his breaking of the fast and a joy on the Day of Resurrection. And the change in the mouth of the fasting person is more fragrant to Allah than the scent of musk" [[Al-Musnad (1/446).]].

Another hadith: Ahmad said: Waki' narrated to us: al-A'mash narrated to us, from Abu Salih, from Abu Hurayrah, who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Every deed of the son of Adam is multiplied: the good deed tenfold up to seven hundred times, up to what Allah wills." Allah says: "Except fasting, for it is for Me and I reward for it. He leaves his food and his desire for My sake. The fasting person has two joys: a joy at his breaking of the fast, and a joy at meeting his Lord. And the change in his mouth is more fragrant to Allah than the scent of musk. Fasting is a shield, fasting is a shield." Muslim also narrated it, from Abu Bakr ibn Abi Shaybah and Abu Sa'id al-Ashaj, both from Waki', with the same wording [[Sahih Muslim no. (1151).]].

Another hadith: Ahmad said: Husayn ibn 'Ali narrated to us, from Za'idah, from al-Rukayn, from Yusayr ibn 'Amilah, from Khuraym ibn Fatik, who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Whoever spends an expenditure in the way of Allah, it is multiplied by seven hundred times." [[Al-Musnad (4/345).]]

Another hadith: Abu Dawud said: Ahmad ibn 'Amr ibn al-Sarh narrated to us: Ibn Wahb narrated to us, from Yahya ibn Ayyub and Sa'id ibn Abi Ayyub, from Zabban ibn Fa'id, from Sahl ibn Mu'adh, from his father, who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Indeed, prayer, fasting and remembrance are multiplied over the expenditure in the way of Allah by seven hundred times" [[Sunan Abi Dawud no. (2498).]].

Another hadith: Ibn Abi Hatim said: My father narrated to us: Harun ibn 'Abdullah ibn Marwan narrated to us: Ibn Abi Fudayk narrated to us, from al-Khalil ibn 'Abdullah, from al-Hasan, from 'Imran ibn Husayn, from the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, who said: "Whoever sends an expenditure in the way of Allah, and remains in his house, for him, for every dirham, there are seven hundred dirhams on the Day of Resurrection. And whoever fights in the way of Allah, and spends in its direction, for him, for every dirham, there are seven hundred thousand dirhams." Then he recited this verse: ﴿And Allah multiplies for whom He wills﴾. This is a gharib (rare) hadith [[Ibn Majah narrated it in his Sunan no. (2761) from Harun ibn 'Abdullah with the same chain.]].

The hadith of Abu 'Uthman al-Nahdi from Abu Hurayrah concerning the multiplication of a good deed to two thousand thousand good deeds has already passed, at His saying: ﴿Who is it that will lend Allah a goodly loan so He may multiply it for him many times over?﴾ [Al-Baqarah 2:245].

Another hadith: Ibn Mardawayh said: 'Abdullah ibn 'Ubaydullah ibn al-'Askari al-Bazzaz narrated to us: al-Hasan ibn 'Ali ibn Shabib informed us: Mahmud ibn Khalid al-Dimashqi informed us: my father informed us, from 'Isa ibn al-Musayyib, from Nafi', from Ibn 'Umar, who said: When this verse was revealed: ﴿The example of those who spend their wealth in the way of Allah﴾, the Prophet ﷺ said: "My Lord, increase my ummah." He said: So Allah revealed: ﴿Who is it that will lend Allah a goodly loan﴾. He said: "My Lord, increase my ummah." He said: So Allah revealed: ﴿Indeed, the patient will be given their reward without account﴾ [Az-Zumar 39:10].

Abu Hatim Ibn Hibban also narrated it in his Sahih, from Hajib ibn Arkin, from Abu 'Umar Hafs ibn 'Umar ibn 'Abd al-'Aziz al-Muqri', from Abu Isma'il al-Mu'addib, from 'Isa ibn al-Musayyib, from Nafi', from Ibn 'Umar, and he mentioned it [[Sahih Ibn Hibban no. (1648), "mawarid".]].

* *

His saying here: ﴿And Allah multiplies for whom He wills﴾ means: according to the sincerity of his deed. ﴿And Allah is All-Encompassing, All-Knowing﴾ means: His bounty is vast and abundant, more than His creation, and He knows who deserves it and who does not.

Ibn Kathir (Tafsir al-Qur'an al-'Azim) on Surah al-Baqarah, verses 262–264:

Almighty Allah praises those who spend their wealth in the way of Allah and then do not follow what they have spent in good deeds and acts of charity with reminders of favour (mann) toward those to whom they have given. So they do not impose obligations on anyone, nor do they remind people of their kindness, neither by word nor by deed.

* *

His saying: ﴿and no injury﴾ means they do not do anything disagreeable to those they have done good to, by which they would nullify the kindness that preceded it. Then Almighty Allah promised them a great reward for this, saying: ﴿For them is their reward with their Lord﴾, meaning their reward is with Allah, not with anyone other than Him. ﴿Nor will they have fear﴾, meaning regarding what they will face of the terrors of the Day of Resurrection, ﴿nor will they grieve﴾, meaning over what they left behind of children and what they lost of the life of this world and its splendour. They do not regret these things, because they have arrived at what is better for them than all of that.

Then Almighty Allah said: ﴿Kind speech﴾, meaning a good word and a prayer for a Muslim, ﴿and forgiveness﴾, meaning pardoning [a wrong] (ghafara [in another manuscript: "a'fa", i.e., pardon]) for a verbal or physical wrong, ﴿is better than charity followed by injury﴾.

Ibn Abi Hatim said: My father narrated to us, Ibn Nufayl narrated to us, saying: I read to Ma'qil ibn 'Ubaydullah, from 'Amr ibn Dinar, who said: "It has reached us that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: 'There is no charity more beloved to Allah than kind speech. Have you not heard His saying: ﴿Kind speech and forgiveness is better than charity followed by injury﴾?'"

﴿And Allah is Free of need﴾ [meaning: ] free of need from His creation.

﴿Forbearing﴾, meaning He is patient, forgives, pardons, and overlooks them.

Hadiths have been reported prohibiting reminders of favour in charity. In Sahih Muslim, from the narration of Shu'bah, from al-A'mash, from Sulayman ibn Musharr, from Kharashah ibn al-Hurr, from Abu Dharr, who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Three will not be spoken to by Allah on the Day of Resurrection, He will not look at them, nor will He purify them, and for them is a painful punishment: the one who reminds of what he has given, the one who lets his garment hang down (below the ankles), and the one who sells his goods with a false oath." [Sahih Muslim, no. 106.]

Ibn Mardawayh said: Ahmad ibn 'Uthman ibn Yahya narrated to us, 'Uthman ibn Muhammad al-Duri informed us, Hushaym ibn Kharijah informed us, Sulayman ibn 'Uqbah informed us, from Yunus ibn Maysarah, from Abu Idris, from Abu al-Darda', from the Prophet ﷺ who said: "No disobedient child (of parents), no one who reminds of favours, and no habitual drinker of wine, nor one who denies divine decree, will enter Paradise." Ahmad and Ibn Majah narrated similarly from the narration of Yunus ibn Maysarah. [Musnad Ahmad (6/441) and Sunan Ibn Majah, no. 3376. Al-Busiri said in al-Zawa'id (3/103): "This chain is good; Sulayman ibn 'Utbah is disputed, and the rest of the narrators are trustworthy."]

Then Ibn Mardawayh, Ibn Hibban, al-Hakim in his al-Mustadrak, and al-Nasa'i narrated from the narration of 'Abdullah ibn Yasar al-A'raj, from Salim ibn 'Abdullah ibn 'Umar, from his father, who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Three, Allah will not look at them on the Day of Resurrection: the one who is disobedient to his parents, the habitual drinker of wine, and the one who reminds of what he has given." [al-Mustadrak (4/146) and Sunan al-Nasa'i (5/80).]

Al-Nasa'i narrated, from Malik ibn Sa'd, from his paternal uncle Rawh ibn 'Ubadah, from 'Attab ibn Bashir, from Khusayf al-Jazari, from Mujahid, from Ibn 'Abbas, from the Prophet ﷺ who said: "No habitual drinker of wine, no disobedient child, and no one who reminds of favours will enter Paradise." [Sunan al-Nasa'i al-Kubra, no. 4921.]

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated this from al-Hasan ibn al-Minhal, from Muhammad ibn 'Abdullah ibn 'Ammar al-Mawsili, from 'Attab, from Khusayf, from Mujahid, from Ibn 'Abbas.

Al-Nasa'i narrated it from the narration of 'Abd al-Karim ibn Malik al-Jazari, from Mujahid, as his own statement. It has also been reported from Mujahid, from Abu Sa'id [al-Nasa'i al-Kubra, no. 4920], and from Mujahid, from Abu Hurayrah, similarly [al-Nasa'i al-Kubra, no. 4922].

For this reason Allah the Exalted said: ﴿O you who have believed, do not invalidate your charities with reminders and injury﴾. So He informed us that charity is nullified by what follows it of reminder and injury, for the reward of charity cannot withstand the sin of reminder and injury.

Then Almighty Allah said: ﴿like one who spends his wealth to be seen by the people﴾, meaning: do not nullify your charities with reminders and injury, just as the charity of one who does it to show off to people is nullified. He displays to them that he seeks the Face of Allah, while his real aim is the people's praise of him, or his fame for beautiful qualities, so that he is thanked among the people, or so it is said that he is generous, and similar worldly aims, while disregarding dealing with Allah the Exalted and seeking His pleasure and great reward. For this reason He said: ﴿and does not believe in Allah and the Last Day﴾.

Then Almighty Allah struck a parable for that showy person in his spending. [Al-Dahhak said: "And the one who follows his spending with reminder or injury."] He said: ﴿So his example is like that of a smooth rock﴾. Safwan is the plural of safwanah, and some say that safwan is also used in the singular, meaning a flat stone, which is a smooth rock. ﴿Upon it is dust, and then a heavy rain strikes it﴾, which is a violent downpour, ﴿and leaves it bare﴾, meaning the heavy rain leaves that rock bare, that is, smooth and dry, with nothing on it of that dust. Rather, all of it has gone. Likewise, the deeds of those who show off are lost and vanish in the sight of Allah, even if they appear to the people like dust. For this reason He said: ﴿They are unable to obtain anything of what they have earned. And Allah does not guide the disbelieving people.﴾
